parole.significato: An authoritative principle, belief or statement of opinion, especially one considered to be absolutely true and indispu…
parole.testo: From Latin dogma (“philosophical tenet”), from Ancient Greek δόγμα (dógma, “opinion, tenet”), from δοκέω (dokéō, “to seem good, think”). Treated in the 17th and 18th century as Greek, with plural dogmata. Compare decent.

parole.significato: To treat something as dogma.
parole.testo: From Late Latin dogmatizō.

parole.significato: A carnivorous cetacean, typically with a beak-like snout, famed for their intelligence and occasional willingness to ap…
parole.testo: From Middle English delphyn, from Latin delphīnus, from Ancient Greek δελφίς (delphís), from δελφύς (delphús, “womb”); the modern form in -ol- is probably influenced by the pronunciation of Middle French dauphin. Compare Swedish delfin. Doublet of dauphin. Displaced native Old English mereswīn (lite

parole.significato: Evil intent: malice or fraud.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin dolus (“deceit, trickery”); akin to Ancient Greek δόλος (dólos, “bait, ruse”). Compare dolose, dolosity.

parole.significato: A chamber produced by a plant in which insects, mites, or fungi live.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin dōmatium, from Ancient Greek δωμάτιον (dōmátion, “chamber, bedroom”), diminutive of δῶμα (dôma, “house, dwelling place of animals”); akin to δόμος (dómos, “house”).

parole.significato: A canelike grass of southern Europe (Arundo donax), used for fishing rods, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin donax (“reed; also a marine fish”), from Ancient Greek δόναξ (dónax).

parole.significato: Gazella dorcas, a gazelle native to northern Africa and western Asia.
parole.testo: From Latin dorcas from Ancient Greek δορκάς (dorkás) + gazelle.

parole.significato: A spear-bearing soldier (nowadays, a statue of a man holding a spear, or appearing to do so).
parole.testo: From Latin doryphoros, from Ancient Greek [Term?], literally "spear-bearing".

parole.significato: A classical historian who describes the opinions of Ancient Greek philosophers and scientists.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin doxographus, itself coined by German classicist Hermann Diels in 1879 from Ancient Greek δόξα (dóxa, “opinion, belief”) + -γράφος (-gráphos, “writer”), originally in reference specifically to the tradition stemming from Theophrastus, + -er. By surface analysis, doxography + -

parole.significato: An expression of praise to God, especially a short hymn sung as part of a Christian worship service.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin doxologia, from Ancient Greek δοξολογία (doxología, “a praising”), from δοξολόγος (doxológos, “giving or uttering praise”), from δόξα (dóxa, “glory, honor, repute”), from δοκέω (dokéō, “to think, expect”).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Dracaena of liliaceous plants with woody stems and funnel-shaped flowers.
parole.testo: From the genus name Dracaena, from Latin dracaena, from Ancient Greek δράκαινᾰ (drákaină, “she-dragon”).

parole.significato: A legendary being with a human head, and sometimes also human arms and a torso, and the rest of the body of a snake.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin dracontopedis, draconcopedis, from Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn, “serpent”) + πούς (poús, “foot, leg”).

parole.significato: Very severe, cruel, or harsh.
parole.testo: From Latin Dracō (stem Dracōn-) + -ian, from Ancient Greek Δράκων (Drákōn), after the Athenian lawmaker Draco, known for making harsh laws. See δράκων (drákōn, “dragon”).

parole.significato: The roots and rhizomes of skunk cabbage, Symplocarpus foetidus
parole.testo: From the genus in which Symplocarpus foetidus was formerly classified, Dracontium, from Latin dracontium (“dragon-wort”), from Ancient Greek δρακόντιον (drakóntion).

parole.significato: A composition, normally in prose, telling a story and intended to be represented by actors impersonating the characters…
parole.testo: From Late Latin drāma, from Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma, “an act, a theatrical act, a play”), from δράω (dráō, “to act, to take action, to achieve”). Doublet of dorama.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the drama.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin drāmaticus. By surface analysis, drama + -tic.

parole.significato: A kind of fruit, with a fleshy exterior, formed from the exocarp and mesocarp, surrounding a hardened endocarp which pr…
parole.testo: Scientific Latin, from Latin drūpa (“wrinkled olive”), from Ancient Greek δρύππᾱ (drúppā).

parole.significato: The veneration of saints, distinguished from latria, the worship of God.
parole.testo: From Latin dulia, from Ancient Greek δουλεία (douleía, “slavery”), from δοῦλος (doûlos, “slave”).

parole.significato: A period of twelve years.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin duodecas (“twelve”), from Ancient Greek δυωδεκάς (duōdekás, “twelve”). Equivalent to duodec- + -ade.

parole.significato: A series comprising two parts, particularly in genre fiction.
parole.testo: Coined based on Latin duo (“two”) + Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos, “word”).

parole.significato: A ruler or governor, especially a hereditary ruler or someone who founded or is part of a dynasty.
parole.testo: From Late Latin dynastēs, from Ancient Greek δυνάστης (dunástēs, “lord, ruler”), from δύναμαι (dúnamai, “to be powerful”).

parole.significato: difficult
parole.testo: From New Latin dys-, from Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-, “hard, difficult, bad”). Often confused with the separately derived prefix dis-.

parole.significato: Of or relating to, or causing degeneration or deterioration in offspring.
parole.testo: From dys- + -genic, produced from New Latin dys- from Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) and γένος (génos, “offspring”).

parole.significato: Difficult or laboured breathing.
parole.testo: Variant spelling of dyspnoea, a learned borrowing from Latin dyspnoea (“difficulty breathing”), from Ancient Greek δῠ́σπνοιᾰ (dŭ́spnoiă, “difficulty breathing, shortness of breath”), from δῠ́σπνοος (dŭ́spnoos, “short of breath, breathing with difficulty”, adjective) (also δῠ́σπνους (dŭ́spnous) by co

parole.significato: A hard, dense, deep black wood from various subtropical and tropical trees, especially of the genus Diospyros.
parole.testo: From earlier heben, hebeny, from Middle English ebenif, hebenyf (influenced by Late Latin hebeninus), from Ecclesiastical Latin ebenius (“of ebony”), from Latin hebenus (“ebon tree”), from Ancient Greek ἔβενος (ébenos), from Egyptian hbnj, U13:n-Z4:M3

parole.significato: A picture representing Jesus Christ wearing a crown of thorns, before his crucifixion.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ecce homō̆ (“behold the man!”). See John 19:5 in the Bible.

parole.significato: A skin discoloration caused by bleeding underneath the skin, especially one that is remote from a site of trauma or cau…
parole.testo: From New Latin ecchymōsis, from Ancient Greek ἐκχύμωσις (ekkhúmōsis), from ἐκχέω (ekkhéō, “I pour out”), from ἐκ- (ek-, “out”) + χέω (khéō, “I pour”).

parole.significato: The public legislative assembly of the Athenians.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ecclēsia, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía). Doublet of Eccles.

parole.significato: An official of the Eastern Church, equivalent to a sacristan in the Western Church.
parole.testo: Latin ecclesiarcha, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A member of the Athenian ecclesia (public legislative assembly).
parole.testo: From Middle English ecclesiaste, from Latin ecclēsiastēs, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησιαστής (ekklēsiastḗs). By surface analysis, ecclesia + -ast.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the church; ecclesiastical.
parole.testo: From Middle English ecclesyastyke, from Late Latin ecclēsiasticus (“of the church”), from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησιαστικός (ekklēsiastikós). By surface analysis, ecclesiast + -ic. Doublet of Ecclesiasticus.

parole.significato: church
parole.testo: From Latin ecclēsia, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía), + -o-.

parole.significato: A sea urchin.
parole.testo: From Latin echīnus (“hedgehog; sea urchin”), from Ancient Greek ἐχῖνος (ekhînos).

parole.significato: Of a sound or sound waves: to reflect off a surface and return; to reverberate or resound.
parole.testo: From Middle English eccho, ecco, echo, ekko, from Medieval Latin ēccō, from Latin ēchō, from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ), from ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound”). Possibly from the same Proto-Indo-European root as sough.

parole.significato: Relating to an eclipse or the ecliptic.
parole.testo: From Middle English ecliptik, from Latin eclīpticus, from Ancient Greek ἐκλειπτικός (ekleiptikós).

parole.significato: A pastoral poem, often in the form of a shepherd's monologue or a dialogue between shepherds.
parole.testo: From Middle English eclog, from Latin ecloga, from Ancient Greek ἐκλογή (eklogḗ, “selection”).

parole.significato: A woman perceived to have a highly sensitive emotional state, or prone to quasi-mystical trances.
parole.testo: From New Latin ecstatica, from Ancient Greek ἐκστατικός (ekstatikós).

parole.significato: The condition where an organ or other body part has an abnormal position.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin ectopia, derived from Ancient Greek ἔκτοπος (éktopos, “away from a place”), from ἐκ- (ek-) + τόπος (tópos). By surface analysis, ec- + -topia.

parole.significato: Ecumenical.
parole.testo: From Latin oecūmenicus, from Ancient Greek οἰκουμενικός (oikoumenikós, “concerning ἡ οἰκουμένη (hē oikouménē, “the inhabited (earth)”)”, “the whole (known) world”). Cognate with French œcuménique. By surface analysis, ecumene + -ic.

parole.significato: A non-contagious acute or chronic inflammation of the skin, characterized by redness, itching, and the outbreak of oozi…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin eczema, from Ancient Greek ἔκζεμᾰ (ékzemă, “cutaneous eruption”), from ἐκζέω (ekzéō, “to boil out, break out”) + -μᾰ (-mă, nominal suffix).

parole.significato: An excessive accumulation of serum in tissue spaces or a body cavity.
parole.testo: From New Latin oedēma, from Ancient Greek οἴδημα (oídēma, “swelling”), from οἰδέω (oidéō, “I swell”).

parole.significato: Of or from Edessa.
parole.testo: From Latin Edessēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἐδεσσηνός (Edessēnós). By surface analysis, Edessa + -ene.

parole.significato: A Thracian people who dwelt mostly between the Nestus and the Strymon rivers in southern Thrace, but also once dwelt we…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Ēdōnī, from Ancient Greek Ἠδωνοί (Ēdōnoí). Doublet of hedon.

parole.significato: of or relating to Ancient Egypt, Egyptian
parole.testo: From the Late Latin aegyptiacus (“Egyptian”), from the Ancient Greek Αἰγῠπτῐᾰκός (Aigŭptĭăkós, “of or for the Egyptians”), from Αἰγῠ́πτῐος (Aigŭ́ptĭos, “Egyptian”) + -ᾰκός (-ăkós). Equivalent to Latin Aegyptius (“Egyptian”) + -acus.

parole.significato: elastic
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἐλᾰστός (elăstós, “ductile”).

parole.significato: Elasticity; especially the expansibility of a gas.
parole.testo: From New Latin elatēr, from Ancient Greek ἐλατήρ (elatḗr, “driver, that which drives away”).

parole.significato: The mineral wurtzilite.
parole.testo: From New Latin elatēr, from Ancient Greek ἐλατήρ (elatḗr, “driver, that which drives away”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a certain school in Elea of Ancient Greek philosophers who taught that reality is stable and unchangi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Eleāticus, from Ancient Greek ’Ελεατικός (’Eleatikós), from Ἐλέα (Eléa, “Elea, Velia”).

parole.significato: Amber.
parole.testo: From Latin ēlectrum, from Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron).

parole.significato: Any preparation of a medicine mixed with honey or other sweetener in order to make it more palatable to swallow.
parole.testo: From Middle English electuarie, eletuarie, electuary, from Latin electuarium, from Ancient Greek ἐκλείκτον (ekleíkton, “medicine which is licked away”), from ἐκλείχω (ekleíkhō, “to lick up”), from ἐκ (ek, “out, from”) + λείχω (leíkhō, “to lick”). Doublet of lekvar.

parole.significato: Relating to charity, alms, or almsgiving.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin eleēmosynārius (“alms dispenser”), from Late Latin eleēmosyna (“alms”), from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē, “alms”), from ἐλεήμων (eleḗmōn, “merciful”) + -σῠ́νη (-sŭ́nē, “suffix denoting an abstract noun”). Compare Italian elemosina.

parole.significato: That part of an argument on which its conclusiveness depends; that which convinces or refutes an antagonist; a refutati…
parole.testo: Latin elenchus, from Ancient Greek ἔλεγχος (élenkhos, “refutation, scrutiny”); compare Old French elenche. Doublet of elenchus.

parole.significato: A technique of argument associated with Socrates wherein the arguer asks the interlocutor to agree with a series of pre…
parole.testo: From Latin elenchus, from Ancient Greek ἔλεγχος (élenkhos, “refutation, scrutiny, control”). Doublet of elench.

parole.significato: A complication of chronic filariasis, in which nematode worms block the lymphatic vessels, usually in the legs or scrot…
parole.testo: From Latin elephantiasis or directly from Ancient Greek ἐλεφᾰντῐ́ᾱσῐς (elephăntĭ́āsĭs).

parole.significato: A member of a minor biblical tribe mentioned in Nahum 1:1.
parole.testo: First attested in 1568 in the Bishops' Bible translation (see quotations); earlier English Bible translations instead used “of Elkosh”. From Middle English Helcesei, borrowed from Vulgar Latin Helcesei, from Ancient Greek Έλκεσαίου (Élkesaíou), from Hebrew אֶלְקֹשִׁי. Analysable as Elkosh (“the unid

parole.significato: A mark consisting of multiple full stops (with or without spaces), used to indicate omitted, missing, or illegible word…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ellīpsis, from Ancient Greek ἔλλειψις (élleipsis, “omission”). Doublet of ellipse.

parole.significato: a eulogy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ēlogium (“short saying, inscription”), from Ancient Greek ἐλεγεῖον (elegeîon, “elegy”), from ἔλεγος (élegos, “song, melody”). Doublet of elogy.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Elysian or Elysium, the location.
parole.testo: From Latin Elysium (from Ancient Greek Ἠλύσιον (Ēlúsion, “Elysium; one of the Elysian Fields”)) + -an (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A mineral consisting of silver chloride and silver bromide; a variety of bromian chlorargyrite.
parole.testo: From Latin embolus (“piston”), from Ancient Greek ἔμβολος (émbolos, “peg, wedge, stopper”).

parole.significato: A narrow piece separating the costa and corium in certain insects of the suborder Heteroptera.
parole.testo: From New Latin embolium, from Ancient Greek ἐμβόλιον (embólion, “insertion”).

parole.significato: An obstruction causing an embolism: a blood clot, air bubble or other matter carried by the bloodstream and causing a b…
parole.testo: The term was coined in 1848 by Rudolf Virchow From Latin embolus (“piston”), from Ancient Greek ἔμβολος (émbolos, “peg, stopper”).

parole.significato: To rub (a diseased part) with a moistened or liquid substance, usually an oil, on a cloth or sponge.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin embrocatus, past participle of Late Latin embrocare, from embrocha, from Ancient Greek ἐμβροχή (embrokhḗ, “lotion, fomentation”).

parole.significato: In the reproductive cycle, the stage after the fertilization of the egg that precedes the development into a fetus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin embryō, from Ancient Greek ἔμβρυον (émbruon, “fetus”), from ἐν (en, “in-”) + βρύω (brúō, “to grow, swell”).

parole.significato: Embryonic.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin embryon, from Ancient Greek ἔμβρυον (émbruon, “newborn animal, embryo”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Emesa or its region.
parole.testo: From Latin Emesēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἐμεσηνός (Emesēnós).

parole.significato: Special weight or forcefulness given to something considered important.
parole.testo: From Latin emphasis, from Ancient Greek ἔμφασις (émphasis, “significance”), from ἐμφαίνω (emphaínō, “to present; to indicate”), from ἐν- (en-, “in”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to show”).

parole.significato: To stress, give emphasis or extra weight to (something).
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek – see emphasis. By surface analysis, emphasis + -ize.

parole.significato: Having the quality of closing the pores of the skin.
parole.testo: From Latin emphracticus, from Ancient Greek ἐμφρακτικός (emphraktikós), from ἐμφράσσω (emphrássō), from ἐν- (en-) + φράσσω (phrássō).

parole.significato: A right to enjoyment of property with a given stipulation that the property will be improved or maintained in an agreed…
parole.testo: From Latin emphyteusis, from Ancient Greek ἐμφύτευσις (emphúteusis, “tenure of a type of leasehold”).

parole.significato: Empirical.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin empiricus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπειρῐκός (empeirĭkós, “experienced”), from ἐμπειρία (empeiría, “experience, mere experience or practice without knowledge, especially in medicine, empiricism”), from ἔμπειρος (émpeiros, “experienced or practised in”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + πεῖρα (pe

parole.significato: A city or region which is a major trading centre; also, a place within a city for commerce and trading; a marketplace.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin emporium (“trading station; business district in a city; market town”), from Ancient Greek ἐμπόριον (empórion, “factory, trading station; market”), from ἔμπορος (émporos, “merchant, trader; traveller”) + -ιον (-ion, suffix forming nouns). ἔμπορος is derived from ἐμ- (em-) (varian

parole.significato: A phantom; ghost; spectre.
parole.testo: Latin empusa, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the highest heaven or the empyrean.
parole.testo: From Latin empyreus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπύριος (empúrios, “fiery”), from ἐν (en, “en-”) + πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) (English pyre).

parole.significato: The highest heaven, supposed by the ancients to be a region of pure light and fire or else composed of ether, and somet…
parole.testo: From Latin empȳreus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπύριος (empúrios), from ἐν (en, “in”) + πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) (whence English pyre).

parole.significato: Containing the combustible principle of coal.
parole.testo: From Latin empyricus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπύριος (empúrios, “fiery”), from ἐν (en, “en-”) + πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).

parole.significato: Ambitious or competitive.
parole.testo: From Middle English emulous, from Latin aemulus (“striving to equal or excel, rivaling; in a bad sense, envious, jealous”) + -ous, from Ancient Greek ἁμιλλάομαι (hamilláomai, “strive, contend”), akin to Latin imitari (“to imitate”); see imitate.

parole.significato: Vivid, lively description.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin enargīa, from Ancient Greek ἐνάργεια (enárgeia, “sensory vividness”).

parole.significato: The eight days of celebration for the dedication of the church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.
parole.testo: From Latin encaenia, from Ancient Greek ἐγκαίνια (enkaínia, “a festival of renewal or dedication”).

parole.significato: A festival held to mark the anniversary of the dedication of a church or temple; (especially), of the Temple at Jerusal…
parole.testo: From Latin encaenia, from Ancient Greek (τὰ) ἐγκαίνια ((tà) enkaínia, “dedication festival”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + καινός (kainós, “new”).

parole.significato: An ornament on a frieze or capital, consisting of festoons of fruit, flowers, leaves, etc.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἔγκαρπος (énkarpos, “containing fruit”) (ἐν- (en-) + καρπός (karpós)).

parole.significato: A clitic that joins with the preceding word phonetically, graphically, or both.
parole.testo: From Late Latin encliticus, from Ancient Greek ἐγκλιτικός (enklitikós, “inclined towards”), from ἐγκλίνειν (enklínein, “lean on”), from ἐν (en, “upon”) + κλίνειν (klínein, “to lean, incline”).

parole.significato: Warm praise, especially a formal expression of such praise; a tribute.
parole.testo: From Latin encōmium (“praise, eulogy”), from Ancient Greek ἐγκώμιον (enkṓmion, “laudatory ode, praise”), from ἐγκώμιος (enkṓmios, “of or pertaining to the victor”), from κῶμος (kômos, “festival, revel, ode”).

parole.significato: One of an ascetic 2nd-century sect of Christians who forbade marriage and counselled abstinence from meat.
parole.testo: Latin Encratitae (plural) from Ancient Greek ἐγκρατής (enkratḗs, “self-disciplined”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + κρᾰ́τος (krắtos, “strength”).

parole.significato: Commonwealth standard spelling of encyclopedia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin encyclopaedia; the English word is an etymologically restored spelling variant of earlier encyclopedia, q.v.

parole.significato: A comprehensive reference work (often spanning several printed volumes) with articles (usually arranged in alphabetical…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin encyclopēdīa, encyclopaedīa (“general education”), a univerbated form of Koine Greek ἐγκύκλιος παιδείᾱ (enkúklios paideíā, “education in the circle of arts and sciences”), from Ancient Greek ἐγκύκλιος (enkúklios, “circular”) + παιδείᾱ (paideíā, “childrearing; education”) (q.v

parole.significato: The mucous membrane that lines the uterus in mammals and in which fertilized eggs are implanted.
parole.testo: From endo- (“inner”) + Late Latin metrium (“womb”), from Ancient Greek μήτριον (mḗtrion, “of a mother”). Compare μήτρᾱ (mḗtrā, “womb”).

parole.significato: An injection of fluid into the large intestine by way of the rectum, usually for medical purposes.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin enema, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἔνεμα (énema, “injection”), from ἐνίημι (eníēmi, “to send in, inject”).

parole.significato: Possessing or pertaining to energy.
parole.testo: From New Latin energeticus (16th c.), or its source, Ancient Greek ἐνεργητικός (energētikós), from ἐνεργέω (energéō, “to be active”), from ἐνεργός (energós, “active”). By surface analysis, energy + -etic.

parole.significato: A person possessed by an evil ghost, spirit, or entity.
parole.testo: From Latin energumenus, from Ancient Greek ἐνεργούμενος (energoúmenos), from verb ἐνεργέω (energéō, “to influence”).

parole.significato: The state of the human nature of Jesus Christ being entirely dependent on, and not existing independently of, the divin…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin enhypostasia, from Ancient Greek ἐν (en, “in”) + ὑπόστασις (hupóstasis, “existence; essence; substance”) + -ία (-ía, suffix forming nouns). ὑπόστασις is in turn derived from ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-, “below, under”) + στάσις (stásis, “standing”). Compare Ancient Greek ἐνυπόστα

parole.significato: The commander of an enomoty.
parole.testo: From Latin enōmotarcha, from Ancient Greek ἐνωμοτάρχης (enōmotárkhēs).

parole.significato: A slight convex curvature introduced into the shaft of a column for aesthetic reasons, or to compensate for the illusio…
parole.testo: From Latin entasis, from Ancient Greek ἔντασις (éntasis, “tension, straining”), from ἐντείνω (enteínō, “to stretch or strain tight”).

parole.significato: The complete realisation and final form of some potential concept or function; the conditions under which a potential t…
parole.testo: From Late Latin entelechia, from Ancient Greek ἐντελέχεια (entelékheia), coined by Aristotle from ἐντελής (entelḗs, “complete, finished, perfect”) (from τέλος (télos, “end, fruition, accomplishment”)) + ἔχω (ékhō, “to have”).

parole.significato: relating to the intestines.
parole.testo: From New Latin entero-, combining form from Ancient Greek ἔντερον (énteron, “intestine”).

parole.significato: The gut, the whole intestine (alimentary) canal
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἔντερον (énteron, “intestine”).

parole.significato: Divinely inspired.
parole.testo: From Latin entheātus (“divinely inspired”), from Ancient Greek ἔνθεος (éntheos, “inspired, possessed by (a) god”) + -ātus.

parole.significato: Involuntary urination: urinary incontinence.
parole.testo: From Latin enuresis, from Ancient Greek ἐνούρησις (enoúrēsis); surface analysis parses uresis as a constituent.

parole.significato: An extinct early Eocene mammal (Hyracotherium leporinum), ancestral to the modern horse.
parole.testo: Originally a genus name, Eohippus, formed in New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”) + ἵππος (híppos, “horse”). By surface analysis, eo- + Latin hippus.

parole.significato: Any effect of wind on land.
parole.testo: Likely from Eolus (“god of wind”), Aeolian (“relating to Eolus”), or aeolo- (“of woodwind instruments”), all via Latin Aeolus from Ancient Greek Αἴολος (Aíolos), plus -ation, a suffix denoting a process or the result of a process.

parole.significato: Of the wind; referring to the action or the power of wind.
parole.testo: From Latin Aeolicus, from Ancient Greek Αἴολος (Aíolos, “Aeolus, god of the winds”).

parole.significato: Eternity, the duration of the universe.
parole.testo: From Latin aeon, from Ancient Greek αἰών (aiṓn, “age, era”).

parole.significato: The adducing of particular examples so as to lead to a universal conclusion; the argument by induction.
parole.testo: From Latin epagōgē, from Ancient Greek ἐπᾰγωγή (epăgōgḗ, “a bringing in”). See epact.

parole.significato: A figure of speech by which the same word is used both at the beginning and at the end of a sentence.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin epanadiplōsis, from Ancient Greek ἐπαναδίπλωσις (epanadíplōsis, “doubling, folding”).

parole.significato: The repetition of the same word or clause after intervening matter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin epanalepsis, from Ancient Greek ἐπανάληψις (epanálēpsis), from ἐπαναλαμβάνω (epanalambánō), from ἐπί (epí) + ἀνά (aná) + λαμβάνω (lambánō).

parole.significato: anaphora
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek ἐπαναφορά (epanaphorá, “reference”).

parole.significato: The insertion of a phoneme, letter, or syllable into a word, usually to satisfy the phonological constraints of a langu…
parole.testo: Middle of 16th century: via Late Latin, from Ancient Greek ἐπένθεσις (epénthesis), from ἐπεντίθημι (epentíthēmi, “to insert”), from ἐπί (epí) + ἐντίθημι (entíthēmi, “to put in”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to put, place”).

parole.significato: An 18- to 20-year-old man in ancient Greece undergoing military training.
parole.testo: Via Latin ephēbus, from Ancient Greek ἔφηβος (éphēbos, “adolescent”), from ἐπί (epí, “early”) + ἥβη (hḗbē, “manhood”), late 19th c.

parole.significato: Synonym of freckle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ephēlis, from Ancient Greek ἔφηλῐς (éphēlĭs, “a freckle”), from ἐπ- (ep-, “upon, over, epi-”) + ἥλῐος (hḗlĭos, “the sun”) + -ῐς (-ĭs, nominal suffix).

parole.significato: Lasting for a short period of time.
parole.testo: From New Latin ephemerus, from Ancient Greek ἐφήμερος (ephḗmeros), the more common form of ἐφημέριος (ephēmérios, “of, for, or during the day, living or lasting but for a day, short-lived, temporary”), from ἐπί (epí, “on”) + ἡμέρα (hēméra, “day”).

parole.significato: A journal or diary.
parole.testo: From New Latin ephēmeris, from Ancient Greek ἐφημερίς (ephēmerís, “diary, calendar”), from ἐφήμερος (ephḗmeros, “daily”).

parole.significato: A depression in the sphenoid bone; the pituitary fossa.
parole.testo: From Latin ephippium (“saddlecloth”), from Ancient Greek ἐφίππιον (ephíppion), from ἐπῐ́ (epĭ́) + ἵππος (híppos, “horse”).

parole.significato: An allegiant of the Israelite tribal patriarch Ephraim, a member of the tribe purportedly descended from him, or an inh…
parole.testo: An adaptation of the Latin Ephraimītēs, Ephraimīta, from the Ancient Greek Ἐφραιμῑ́tης (Ephraimī́tēs), from Ἐφραίμ (Ephraím, “Ephraim”) + -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs, “one connected to, a member of”). Equivalent to Ephraim + -ite.

parole.significato: The layer of tissue between the pericardium and the heart.
parole.testo: New Latin, from Latin epi- (“over”) + Ancient Greek καρδία (kardía, “heart”). Attested in English from the 19th century.

parole.significato: An elegy; an ode to someone deceased.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin epicēdīon, from Ancient Greek ἐπικήδειον (epikḗdeion), neuter singular form of ἐπικήδειος (epikḗdeios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + κῆδος (kêdos, “care”). Doublet of epicedium.

parole.significato: A syllogism in which the proof of the major or minor premise, or both, is introduced with the premises themselves, and…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπιχείρημα (epikheírēma).

parole.significato: The pattern of cell wall thickening which forms the ornamentation on spores of certain types of mushroom (especially of…
parole.testo: From Latin cŏrĭum ("skin") with the Ancient Greek prefix ἐπί- ("on top of").

parole.significato: A small circle whose centre is on the circumference of a larger circle; in Ptolemaic astronomy it was seen as the basis…
parole.testo: From Latin epicyclus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίκυκλος (epíkuklos), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”). The ad hoc complication sense is a generalization from the archetype supplied by the Ptolemaic astronomy sense.

parole.significato: The outer, protective layer of the skin of vertebrates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin epidermis, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδερμίς (epidermís), ἐπί (epí, “on top of”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”). Equivalent to epi- + dermis.

parole.significato: A cartilaginous organ in the throat of terrestrial vertebrates covering the glottis when swallowing to prevent food and…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin epiglōttis, from Ancient Greek ἐπῐγλωττῐ́ς (epĭglōttĭ́s, “valve covering the larynx”), from ἐπῐ- (epĭ-, “upon, over”) + γλωττῐ́ς (glōttĭ́s, “glottis, mouth of the windpipe”); equivalent to epi- (“upon; above”) + glottis.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an epigraph or to epigraphy.
parole.testo: From New Latin epigraphicus, from Ancient Greek ἐπῐγρᾰφῐκός (epĭgrăphĭkós). By surface analysis, epigraph + -ic.

parole.significato: The connective tissue framework and sheath of a nerve which bind together the nerve bundles, each of which has its own…
parole.testo: From New Latin epineurium, from Ancient Greek ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) + νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”).

parole.significato: An activity, process, or state that is the result of another; a by-product, a consequence.
parole.testo: From epi- (prefix meaning ‘above, on, over; in addition to’) + phenomenon. Phenomenon is derived from Late Latin phaenomenon (“appearance”), from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, “thing that appears in one’s view; appearance; phenomenon”), a noun use of the neuter singular form of φαινόμενος (

parole.significato: An exclamation or reflection used to summarise or round off an argument or discourse.
parole.testo: From Latin epiphonema, from Ancient Greek ἐπιφώνημα (epiphṓnēma), from ἐπιφωνείν (epiphōneín, “call to”).

parole.significato: A rhetorical device where a sequence of rhetorical questions is used to criticise or blame, or more generally, to elici…
parole.testo: From Latin epiplexis (“rebuke”), from Ancient Greek ἐπίπληξις (epíplēxis, “rebuke”), from ἐπιπλήσσω (epiplḗssō, “to chastise”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) (see epi-) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “to strike”).

parole.significato: A figure of speech by which one striking circumstance is added, in due gradation, to another; escalation to a climax.
parole.testo: From Latin epiplocē (“(rhetoric) connection”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιπλοκή (epiplokḗ, “plaiting together”), from ἐπιπλέκω (epiplékō, “to interweave”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) (see epi-) + πλέκω (plékō, “to plait”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the affairs of a bishop in various Christian churches.
parole.testo: From Middle English episcopal, from Late Latin episcopālis, from Latin episcopus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “watchman, overseer”).

parole.significato: Bishops seen as a group.
parole.testo: From Late Latin episcopatus, from Latin episcopus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “watching over”).

parole.significato: A literary composition in the form of a letter or series of letters, especially one in verse.
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₁epi The noun is derived from Middle English epistel, epistole, pistel (“letter; literary work in letter form; written legend or story; spoken communication; (Christianity) one of the letters by an apostle in the New Testament; extract from such a letter read as part of the Mass”) [and o

parole.significato: Of or relating to letters, or the writing of letters.
parole.testo: 1627, from Latin epistolārius, from epistola (“letter”) (English epistle) + -ārius, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ) from ἐπιστέλλω (epistéllō, “to send a message”) from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to prepare, send”). For the noun, compare Middle English pistelarie and Old English pis

parole.significato: Relating to letters or epistles, or in the form or style of them
parole.testo: From Latin epistolicus, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολικός (epistolikós, “suited to or in the style of a letter”).

parole.significato: The study of letters and epistles.
parole.testo: From Latin epistola or its etymon Ancient Greek ἐπῐστολή (epĭstolḗ) + -ology.

parole.significato: The repetition of the same word or words at the end of successive phrases, clauses or sentences.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin epistrophē, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπιστροφή (epistrophḗ).

parole.significato: A massive piece of stone or wood laid immediately on the abacus of the capital of a column or pillar; an architrave.
parole.testo: Latin epistylium, Ancient Greek: compare French épistyle.

parole.significato: A song or poem celebrating a marriage.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin epithalamium, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐπιθαλάμιον (epithalámion, “bridal song”), neuter form of ἐπιθαλάμιος (epithalámios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + θάλαμος (thálamos, “inner chamber, wedding chamber”).

parole.significato: A horny excrescence on the top of the beak of some birds, notably the hornbill.
parole.testo: From New Latin epithema, from Ancient Greek ἐπίθεμα (epíthema, “lid, cover”).

parole.significato: a hurried accumulation or enumeration of several points.
parole.testo: From Late Latin epitrochasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐπιτροχασμός (epitrokhasmós), from ἐπιτροχάζω (epitrokházō, “run swiftly over”).

parole.significato: A figure by which permission is either seriously or ironically granted to someone to do what he or she proposes to do,…
parole.testo: From Latin epitrope, from Ancient Greek ἐπιτροπή (epitropḗ, “reference, arbitration”), from ἐπιτρέπω (epitrépō).

parole.significato: A particular period of history, or of a person's life, especially one considered noteworthy or remarkable.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin epocha, from Ancient Greek ἐποχή (epokhḗ, “a check, cessation, stop, pause, epoch of a star, i.e., the point at which it seems to halt after reaching the highest, and generally the place of a star; hence, a historical epoch”), from ἐπέχω (epékhō, “to hold in, check”), from ἐπι- (

parole.significato: A person who gave or supposedly gave their name to a people, place, institution, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin eponymus, from Ancient Greek ἐπώνῠμος (epṓnŭmos), from ἐπί (epí, “upon, epi-”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”) + -ος (-os, suffix forming adjectives and nouns). Equivalent to epi- + -nym.

parole.significato: An epic.
parole.testo: From Latin epos, from Ancient Greek ἔπος (épos, “word, song, epic”).

parole.significato: A gradual decay through slow combustion or oxidation, like that of old trees or dead animals.
parole.testo: From New Latin ēremacausis, from Ancient Greek ἠρέμα (ēréma, “quietly”) + καῦσις (kaûsis, “burning”).

parole.significato: A hermit; a religious recluse, someone who lives alone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin eremita, from Ancient Greek ἐρημίτης (erēmítēs), from ἐρῆμος (erêmos, “uninhabited”) + -ίτης (-ítēs). Doublet of hermit.

parole.significato: A figure of speech whereby a question is asked in confident expectation of a negative answer.
parole.testo: From Late Latin erotesis, from Ancient Greek ἐρώτησις (erṓtēsis), from ἐρωτάω (erōtáō, “I question”).

parole.significato: Erotic literature, art, decoration, or other such work.
parole.testo: From neuter plural of Latin eroticus (“amatory”), from Ancient Greek ἐρωτικός (erōtikós). By surface analysis, erotic + -ica.

parole.significato: Causing an increase in mucus within the nose, and hence causing one to sneeze.
parole.testo: From Latin errhīnum, from Ancient Greek ἔρρινον (érrhinon), from ἐν (en, “in”) + ῥίς (rhís, “nostril”).

parole.significato: The root of sea holly, Eryngium maritimum, formerly candied and taken as confectionery and held to have aphrodisiac pro…
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin ēryngion, from Ancient Greek ἠρύγγιον (ērúngion), from ἤρυγγος (ḗrungos).

parole.significato: An acute, sometimes recurrent febrile disease caused by infection of a hemolytic streptococcus, associated with intense…
parole.testo: From Middle English erisipila, borrowed from Latin erysipelas, from Ancient Greek ἐρῠσῐ́πελᾰς (erŭsĭ́pelăs), probably related to ἐρῠθρός (erŭthrós, “red”) and πέλμᾰ (pélmă, “the sole of a foot”).

parole.significato: Abnormal redness and inflammation of the skin, due to vasodilation.
parole.testo: From New Latin erythēma, from Ancient Greek ἐρύθημα (erúthēma, “a redness or flush on the skin”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”)..

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Erythrae
parole.testo: From Latin Erythraeus (from Ancient Greek Ἐρυθραῖος (Eruthraîos)) + -an.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Erythraean Sea
parole.testo: From Latin erythraeus (“reddish”) (as it was used in Erythraeum mare (“the Erythraean Sea”), from Ancient Greek ἐρυθρός (eruthrós, “red”)) + -an.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a dry north wind which blows in the eastern Mediterranean.
parole.testo: From Latin etesius (“annual”), from Ancient Greek ἐτήσιος (etḗsios, “annual”), from ἔτος (étos, “year”).

parole.significato: The substance formerly supposed to fill the upper regions of the atmosphere above the clouds, in particular as a medium…
parole.testo: From Middle English ēther (“the caelum aetherum of ancient cosmology in which the planets orbit; a shining, fluid substance described as a form of air or fire; air”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman ether and Middle French ether, ethere, aether, from Old French aether (“highest and purest part of the atm

parole.significato: Pertaining to the presupposition of an invisible air-like element permeating all of space, or to the higher regions bey…
parole.testo: From Latin aetherius (“of or pertaining to the ether, the sky, Heaven or the air or upper air”), from Ancient Greek αἰθέριος (aithérios, “of or pertaining to the upper air”). By surface analysis, ether + -ial.

parole.significato: Formed of ether; ethereal.
parole.testo: Latin aethereus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Moral, relating to morals.
parole.testo: From Middle English etik, from Late Latin ēthicus, from Ancient Greek ἠθῐκός (ēthĭkós).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the study of ethics.
parole.testo: From ethic + -al, from Late Latin ethicus (“moral, ethical”), from Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Ethiopia.
parole.testo: From Latin Aethiops from Ancient Greek Αἰθίοψ (Aithíops, “charred complexion”).

parole.significato: Ethiopian
parole.testo: From Latin aethiopicus, from Ancient Greek Αἰθιοπικός (Aithiopikós). By surface analysis, Ethiop + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a group of people having common racial, ancestral, national, religious or cultural origins.
parole.testo: From Middle English ethnik, from Latin ethnicus ("pagan", "heathen"), from Ancient Greek ἐθνικός (ethnikós, “of or for a nation, heathen”), from ἔθνος (éthnos, “a company", later "a people or nation, heathens”). By surface analysis, ethno- + -ic.

parole.significato: The scientific study of animalian behavior, especially that of nonhuman animals.
parole.testo: From the Latin ēthologia (“the art of depicting or imitating character”), from the Ancient Greek ἠθολογία (ēthología, “painting of character, especially by mimic gestures”), from ἠθολόγος (ēthológos, “painting character by mimic gestures”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, especially moral character”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to Etna, a volcano in Sicily.
parole.testo: From Latin Aetnaeus, from Ancient Greek Αἰτναῖος (Aitnaîos), from Αἴτνη (Aítnē) + -αῖος (-aîos), equivalent to Etna + -ean.

parole.significato: Synonym of Euboean.
parole.testo: From Latin Euboicus, from Ancient Greek Εὐβοϊκός (Euboïkós). By surface analysis, Euboea + -ic.

parole.significato: A member of the eudicots.
parole.testo: Probably a back-formation from eudicots, short for eudicotyledons, from the New Latin coinage eudicotylēdōn, from the Ancient Greek components εὐ- (eu-, “good, well”) + δι- (di-, “two”) + κοτυληδών (kotulēdṓn, “cup-shaped cavity”); equivalent to eu- (“true”) + dicot.

parole.significato: applause
parole.testo: From Latin euge, from Ancient Greek εὖγε (eûge).

parole.significato: The belief that legends and mythology arise from exaggerated descriptions of historical people and events.
parole.testo: From Euhemerus + -ism, ultimately from Latin Euhēmerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros), an ancient Greek Sicilian Skeptic who proposed most or all mythology derived from historical figures and natural events which received supernatural characteristics only through retelling.

parole.significato: Someone who practices or upholds euhemerism, a person who believes all or most myths and legends arose from historical…
parole.testo: From euhemerism + -ist, from Latin Euhemerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros), an ancient Greek Sicilian Skeptic who proposed most or all mythology derived from historical figures and natural events which received supernatural characteristics only through retelling.

parole.significato: Of or relating to euhemerism.
parole.testo: From euhemerist + -ic, from euhemerism, from Latin Euhemerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros), an ancient Greek Sicilian Skeptic who proposed most or all mythology derived from historical figures and natural events which received supernatural characteristics only through retelling.

parole.significato: The fanciful invention of plausible historical figures and events as an attempt to rationalize mythology and legends
parole.testo: From euhemerize + -ation, ultimately from Latin Euhēmerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros), an ancient Greek Sicilian Skeptic who proposed most or all mythology derived from historical figures and natural events which received supernatural characteristics only through retelling.

parole.significato: To invent a plausible but fanciful historical origin for something in order to rationalize mythology and legends.
parole.testo: From euhemerism + -ize, ultimately from Latin Euhēmerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros), an ancient Greek Sicilian Skeptic who proposed most or all mythology derived from historical figures and natural events which received supernatural characteristics only through retelling.

parole.significato: The practice of sending the consecrated Eucharist to those not present, or the Eucharist itself so sent.
parole.testo: From Latin eulogia, from Ancient Greek εὐλογῐ́ᾱ (eulogĭ́ā).

parole.significato: An oration to honor a deceased person, usually at a funeral.
parole.testo: From Latin eulogium, apparently from a confusion between ēlogium (whence English elogium, elogy) and eulogia (from Ancient Greek εὐλογία (eulogía, “praise”), whence English eulogia); equivalent to eu- + logia ("good words"). Doublet of eulogium.

parole.significato: A castrated man.
parole.testo: From Middle English eunuk, from Middle French eunuque, from Latin eunūchus, from Ancient Greek εὐνοῦχος (eunoûkhos), from εὐνή (eunḗ, “bed”) + ἔχω (ékhō, “to have, keep”). Originally probably used to refer to a bed chamber attendant.

parole.significato: An acrid dull yellow or brown resin consisting of the concreted milky juice of several species of Euphorbia, formerly u…
parole.testo: From Latin euphorbium, from Ancient Greek εὐφόρβιον (euphórbion), from Εὔφορβος (Eúphorbos, “Euphorbus, physician to the Mauretanian king Juba II”) + -ιον (-ion, “related to”). The name is from εὔφορβος (eúphorbos, “well-fed”), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + φορβή (phorbḗ, “food, fodder”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Euripides (an ancient Greek tragedian).
parole.testo: Latin Eurīpidēus (from the Ancient Greek Εὐρῑπῐ́δειος, from Εὐρῑπῐ́δης, whence Euripides) + English -an

parole.significato: A strait; a narrow tract of water, where the tide or a current flows and reflows with violence, like the ancient firth…
parole.testo: From Latin eurīpus, from Ancient Greek εὔριπος (eúripos); from εὖ (eû, “well”) + ῥιπή (rhipḗ, “rushing motion”).

parole.significato: The east wind.
parole.testo: From Middle English Eurus, ewrus, from Latin eurus, from Ancient Greek εὖρος (eûros).

parole.significato: One who is comparable to Eusebius of Caesarea; an ecclesiastic historian.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Eusebius, borrowed from Ancient Greek Εὐσέβιος (Eusébios), from εὐσεβής (eusebḗs) + -ῐος (-ĭos).

parole.significato: An operation involving the removal of a part or parts of the body; excision, ectomy.
parole.testo: From New Latin exaeresis, from Ancient Greek ἐξαίρεσῐς (exaíresĭs, “a taking out, an extraction”).

parole.significato: A widespread rash usually occurring in children.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin exanthema, from Ancient Greek ἐξάνθημα (exánthēma), from ἐξανθέω (exanthéō), from ἐξ (ex) + ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).

parole.significato: A rash on the skin.
parole.testo: From New Latin exanthesis, from Ancient Greek ἐξάνθεσις (exánthesis). See exanthema.

parole.significato: departure; exodus, especially the exodus of the Israelites from Egypt
parole.testo: From Latin exodium, from Ancient Greek ἐξόδιον (exódion).

parole.significato: A sudden departure of a large number of people.
parole.testo: From Latin exodus, from Ancient Greek ἔξοδος (éxodos, “expedition, procession, departure”). Doublet of exodos. From late Old English only as a proper noun, Exodus, the biblical book; use as a common noun is from the early 17th century.

parole.significato: To drive out (an evil spirit) from a person, place or thing, especially by an incantation or prayer.
parole.testo: From Middle English exorcisen, exorzisen, from Medieval Latin exorcizō, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζω (exorkízō, “to banish an evil spirit; bind by oath”), from ἐξ (ex) + ὅρκος (hórkos). Compare Old French exorciser.

parole.significato: Of a doctrine, information, etc.: suitable to be imparted to the public without secrecy or other reservations.
parole.testo: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Late Latin exōtericus + English -ic (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’). Exōtericus is borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐξωτερῐκός (exōterĭkós, “exterior, external, outside”, adjective), from ἐξωτέρω (exōtérō, “more exterior”) (the co

parole.significato: The act of bewitching, or enchanting
parole.testo: From Latin fascinare ("to bewitch"), possibly from Ancient Greek βασκαίνιεν (baskaínien, “to speak ill of; to curse”). Morphologically fascinate + -ion.

parole.significato: A transparent form of marble or alabaster, formerly sometimes used for windows.
parole.testo: Like phengite from Latin phengites, from Ancient Greek φέγγος (phéngos). Superficially contains -ite.

parole.significato: A kind of medieval reliquary or shrine containing the sacred effigies and relics of a saint.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin feretrum, from Ancient Greek φέρετρον (phéretron). Doublet of feretory.

parole.significato: Forms of pronouns or verbs used for the speaker or writer of the sentence in which they occur.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin prīma persōna, itself a calque of Ancient Greek πρῶτον πρόσωπον (prôton prósōpon). Displaced native Old English forma had, literally, "form hade".

parole.significato: Resembling the genus Fistularia (cornetfishes); having a long, tubular body.
parole.testo: From Fistulari(a) (“genus of cornetfishes”) + -oid (“resembling”), from Latin fistula (“pipe, tube”) and Ancient Greek εἶδος (eîdos, “form, likeness”). By surface analysis, fistule + -arioid.

parole.significato: An operation to create a surgical connection between a fistula and the intestine.
parole.testo: From fistulo- (“fistula”) + entero- (“intestine”) + -stomy (“mouth, surgical connection”), from Latin fistula (“pipe, tube”), Ancient Greek ἔντερον (énteron, “intestine”), and Ancient Greek στόμα (stóma, “mouth”).

parole.significato: A collection of flowers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Renaissance Latin flōrilegium, calque of Ancient Greek ἀνθολογία (anthología, “flower-gathering”) (compare English anthology), so called because flowers were used as symbols of the finer sensibility of literature.

parole.significato: Synonym of form (“the component of a thing that determines its kind”).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin fōrma. Doublet of form.

parole.significato: A carotenoid pigment found in the chloroplasts of brown algae.
parole.testo: From Latin fūcus (from Ancient Greek φῦκος (phûkos, “seaweed”)) + ξανθός (xanthós, “yellow”) + -in.

parole.significato: Any alga of the genus Fucus.
parole.testo: From New Latin Fūcus, from Ancient Greek φῦκος (phûkos).

parole.significato: An offspring of a fundatrix.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from fundatri- (from fundātrīx) + -genia (irregular from Ancient Greek -γενής (-genḗs, “born”)).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the ancient city of Gadara (near modern-day Umm Qais, in Jordan).
parole.testo: From the Late Latin Gadarēnus, from the Ancient Greek Γαδαρηνός (Gadarēnós, “inhabitant of Gadara”), from Γάδαρα (Gádara, “Gadara”, now “Umm Qais”).

parole.significato: An ancient Berber tribe inhabiting Gaetulia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Gaetūlī, from Ancient Greek Γαίτουλοι (Gaítouloi).

parole.significato: Used to form medical and biochemical terms related to galactose
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek stem γάλακτ- (gálakt-) of γάλα (gála, “milk, milky sap, the Milky Way”).

parole.significato: A bitter, aromatic resin or gum, extracted from plants of the genus Ferula, that resembles assafoetida and has been use…
parole.testo: From Latin galbanum (“galbanum”), from Ancient Greek χαλβάνη (khalbánē, “galbanum”).

parole.significato: A physician.
parole.testo: From Middle English Galen, from Latin Galēnus, from Ancient Greek Γαληνός (Galēnós), from γαλήνη (galḗnē, “calm, tranquillity”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Galilee, or a native or inhabitant thereof.
parole.testo: Originated 1605–15 from Latin Galilaeus [from Ancient Greek Γαλιλαῖος (Galilaîos)] + -an.

parole.significato: A verse consisting of four Ionics a minore, with variations and substitutions.
parole.testo: From Latin Galli + iambus. Used by the Galli, priests of the Phrygian goddess Cybele. The first element, Ancient Greek γάλλος (gállos), was said by Ovid to be named after a Phrygian river.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the river Ganges.
parole.testo: From Latin Gangēticus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek Γαγγητικός (Gangētikós), from Γάγγης (Gángēs, “(River) Ganges”).

parole.significato: a gargle; a liquid used to gargle with.
parole.testo: From Latin gargarisma, from Ancient Greek γαργάρισμα (gargárisma).

parole.significato: To gargle (rinse or wash mouth and throat).
parole.testo: From Latin gargarizo, from Ancient Greek γαργαρίζω (gargarízō).

parole.significato: A fermented fish sauce popular as a condiment in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin garum, from Ancient Greek γάρον (gáron, “the fish whose intestines were originally used in the condiment's production”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the stomach.
parole.testo: From New Latin gastricus, from Ancient Greek γαστήρ, γαστρός (gastḗr, gastrós, “stomach”). By surface analysis, gastr- + -ic; Doublet of gastrique.

parole.significato: The muscle at the back of the calf, whose insertion is the Achilles tendon at the heel.
parole.testo: 1670s, borrowed from New Latin gastrocnēmius, from Ancient Greek γαστροκνημία (gastroknēmía, “calf of the leg”), from γαστήρ (gastḗr, “paunch, belly”) + κνήμη (knḗmē, “leg”).

parole.significato: A tribe of Scythia settled near the river Borysthenes
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Gelōnī, from Ancient Greek Γελωνοί (Gelōnoí).

parole.significato: Someone who has the Gemini star sign.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin geminī, plural of geminus (“twin”), calque of Ancient Greek Δίδυμοι (Dídumoi), calque of Akkadian 𒀯𒈠𒀸 (māšu), calque of Sumerian 𒀯𒈦𒋰𒁀 (ᵐᵘˡMAŠ.TAB.BA, “the Divine Twins, in Mesopotamia identified as Lugal-irra and Meslamta-ea; name of constellation”). See Lugal-irra and Meslamta-e

parole.significato: The origin, start, or point at which something comes into being.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin genesis (“generation, nativity”), from Ancient Greek γένεσις (génesis, “origin, source, beginning”). Related to Ancient Greek γίγνομαι (gígnomai, “to be produced, become, be”). Doublet of kind, gens, and jati.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the casting of horoscopes at a person's birth
parole.testo: From Latin genethliacus, from Ancient Greek γενεθλιακός (genethliakós, “belonging to a birthday”).

parole.significato: A birthday ode.
parole.testo: Via Latin genethliacon from Ancient Greek γενεθλιακόν (genethliakón, “of or related to a birthday”, neuter sg.).

parole.significato: Any of various herbs of the family Gentianaceae found in temperate and mountainous regions with violet or blue flowers.
parole.testo: Via Middle English from Latin gentiāna, which, according to Pliny the Elder, was named after Gentius (Ancient Greek Γένθιος (Génthios)), the last king of Illyria, who supposedly discovered the plant's medicinal benefits. This has been dismissed as folk etymology but the word may still ultimately be

parole.significato: The science that studies the structure of the Earth (or other planets), together with its origin and development, espec…
parole.testo: From geo- + -logy, partly after Renaissance Latin geōlogia, from Ancient Greek γεω- (geō-, “earth”) + Latin -logia (“the study of”), from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía).

parole.significato: A method of divination using earth or the ground, such as interpreting markings on the ground or how handfuls of dirt l…
parole.testo: From Middle English geomancie, from Medieval Latin geomantia from late Ancient Greek γεωμαντεία (geōmanteía). Equivalent to geo- + -mancy.

parole.significato: A mathematician who specializes in geometry.
parole.testo: From Middle English gemeter, geometer, ultimately from Late Latin geōmetrēs, from Ancient Greek γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) + μετρέω (metréō, “to measure”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to geometry.
parole.testo: From Latin geōmetricus, from Ancient Greek γεωμετρικός (geōmetrikós), from γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs). By surface analysis, geometer + -ic or geo- + -metric.

parole.significato: radiotelephony clear-code word for the letter G.
parole.testo: Name of an early saint, from Middle English George, from Latin Geōrgius, from Ancient Greek Γεώργῐος (Geṓrgĭos), from γεωργός (geōrgós, “farmer, earth worker”), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) (combining form γεω- (geō-)) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”) Doublet of Jorge and Geevarghese. The aircraft autopilot sense i

parole.significato: Any flowering plant of the genus Geranium, of family Geraniaceae.
parole.testo: From Latin geranium, from Ancient Greek γερᾰ́νῐον (gerắnĭon), from γέρᾰνος (gérănos, “crane”) + -ῐον (-ĭon, diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Gerasa
parole.testo: From the Late Latin Gerasēnus, Gergesēnus, from the Ancient Greek Γερασηνός (Gerasēnós), Γεργεσηνός (Gergesēnós), from Γέρασα (Gérasa), Γέργεσα (Gérgesa). By surface analysis, Gerasa + -ene.

parole.significato: magistrates in Sparta who, with the kings, constituted the Gerousia
parole.testo: From New Latin Gerontes, from Ancient Greek γέροντες (gérontes, literally “elders”).

parole.significato: Do not tempt or torment me; I reject you, your statements, or your beliefs.
parole.testo: Originally uttered by Christ in the King James Bible, Matthew 16:23: “get thee behind me, Satan”; Latin vāde retrō, Satanā; Ancient Greek ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου, Σατανᾶ (húpage opísō mou, Satanâ).

parole.significato: A Dacian tribe inhabiting the regions of the lower Danube.
parole.testo: From Latin Getae, from Ancient Greek Γέται (Gétai).

parole.significato: A hinge joint.
parole.testo: From Late Latin, from Ancient Greek γίγγλυμος (gínglumos, “hinge”).

parole.significato: A member of a certain group of descendants of Canaan who inhabited the land of Canaan.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin Gergeseum, from Ancient Greek Γεργεσαῖον (Gergesaîon), from Biblical Hebrew גִּרְגָּשִׁי (girgāšî). Further etymology is unknown.

parole.significato: Of a pale grey or bluish-green, especially when covered with a powdery residue.
parole.testo: From Latin glaucus, from Ancient Greek γλαυκός (glaukós, “blue-green, blue-grey”), 1670s. See Irish glas.

parole.significato: A list of difficult words or specialized terms used in a particular book or document, or in a particular domain of know…
parole.testo: From Middle English glosarie, from Latin glossārium, from Ancient Greek γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”). Doublet of glossarium.

parole.significato: The opening between the true vocal cords which is located in the larynx and affects voice modulation through expansion…
parole.testo: Late 16th century borrowing from New Latin glōttis, from Ancient Greek γλωττῐ́ς (glōttĭ́s, “mouth of the windpipe”), from γλῶττᾰ (glôttă, “tongue”) + -ῐς (-ĭs, feminine noun suffix). Cognates include Latin gula.

parole.significato: sweetness
parole.testo: From the New Latin combining form from Ancient Greek γλυκύς (glukús, “sweet”).

parole.significato: Any legume (such as liquorice) of the genus Glycyrrhiza.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek γλυκύρριζα (glukúrrhiza, “sweet root, licorice”). Doublet of licorice.

parole.significato: A member of the genus Glyptodon of extinct giant armadillos.
parole.testo: From the New Latin genus name Glyptodon (from Ancient Greek Ancient Greek γλυπτός (gluptós, “sculptured”) + -odon (“tooth”), 'grooved or carved tooth').

parole.significato: Deceitful and flattering; toadying.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Gnathōnicus, from Gnathō (genitive Gnathōnis), name of a parasitical character in the Eunuchus of Terence. Gnathō is from Ancient Greek γνάθος (gnáthos, “jaw”), used in the genitive γνάθου (gnáthou, “of a jaw”) to mean “greedy”; hence, a parasite in general.

parole.significato: Showing all great circles as straight lines, and thus preserving the shortest distances between any two locations.
parole.testo: From Latin gnōmonicus, Ancient Greek γνωμονικός (gnōmonikós, “judging by rule”). Compare French gnomonique. See gnomon.

parole.significato: Any of various small fish from the large family Gobiidae, in which the pelvic fins are fused to form a disc-shaped suck…
parole.testo: From Latin gobius (“gudgeon”), from Ancient Greek κωβιός (kōbiós), a type of small fish, of unknown ultimate origin. See also gudgeon.

parole.significato: witchcraft, demonic magic, necromancy.
parole.testo: From Latin goetia, from Ancient Greek γοητεία (goēteía, “witchcraft”), from γόης (góēs, “sorceror”).

parole.significato: One of the bluish-green granules that replace the more usual gonidia in certain lichens.
parole.testo: From New Latin gonimium, possibly from Ancient Greek γόνιμος (gónimos, “productive”).

parole.significato: A sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a species of bacteria (the gonococcus) that affects t…
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Late Latin gonorrhoea, from Ancient Greek γονόρροια (gonórrhoia), from γόνος (gónos, “sperm, seed, offspring”) + ῥοία (rhoía, “flow”) (ca. 1526). By surface analysis, gono- + -rrhea.

parole.significato: A vicious female monster from Greek mythology with sharp fangs and hair of living, venomous snakes. One of the three si…
parole.testo: From Middle English gorgon, from Latin Gorgō, from Ancient Greek Γοργώ (Gorgṓ), from γοργός (gorgós, “terrible”). Possibly from the same root as the Sanskrit word "garğ" (गर्जन), which is defined as a guttural sound, similar to the growling of a beast, thus possibly originating as an onomatopoeia.

parole.significato: The first section of the Christian New Testament scripture, comprising the books of Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, conce…
parole.testo: From Middle English gospel, gospell, godspel, godspell, goddspell, from Old English godspell (“gospel”), corresponding to God + spell (“talk, tale, story”), literally “the message of God”, believed to be an alteration of earlier *gōdspell (literally “good news”), used to translate ecclesiastical Lat

parole.significato: Relating to goth music or people.
parole.testo: From gothic rock, first used by John Stickney in reference to The Doors in 1967 and used by the late 1970s to describe the musical scene that gave rise to the goth subculture, both from a supposed aesthetic similarity to dark and moody 19th century gothic fiction and earlier gothic art and architect

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Goths or their language.
parole.testo: From Late Latin gothicus (“Gothic, barbaric”), from Ancient Greek Γοτθικός (Gotthikós), from Ancient Greek Γότθοι (Gótthoi, “Goths”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”), proposed to derive from unattested Gothic *𐌲𐌿𐍄𐌰 (*guta). Equivalent to Goth + -ic. The various usages of the adjective are introduced nearly si

parole.significato: Drawn, pictorial.
parole.testo: From Latin graphicus (“belonging to painting or drawing”), from Ancient Greek γραφικός (graphikós, “belonging to painting or drawing, picturesque, of or for writing; of style, lively”), from γραφή (graphḗ, “drawing, painting, writing, a writing, description, etc.”), from γράφω (gráphō, “scratch, car

parole.significato: Shortened form of Gregory Peck, a neck
parole.testo: Via Latin Grēgorius, from post-classical Ancient Greek Γρηγόριος (Grēgórios, “watchful, vigilant”), from Ancient Greek ἐγείρω (egeírō, “awaken, arouse”).

parole.significato: A Roman surveying instrument having plumb lines hanging from four arms at right angles.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin grōma, from Ancient Greek γνῶμᾰ (gnômă)

parole.significato: Abnormal curvature or hooked appearance.
parole.testo: From Late Latin grȳpōsis (“hooking”) (from grȳpus (“hook-nosed”)), from Ancient Greek γρυπῶσις (grupôsis, “hooking”), from γρύπεσθαι (grúpesthai, “become hooked”), from γρύπος (grúpos, “hook-nosed”).

parole.significato: a soft, non-cancerous growth, a form of granuloma, resulting from the tertiary stage of syphilis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin gumma, extended in meaning from Late Latin gumma (“gum, resin”), a late form of cummis, cummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi), of Egyptian origin. Doublet of gum (Etymology 2).

parole.significato: An officer who had various powers and duties connected with the gymnasia, such as the payment of training, oil, or othe…
parole.testo: From Latin gymnasiarchus, from Ancient Greek γυμνασίαρχος (gumnasíarkhos).

parole.significato: A large room or building for indoor sports.
parole.testo: From Latin gymnasium, from Ancient Greek γυμνάσιον (gumnásion, “exercise, school”), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”), because Greek athletes trained naked.

parole.significato: A sport involving the performance of sequences of movements requiring physical strength, flexibility, and kinesthetic a…
parole.testo: From gymnastic: see -ics; from Latin gymnasticus, from Ancient Greek γυμναστικός (gumnastikós), from γυμναστής (gumnastḗs, “athlete, gymnast”), from γῠμνᾰ́ζω (gŭmnắzō, “to train, exercise”), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”), because Greek athletes trained naked. By surface analysis, gymnast + -ics.

parole.significato: Gymnastic; athletic.
parole.testo: From Latin gymnicus, from Ancient Greek γυμνικός (gumnikós), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”).

parole.significato: A small carnivorous mammal, subfamily Galericinae, related to the hedgehogs and resembling a large rat, which inhabits…
parole.testo: From New Latin Gymnura, former genus name, from Ancient Greek γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”).

parole.significato: The women's quarters in a household; (hence, loosely) any building or area for women.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gynaecēum, gynaecīum, from Ancient Greek γυναικεῖον (gunaikeîon), from γυνή (gunḗ, “woman”) (stem: γῠναικ- (gŭnaik-)) + -εῖον (-eîon, noun-forming suffix meaning “place or building associated with a specific purpose or person”).

parole.significato: A gynaeceum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gynaecōnītis, from Ancient Greek γυναικωνῖτις (gunaikōnîtis).

parole.significato: The pistils/carpels of a flower considered as a group
parole.testo: From New Latin; from gyno- + oecium (from Ancient Greek οἰκῐ́ον (oikĭ́on), diminutive of οἶκος (oîkos, “house”)).

parole.significato: A mineral consisting of hydrated calcium sulphate. When calcinated, it forms plaster of Paris.
parole.testo: From Latin gypsum, from Ancient Greek γύψος (gúpsos). Doublet of gesso.

parole.significato: A swirling vortex.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gȳrus (“circle; circular motion”), from Ancient Greek γῦρος (gûros, “circle; ring”), from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to bend; to curve”). The English word is a doublet of gyro and gyrus.

parole.significato: A magical plant mentioned by John Milton, said to be good against enchantments.
parole.testo: Coined by John Milton for the play Comus around 1634 (see quotation below). Various scholars suggest that the word comes from a classical source such as Latin Haemonia (“Thessaly”, a place associated with magic), Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma, “blood”), or Ancient Greek αἵμων (haímōn, “skillful”).

parole.significato: A kingfisher whose nesting by the sea was said, in classical mythology, to cause the Gods to restrain the wind and wave…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Alceoun, from Latin halcyōn, alcyōn (“kingfisher”), from Ancient Greek ἀλκυών (alkuṓn).

parole.significato: A period of calm during the winter, when storms do not occur.
parole.testo: From halcyon, from Latin Alcyone, from Ancient Greek Ἀλκυόνη (Alkuónē), daughter of Aeolus and wife of Ceyx. When her husband died in a shipwreck, Alcyone threw herself into the sea whereupon the gods transformed them both into halcyon birds (kingfishers). When Alcyone made her nest on the beach, wa

parole.significato: The dugong.
parole.testo: From Late Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek ἅλς (háls, “sea”) + κόρη (kórē, “girl, maiden”).

parole.significato: A treatise upon fish or the art of fishing, especially in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin halieuticus ("halieutic, of or about fishing"), from Ancient Greek ἁλιευτικός (halieutikós) (alieutikós, "of or about fishermen"), from ἁλιεύς (halieús, “fisherman”). The Christianity definition comes from the fish being a symbol of the Christian faith.

parole.significato: The condition of having stale or foul-smelling breath.
parole.testo: Coined by doctor Joseph William Howe in 1874 and described as being derived from the Latin hālitus (literally “whiff, breath”) and the Ancient Greek νόσος (nósos, literally “disease”). It can be also understood as combination of the Latin hālitus and the English suffix -osis.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Haloragaceae.
parole.testo: From translingual Haloragaceae + -ous, from New Latin Haloragis + -aceae, formed irregularly from Ancient Greek ἅλς (háls, “salt”) + ῥάξ (rháx, “berry”) (a Pre-Greek / Mediterranean loan).

parole.significato: A wood-nymph who was physically a part of her tree; she would die if her tree were felled.
parole.testo: From Latin Hamadryas, from Ancient Greek Ἁμαδρυάς (Hamadruás), from ἅμα (háma, “together”) + δρῦς (drûs, “tree”).

parole.significato: Any of the flowering plant genus Hamamelis, the witch hazels.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἁμαμηλίς (hamamēlís, “medlar”).

parole.significato: A certain stone with spangles of gold color in it, known to Pliny, perhaps golden mica or yellow mica schist.
parole.testo: From Latin hammochrȳsos, (h)ammochrȳsus, from Ancient Greek ἀμμόχρῡσος (ammókhrūsos), from ἄμμος (ámmos, “sand”) + χρῡσός (khrūsós, “gold”).

parole.significato: Being or relating to a form of arthrodontous peristome:
parole.testo: From New Latin haplolepideus, from Ancient Greek ἁπλόος (haplóos, “two-fold, single”) + λεπίδιον (lepídion, “small plate used to close a tube”).

parole.significato: Any primate of the evolved clade (half of the order) which comprises all apes (including hominoids), monkeys and even (…
parole.testo: From Neo-Latin Haplorrhini, from Ancient Greek ἁπλόος (haplóos, “simple”) + ῥίς (rhís, “nose”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to harmony.
parole.testo: From Latin harmonicus, from Ancient Greek ἁρμονικός (harmonikós), from ἁρμονία (harmonía, “harmony”). By surface analysis, harmony + -ic. Doublet of armónico.

parole.significato: A grappling hook.
parole.testo: Adapted from Latin harpagō, gen. harpagōnis, from Ancient Greek ἁρπάγη (harpágē, “hook”), from ἁρπάζω (harpázō, “to snatch away, to carry off, to seize, to captivate”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of harpoon.

parole.significato: A student of law or medicine at Cambridge who, being of the same standing as the students in arts in his year, is allow…
parole.testo: According to a 17th century chronicler, from Latin sophister Henricianus after King Henry VIII, but remodeled to fit a fanciful Ancient Greek *ἐρίσοφος (*erísophos, “very wise indeed”), from ἐρι- (eri-) + σοφός (sophós).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the patriotic Jewish family to which the Maccabees belonged; Maccabean.
parole.testo: From Latin Asmonaeus (latinized name of the family's founder) + English -an, from (Hellenic) Ancient Greek Ἀσαμωναῖος (Asamōnaîos), from Hebrew חַשְׁמוֹנַאי (ḥašmōnay).

parole.significato: A group of seven.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hebdomada (“number seven; group of seven; seven days”), hebdomas (“number seven; seven days; seventh day”), from Ancient Greek ἑβδομάς (hebdomás, “group of seven, especially seven days or seven years”), from ἕβδομος (hébdomos, “seventh”) + -ᾰ́ς (-ắs, suffix forming abstract nouns of

parole.significato: Ebony.
parole.testo: From Middle English ebenif, hebenyf (influenced by Late Latin hebeninus), from Ecclesiastical Latin ebenius (“of ebony”), from Latin hebenus (“ebon tree”), from Ancient Greek ἔβενος (ébenos), from Egyptian hbnj, U13:n-Z4:M3

parole.significato: Texts or artifacts containing Hebrew writing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin hebraica, neuter plural of hebraicus (“Hebrew”), from Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος (Hebraîos), from Hebrew עִבְרִי (ʿiḇrī, “Hebrew”) (likely through Aramaic עִבְרַי (ʿiḇray, “Hebrew”)), traditionally from עֵבֶר ('éver, “Eber”), the ancestor of the Israelites. By surface an

parole.significato: A great public sacrifice to the gods, originally of a hundred oxen; also, a great number of animals reserved for such a…
parole.testo: The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin hecatombē (“great sacrifice of a hundred oxen, hecatomb”), from Ancient Greek ἑκατόμβη (hekatómbē, “great sacrifice of a hundred oxen, hecatomb; any animal sacrifice or large sacrifice”, from ἑκᾰτόν (hekătón, “hundred”) + βοῦς (boûs, “cattle, cow, ox”)). Th

parole.significato: A modified arm of any of several male cephalopods that functions as a reproductive organ by transferring sperm to the m…
parole.testo: From New Latin, corresponding to hecto- + Ancient Greek κότυλος (kótulos, “small cup”).

parole.significato: Sometimes in the form Hector: a blustering, noisy, turbulent fellow; a braggart, bully.
parole.testo: From Hector (“in Greek and Roman mythology, a character in Homer’s Iliad who is the greatest warrior of Troy”), from Late Middle English Hector (“warrior with the qualities of Hector”), from Latin Hectōr or Ancient Greek Ἕκτωρ (Héktōr), from ἕκτωρ (héktōr, “holding fast”), from ἔχειν (ékhein), prese

parole.significato: snail farming
parole.testo: From helici- + culture, from the genus of snails Helix, from helix, from Latin helix, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix, “something twisted”).

parole.significato: helix, spiral
parole.testo: From Latin helic- + -o-, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix).

parole.significato: A device that includes a plane mirror which turns so as to keep reflecting sunlight toward a predetermined target, comp…
parole.testo: First use appear c. 1747, from New Latin heliostata, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”) + Latin status (“stationary”). By surface analysis, helio- + -stat.

parole.significato: The second-lightest chemical element (symbol He), with an atomic number of 2 and atomic weight of 4.002602, a colorless…
parole.testo: From New Latin helium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”) (because its presence was first theorised in the Sun's atmosphere) with the suffix + -ium. Probably coined by Norman Lockyer. This suffix is unusual, because it is usually used only for metallic elements. It is likely that Lockyer, bein

parole.significato: A curve on the surface of a cylinder or cone such that its angle to a plane perpendicular to the axis is constant; the…
parole.testo: From Latin helix, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix, “something twisted or spiral”).

parole.significato: A variety of agate, sprinkled with spots of red jasper.
parole.testo: From Latin haemachātēs, from Ancient Greek *αἱμᾰχᾱ́της (*haimăkhā́tēs), from αἷμᾰ (haîmă, “blood”) + ᾰ̓χᾱ́της (ăkhā́tēs, “agate”).

parole.significato: The inability to see clearly in bright light; day blindness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin hēmeralōpia, from Ancient Greek ἡμεραλωπία (hēmeralōpía). From ἡμέρα (hēmérā, “day”), ἀλαός (alaos, “blind”), and ὄψ (ops, “eye”).

parole.significato: A headache affecting one side of the head.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hemicrania (“pain in one half of the head”), from Ancient Greek ἡμικρᾱνίᾰ (hēmikrāníă), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “hemi-, half”) + κρανίον (kraníon, “skull”) (from whence also cranium). Cognate to megrim and migraine, which also derive from the Latin.

parole.significato: A Roman unit of liquid measure reckoned as the volume of ⁵⁄₆ Roman pound of wine, equivalent to around 0.27 L.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hēmīna (“half-sextarius”), from Ancient Greek ἡμῑ́νᾱ (hēmī́nā).

parole.significato: Equus hemionus, the onager or kiang, a kind of wild ass of Tibet.
parole.testo: From New Latin hēmionus, from Ancient Greek ἡμῐ́ονος (hēmĭ́onos, “half ass, mule”).

parole.significato: Total or partial inability to move one side of the body.
parole.testo: From New Latin hemiplegia, from Ancient Greek ἡμιπλήξ (hēmiplḗx), also ἡμιπληγής (hēmiplēgḗs, “stricken on one side”), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “half”) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “to strike”). By surface analysis, hemi- + -plegia.

parole.significato: Half of the celestial sphere, as divided by either the ecliptic or the celestial equator .
parole.testo: From Latin hemisphaerium, from Ancient Greek ἡμισφαίριον (hēmisphaírion), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “half”) + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”). Equivalent to hemi- + sphere. Displaced native Old English healftrendel (literally “half-sphere”).

parole.significato: A semitone.
parole.testo: Latin hemitonium, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A heavy release of blood within or from the body.
parole.testo: From Latin haemorrhagia, from Ancient Greek αἱμορραγία (haimorrhagía, “a violent bleeding”), from αἱμορραγής (haimorrhagḗs, “bleeding violently”), from αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) + -ραγία (-ragía), from ῥηγνύναι (rhēgnúnai, “to break, burst”); see ῥήγνῡμῐ (rhḗgnūmĭ) for more.

parole.significato: Having eleven syllables.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hendecasyllabus, from Ancient Greek ἑνδεκασύλλαβος (hendekasúllabos), from ἕνδεκα (héndeka, “eleven”) + συλλαβή (sullabḗ, “syllable”).

parole.significato: A line, verse, or word that comprises eleven syllables.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hendecasyllabus, from Ancient Greek ἑνδεκασύλλαβος (hendekasúllabos); equivalent to hendeca- + syllable.

parole.significato: A figure of speech used for emphasis, where two words joined by and are used to express a single complex idea.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin, from Ancient Greek ἕν (hén), stem of εἷς (heîs, “one”) + διά (diá, “through”) + δύο (dúo, “two”), “one [idea] through two [words]”.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the liver.
parole.testo: From Middle English epatik, from Late Latin hepaticus, from Ancient Greek ἡπατικός (hēpatikós, “of the liver”), from ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”).

parole.significato: A variety of barite that emits a foetid odour when rubbed or heated.
parole.testo: From Latin hepatitis, an unknown precious stone, from Ancient Greek ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”); compare French hépatite.

parole.significato: A valuable metal alloy in antiquity, thought to have been an alloy of copper with gold and silver, mixed and treated to…
parole.testo: From the Latin hēpatizon, from the Ancient Greek ἡπᾰτῐ́ζον (hēpătĭ́zon), from ἡπᾰτῐ́ζων (hēpătĭ́zōn, “liver-coloured”).

parole.significato: Any of a people who comprised a nomadic confederation in Central Asia during the 5th–6th centuries CE.
parole.testo: Hypercorrect respelling of Ephthalite, with unetymological initial h-, from Latin Ephthalītēs, from Ancient Greek Ἐφθαλίτης (Ephthalítēs), from Bactrian Ηβοδαλο (Ēbodalo) + Ancient Greek -ίτης (-ítēs).

parole.significato: A government of seven people.
parole.testo: From New Latin heptarchia, from Ancient Greek ἑπτά (heptá, “hepta-: seven”) + -αρχία (-arkhía, “-archy: rule”). Equivalent to hepta- + -archy.

parole.significato: A rectangular pillar bearing a bust of Hermes, once used as a boundary marker and later as decoration.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Herma, a Latinization of Hermēs, from Ancient Greek Ἑρμῆς (Hermês).

parole.significato: A type of root, probably from a plant of the genus Colchicum, as imported and used in Western medicine.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hermodactylus, from Ancient Greek ἑρμοδάκτυλος (hermodáktulos, “Hermes's finger”).

parole.significato: A female hero.
parole.testo: From Latin hērōīna, from late Ancient Greek ἡρωΐνη (hērōḯnē) (2nd century), a feminine equivalent of ἥρως (hḗrōs, “hero, demigod”), equivalent to hero + -ine (suffix forming feminine nouns). * English from 1587. The sense of "female lead character" is from 1715.

parole.significato: A temple dedicated to a hero, often over his supposed tomb.
parole.testo: From Latin hērōon, from Ancient Greek ἡρῷον (hērōîon), from ἡρῷος (hērōîos, “of a hero”).

parole.significato: Seeking infamy.
parole.testo: From Herostratus + -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives from nouns). Herostratus is a learned borrowing from Latin Hērostratus, from Ancient Greek Ἡρόστρατος (Hēróstratos), from Ἥρᾱ (Hḗrā, “Greek goddess of marriage, women, and family”) + στρᾰτός (strătós, “army, military for

parole.significato: Fame (or infamy) won through crime, destruction, or some other misdeed.
parole.testo: Herostratic is derived from Herostratus (learned borrowing from Latin Hērostratus, from Ancient Greek Ἡρόστρατος (Hēróstratos) + -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives from nouns)).
