parole.testo: From Latin metoecus, from Ancient Greek μέτοικος (métoikos, “alien, outsider, foreigner”), combination of μετά (metá) and οἶκος (oîkos, “residency”). Cognate with French métèque.

parole.significato: Meum athamanticum, a European herb.
parole.testo: From Latin mēum (“umbelliferous plant, Meum athamanticum”), from Ancient Greek μῆον (mêon), probably from μεῖον (meîon, “lesser”) for its small size. The English form came perhaps via Middle French meu, a word with a single isolated attestation from the 14th century which only began to appear consis

parole.significato: spignel, Meum athamanticum
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mēum (“Meum athamanticum”), from Ancient Greek μῆον (mêon), probably from μεῖον (meîon, “lesser”) for its small size.

parole.significato: A very large champagne bottle (named after the King) with the capacity of about 30 liters, equivalent to 40 standard bo…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Midās, from Ancient Greek Μίδᾱς (Mídās), from Phrygian midas.

parole.significato: A form of acting without words; pantomime.
parole.testo: Possibly from Middle English mime, from Old English mīma (“a buffoon, jester, mime”), from Latin mimus, from Ancient Greek μῖμος (mîmos, “imitator, actor”), but more likely re-borrowed in modern times from French mime (“mimic actor”), from the same source.

parole.significato: Exhibiting mimesis.
parole.testo: From Latin mīmēticus or its etymon Ancient Greek μῑμητικός (mīmētikós, “imitative”). By surface analysis, mime + -etic.

parole.significato: To imitate, especially in order to ridicule.
parole.testo: From Latin mīmicus, from Ancient Greek μῑμικός (mīmikós, “belonging to mimes”), from μῖμος (mîmos, “imitator, actor”); see mime.

parole.significato: A monetary unit of ancient Greece and the Middle East, originally equivalent to the weight of a mina of silver.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mina, from Ancient Greek μνᾶ (mnâ, “mna”). Compare maneh, from Biblical Hebrew מָנֶה (māne), as well as maund.

parole.significato: A monastic church.
parole.testo: From Middle English mynster (see mynisterie), from Old English mynster, from Latin monastērium (“monastery”), from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion, “monastery; solitary dwelling”). Doublet of monastery.

parole.significato: A member of a race said to be autochthonous to the Aegean area.
parole.testo: From Latin Minyes (from Ancient Greek Μινύες (Minúes)) + -an.

parole.significato: A kind of gladiator, known for wearing a Gallic helmet with the image of a fish.
parole.testo: From Latin mirmillō, from Ancient Greek μόρμυλος (mórmulos).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the dynasty begun by Mithridates I of Pontus or any of its kings named Mithridates, especially Mith…
parole.testo: From Latin Mithridāticus, from Ancient Greek Μιθριδατικός (Mithridatikós), from Μιθριδάτης (Mithridátēs) + -ικός (-ikós), from Old Median *Miθra-dāta (literally “Mithra-given”).

parole.significato: Synonym of mithridate.
parole.testo: From Late Latin mithridatium, from Latin Mithridātīus (“of or related to Mithridates”), from Mithridātēs + -ius, from Ancient Greek Μιθριδάτης (Mithridátēs), the Greek form of the name of Mithridates VI of Pontus. Doublet of mithridate, mithridatum, and mithridaticon.

parole.significato: Synonym of mithridate.
parole.testo: From Late Latin mithridatum, variant of mithridatium, from Latin Mithridātīus (“of or related to Mithridates”), from Mithridātēs + -ius, from Ancient Greek Μιθριδάτης (Mithridátēs), the Greek form of the name of Mithridates VI of Pontus. Doublet of mithridate, mithridatium, and mithridaticon.

parole.significato: Especially of a series of ideas, letters, words, etc.: intended to help in remembering.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin mnemonicus or its etymon Ancient Greek μνημονῐκός (mnēmonĭkós, “pertaining to memory or remembrance, memorial”) + English -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Mνημονῐκός (Mnēmonĭkós) is derived from μνήμων (mnḗmōn, “mindful, remembering”) + -ῐκός (-

parole.significato: Something (especially a series of ideas, letters, words, etc.) used to help in remembering a thing; a memory aid.
parole.testo: Noun sense 1 (“something used to help in remembering a thing”) is borrowed from Latin mnēmonicum (“something used to help in remembering a thing”), from Ancient Greek μνημονικόν (mnēmonikón, “something used to help in remembering a thing”), a noun use of the neuter form of μνημονῐκός (mnēmonĭkós, ad

parole.significato: A metrical foot of three long syllables.
parole.testo: From Latin molossus, from Ancient Greek μολοσσός (molossós), properly "belonging to the Molossians", a people in the eastern part of Epirus.

parole.significato: A magic herb or plant used by Odysseus to overcome Circe.
parole.testo: From Latin mōly, from Ancient Greek μῶλυ (môlu) (probably a loanword).

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol Mo) with an atomic number of 42: a silvery metal, not found as a free element, used in steel…
parole.testo: From New Latin molybdaenum, from molybdaena (“any of various substances resembling lead”), from Ancient Greek μολύβδαινα (molúbdaina, “a plummet, piece of lead”), from μόλυβδος (mólubdos, “lead; graphite”), from an Anatolian word cognate with Lydian 𐤪𐤠𐤭𐤦𐤥𐤣𐤠 (mariwda, “dark”), from Proto-Indo-Europea

parole.significato: One thing, one being, one item.
parole.testo: From Latin monas (“unit”) (from Ancient Greek μονάς (monás), from μόνος (mónos), from Proto-Indo-European *men-). By surface analysis, mono- + -ad.

parole.significato: A rare autosomal-dominant hair disease that results in short, fragile, broken hair with a beaded appearance.
parole.testo: From Latin mŏnīle (“necklace”) + Ancient Greek θρίξ (thríx, “hair”).

parole.significato: The doctrine of the oneness and unity of reality, despite the appearance of diversity in the world.
parole.testo: The word was coined by German philosopher Baron Christian von Wolff and first used in English in 1862, from New Latin monismus, from Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos, “alone”). By surface analysis, mon- + -ism.

parole.significato: A type of cyme on which each single axis bears one flower.
parole.testo: From New Latin monochasium, from Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos, “alone, only, sole, single”) + χάσις (khásis, “chasm, separation”).

parole.significato: A musical instrument for experimenting with the mathematical relations of musical sounds, consisting of a single string…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin monochordon, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μονόχορδον (monókhordon). By surface analysis, mono- + chord.

parole.significato: An ode, as in Greek drama, for a single voice, often specifically a mournful song or dirge.
parole.testo: From Latin monodia, from Ancient Greek μονῳδία (monōidía).

parole.significato: A duel; single combat.
parole.testo: From Latin monomachia, from Ancient Greek μονομαχία (monomakhía); μόνος (mónos, “single, alone”) + μάχομαι (mákhomai, “fight”).

parole.significato: A situation, by legal privilege or other agreement, in which solely one party (company, cartel etc.) exclusively provid…
parole.testo: From Latin monopōlium, from Ancient Greek μονοπώλιον (monopṓlion, “a right of exclusive sale”), from μόνος (mónos, “sole”) + πωλέω (pōléō, “to barter, sell”). By surface analysis, mono- + -poly.

parole.significato: A classical temple made up of one circle of columns supporting a roof.
parole.testo: From Latin monopteros, from Ancient Greek μονόπτερος (monópteros), from μονο- (mono-, “mono-”) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing; circle of columns”).

parole.significato: A noun which only occurs in one case.
parole.testo: From Latin monoptotum, from Ancient Greek μονόπτωτος (monóptōtos).

parole.significato: Consisting of one syllable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin monosyllabicus, from Latin monosyllabus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek μονοσύλλαβος (monosúllabos). By surface analysis, monosyllable + -ic or mono- + syllabic.

parole.significato: Having a single unvaried pitch.
parole.testo: From the post-Classical Latin monotonus (“unvarying in tone”) or its etymon the Ancient Greek μονότονος (monótonos, “steady”, “unwavering”); compare cognate adjectives, namely the French monotone, the German monoton, the Italian monotono, and the Spanish monótono, as well as the slightly earlier Eng

parole.significato: A canoe or boat made from a hollowed out tree.
parole.testo: From New Latin monoxylon, from Ancient Greek μονόξυλος (monóxulos, “made from a solid trunk”). See mono- and xylo-.

parole.significato: An acid derived from the mulberry.
parole.testo: Latin morus (“mulberry tree”) + Ancient Greek ξύλον (xúlon, “wood”) + -ic + acid. Named by Martin Heinrich Klaproth

parole.significato: A blemish or mark on the skin, especially a blister caused by scurvy.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin morphea, perhaps from Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “form, shape”). Doublet of morphea.

parole.significato: The way in which an organism (or an organ) changes form during development.
parole.testo: From Late Latin morphosis, from Ancient Greek μόρφωσις (mórphōsis, “shaping”).

parole.significato: Giving birth to multiple young at one time; synonym of multiparous and polytocous.
parole.testo: From Latin multi- + Ancient Greek τόκος (tókos).

parole.significato: One of the nine Ancient Greek deities of the arts.
parole.testo: From Middle English Muse, from Latin Musa, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa).

parole.significato: A building or institution dedicated to the acquisition, conservation, study, exhibition, and educational interpretation…
parole.testo: From Latin mūsēum (“library, study”), from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon), shrine of the Muses (Μοῦσα (Moûsa)). Doublet of mosaic.

parole.significato: The fear of mice (and rats).
parole.testo: From Latin mūs (“mouse”) or Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs, “mouse”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: The condition of having abnormally large and dilated pupils due to illness or narcotics, particularly stimulants such a…
parole.testo: From Latin mydriasis, from Ancient Greek μυδρίᾱσις (mudríāsis, “undue enlargement of the pupil”), from μύδρος (múdros, “mass of red hot material in a forge”), possibly because the pupil is particularly bright or sparkling when dilated, or because of the red eye effect when exposed to a flash of ligh

parole.significato: megakaryocyte or osteoclast
parole.testo: From New Latin myeloplax, from Ancient Greek μυελός (muelós, “marrow”) + πλάξ (pláx, “plate”).

parole.significato: A shrew or ferret.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin mygale (“field mouse”) (Vetus Latina), from Ancient Greek μυγαλέη (mugaléē, “shrew”) (used in the Septuagint to translate Hebrew אֲנָקָה, now generally thought to indicate a gecko or similar small reptile).

parole.significato: The muscular substance of the heart; the middle of the three layers forming the outer wall of the human heart.
parole.testo: From New Latin myocardium, from Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs, “muscle”) + καρδίᾱ (kardíā, “heart”).

parole.significato: The smooth muscle forming the wall of the uterus.
parole.testo: From myo- + Late Latin metrium (“womb”), from Ancient Greek μήτριον (mḗtrion, “of a mother”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Myosotis, the forget-me-nots.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin myosōtis, from Koine Ancient Greek μυοσωτίς (muosōtís, literally “ears of a mouse”), from genitive of μῦς (mûs, “mouse”) and nominative plural of οὖς (oûs, “ear”).

parole.significato: A protein that acts as an inhibitor to the growth of muscle tissue.
parole.testo: Perhaps from myo- (“muscle”) + Latin statos, status, sto (“remain, stand, fix, set"”) or Ancient Greek στάσις (stásis, “inactivity, a freezing, state of motionlessness, arrest, a standing”). myo- + -statin?

parole.significato: One of a fierce tribe or troop who accompanied Achilles, their king, in the Trojan War.
parole.testo: From Latin Myrmidones, from Ancient Greek Μυρμιδόνες (Murmidónes), a tribe of warriors led by Achilles to the Trojan War. Folk etymology in Ovid's time derived the tribe's name from μυρμηδών (murmēdṓn, “ant-nest”), from μύρμηξ (múrmēx, “ant”)).

parole.significato: A soldier or a subordinate civil officer who executes orders of a superior without protest or pity (sometimes applied t…
parole.testo: From Myrmidon, from Latin Myrmidones, from Ancient Greek Μυρμιδόνες (Murmidónes).

parole.significato: A plum-like fruit from various trees of the genus Terminalia, formerly used in medicine and now in the dyeing industry;…
parole.testo: From Latin myrobalanum, myrobalanus (“ben nut”), from Ancient Greek μυροβάλανος (murobálanos), from μύρον (múron, “perfume”) + βάλανος (bálanos, “acorn”).

parole.significato: A red-brown resinous material, the dried sap of a tree of the genus Commiphora, especially Commiphora myrrha, used as p…
parole.testo: From Middle English mirre, from Old English myrre, from Latin myrrha, from Ancient Greek μύρρα (múrrha), from Semitic. Compare Arabic مُرّ (murr, “myrrh”, literally “bitterness”), Hebrew מור / מֹר (mōr, “myrrh”, literally “bitterness”). Compare מרור : maror.

parole.significato: A set of growth stages in the larvae of Decapoda after protozoea and prior to the juvenile stage, in which pereiopods a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin, from Ancient Greek μῡ́ειν (mū́ein, “to close”, used of the lips or eyes).

parole.significato: A person who prepares an initiate for entry into a mystery cult, or who teaches mystical doctrines.
parole.testo: From Latin mystagōgus, Ancient Greek μυσταγωγός (mustagōgós). By surface analysis, mystic + -agogue.

parole.significato: One who rules over mysteries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin mystēriarchēs (“one who presides over Christian sacraments”), from Ancient Greek μυστηριάρχης (mustēriárkhēs, “one who rules over religious mysteries”), from μυστήριον (mustḗrion) + -άρχης (-árkhēs), corresponding to mystery + -arch.

parole.significato: Mythical; existing in myth.
parole.testo: 1660s; from Latin mȳthicus or Ancient Greek μυθικός (muthikós); equivalent to myth + -ic.

parole.significato: Anything transmitted by word of mouth, such as a fable, legend, narrative, story, or tale (especially a poetic tale).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin mȳthos (“myth”), from Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos, “report, tale, story”). Doublet of myth. The plural form mythoi is from Ancient Greek μῦθοι (mûthoi), and the form mythoses from mythos + -es.

parole.significato: Synonym of mythos.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin mythus, from Late Latin mȳthos (“myth”), from Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos, “report, tale, story”).

parole.significato: The ancient inhabitants of Nabataea, a region of Arabia inhabited by the Nabataeans that covers parts of northern Arabi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Nabataeus (“Nabataean”), which was borrowed from Ancient Greek Ναβαταῖος (Nabataîos, “Nabataean”), which was borrowed from Nabataean Aramaic 𐢕𐢃𐢋𐢈 (nbṭw, “Nabataean”). Possibly cognate with Arabic نَبَطِيّ (nabaṭiyy, “Nabataean, Nabaṭ”), Arabic أَنْبَاط (ʔanbāṭ), and Hebrew נבטים

parole.significato: A Hebrew stringed instrument.
parole.testo: From Latin nabla, from Ancient Greek νάβλα (nábla, “Phoenician harp”), from ancient Hebrew נֵבֶל (nḗḇel) or a Phoenician cognate. Doublet of nebel, which comes via the modern Hebrew נֵ֤בֶל.

parole.significato: A female deity (nymph) associated with water, especially a spring, stream, or other fresh water.
parole.testo: From Latin Nāïas, from Ancient Greek Νᾱϊάς (Nāïás, “naiad”), from νάω (náō, “to flow”).

parole.significato: In the International System of Units and other metric systems of units, multiplying the unit to which it is attached by…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nānus (“dwarf”), borrowed from Ancient Greek νᾶνος (nânos, “dwarf”).

parole.significato: A form of dwarfism characterized by a very short trunk
parole.testo: From nano- (“dwarf”) + Latin cormus, Ancient Greek κορμός (kormós, “trunk”).

parole.significato: Naturally occurring liquid petroleum.
parole.testo: From Latin naphtha, from Ancient Greek νάφθα (náphtha, “naphtha”), from Old Persian *naftah, probably borrowed or assimilated from Akkadian 𒉌𒆳𒊏 (napṭu, “naphtha”) . The Greek mediation is reflected in the spelling – ‘ph’ and ‘th’ (from ‘φ’ and ‘θ’).

parole.significato: Narcissistic, loving oneself excessively.
parole.testo: From Latin narcissinus, from Ancient Greek ναρκίσσινος (narkíssinos), from νάρκισσος (nárkissos, “narcissus”).

parole.significato: The ointment nard.
parole.testo: From Latin nardus, from Ancient Greek νάρδος (nárdos).

parole.significato: A national standard variety of a language spoken in more than one region.
parole.testo: From natio(n) + -lect. The first component is from Latin nātiōn(em), with the second abbreviated from dialect, from Ancient Greek. Coined by Godelieve Laureys in 1997.

parole.significato: A shipmaster, a shipowner, a skipper
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nauclērus, from Ancient Greek ναύκληρος (naúklēros).

parole.significato: The recreation of a sea battle staged for entertainment.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin naumachia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ναυμαχία (naumakhía). Compare naumachy.

parole.significato: A crustacean larva that has three pairs of locomotive organs (corresponding to antennules, antennae, and mandibles), a…
parole.testo: ] Borrowed from New Latin Nauplius (former genus name) (coined by Danish naturalist Otto Friedrich Müller (1730–1784) who mistakenly thought the larvae were a separate genus of animal), from Latin nauplius (“argonaut, paper nautilus (genus Argonauta)”), from Ancient Greek ναύπλιος (naúplios, “type o

parole.significato: A feeling of illness or discomfort in the digestive system, usually characterized by a strong urge to vomit.
parole.testo: From Middle English nausea, a borrowing from Latin nausea, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía, “sea-sickness”), from ναῦς (naûs, “ship”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₂-. Displaced native Old English wlǣtta.

parole.significato: To cause nausea in.
parole.testo: From earlier nauseat, from Latin nauseātus (“nauseated”), perfect past participle of nauseō (“to feel sea sick, nauseate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix, of participial origin)), from nausea, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía), from ναῦς (naûs), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₂-. By surface analys

parole.significato: A marine mollusc, of the family Nautilidae native to the Pacific Ocean and Indian Ocean, which has tentacles and a spir…
parole.testo: From Latin nautilus, from Ancient Greek ναυτίλος (nautílos, “paper nautilus, sailor”).

parole.significato: The commander of a fleet.
parole.testo: From Latin navarchus, from Ancient Greek ναύαρχος (naúarkhos, “leader of the ships”), corresponding to navy + -arch.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the city of Naples, capital and largest city of Campania, Italy, or the surrounding metropolita…
parole.testo: From Latin neāpolītānus, from Neāpolis, from Ancient Greek Νεάπολις (Neápolis, literally “new city”), a Greek city in modern Naples. Doublet of naporitan.

parole.significato: The skin of a fawn, as worn by Dionysus, and as worn in his honor by his male followers and female followers (maenads)…
parole.testo: From Latin nebris, from Ancient Greek νεβρίς (nebrís), earlier νεβρός (nebrós, “fawn”).

parole.significato: The drink of the gods.
parole.testo: From Latin nectar, from Ancient Greek νέκταρ (néktar, “nourishment of the gods”), from Proto-Indo-European *neḱ- (“perish, disappear”) + *-tr̥h₂ (“overcoming”), from *terh₂- (“to overcome, pass through, cross over”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to nectar; nectarous.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nectareus (“of nectar; sweet”), from Ancient Greek νεκτάρεος (nektáreos, “sweet as nectar, fragrant”), from νέκταρ (néktar, “nectar”).

parole.significato: The swede (rutabaga); turnip.
parole.testo: From Middle English neep, from Old English nǣp (“turnip, rape”), borrowed from Latin nāpus. Compare Icelandic næpa (“turnip”). Cognate with English turnip.

parole.significato: A beginner; a person who is new to a subject, skill, or belief.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin neophytus, from Ancient Greek νεόφυτος (neóphutos, “newly planted”), from νέος (néos, “new”) + φυτόν (phutón, “plant, child”). By surface analysis, neo- + -phyte.

parole.significato: Modern, new-fangled.
parole.testo: From Late Latin neotericus, from Hellenistic Greek νεωτερικός (neōterikós), from comparative of Ancient Greek νέος (néos, “new”).

parole.significato: A drug mentioned in Homer's Odyssey (c. 8th century B.C.E.) as bringing relief from anxiety or grief; hence, any drug o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nēpenthes (“a drug bringing relief from grief”), from Ancient Greek νηπενθές (nēpenthés), neuter of νηπενθής (nēpenthḗs, “sorrow-banishing”), from νη- (nē-, “not”) + πένθος (pénthos, “grief”) (from πάσχειν (páskhein), present active infinitive of πάσχω (páskhō, “to be ill or inju

parole.significato: A semi-precious stone, one of the two types of stone commonly referred to as jade (the other being jadeite).
parole.testo: From Latin lapis nephriticus, via Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos) νεφριτικός (nephritikós), meaning kidney stone, because jade was believed to have cured kidney stones.

parole.significato: Any one of the fifty sea-nymphs who were daughters of the sea-god Nereus and attendants upon Poseidon (Neptune), and we…
parole.testo: From the stem of Latin Nērēis, from Ancient Greek Νηρηΐς (Nērēḯs), from Νηρεύς (Nēreús, “Nereus”) + -ις (-is), literally “sprung of Nereus”. By surface analysis, Nereus + -id.

parole.significato: In Ancient Greek musical theory, the highest-pitched fixed note in the farther tetrachord on a lyre, always pitched a p…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin nētē, from Ancient Greek νήτη (nḗtē, literally “lowest [string]”). It was "lowest" in the sense of being the farthest from the player and physically below the other strings, but was the highest in pitch. Compare the high E string in a modern guitar, which is farthest f

parole.significato: An acute, severe, intermittent pain that radiates along a nerve.
parole.testo: From New Latin neuralgia, from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”). By surface analysis, neur- + -algia.

parole.significato: A nomad tribe of Scythia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Neurī, from Ancient Greek Νευροί (Neuroí).

parole.significato: A cell of the nervous system, which conducts nerve impulses; consisting of an axon and several dendrites. Neurons are c…
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”), doublet of nerve and sinew. By surface analysis, neuro- + -on.

parole.significato: A puppet; a marionette
parole.testo: From Latin neurospaston, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: An embryo of vertebrates in the stage when the primitive band is first developed.
parole.testo: From New Latin neurula, diminutive in -ula of Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “sinew, tendon, cord”).

parole.significato: A Nicolaitan.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Nicolaita, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek Νικολαΐτης (Nikolaḯtēs), from Νικόλαος (Nikólaos, “Nicolas”); Nicolas of Antioch was associated with the sect, although the word may have come from a different allegorical use of the name.

parole.significato: The study of nests.
parole.testo: From nido- (“nest”) + -logy (“study of”). From Latin nidus + French -logie (“from Latin -logia, from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía)”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Nile or the people who live on its banks.
parole.testo: From Latin Nīlōticus, from Ancient Greek Νειλώτης (Neilṓtēs, “on the Nile”). Analyzable as Nile + -otic.

parole.significato: A gangrenous disease of humans leading to tissue destruction of the face, especially the mouth and cheek.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin noma from Latin nomē from Ancient Greek νομή (nomḗ, “spreading (of sores)”) from νέμω (némō, “feed, devour, spread (of sores)”).

parole.significato: Of an infection or its cause: arising from the environment of, or treatment in, a hospital.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin nosocomīum (“hospital, infirmary”) + English -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Nosocomīum is borrowed from Ancient Greek νοσοκομεῖον (nosokomeîon, “hospital, infirmary”), from νοσοκομέω (nosokoméō, “to tend the sick”) + -εῖον (-eîon, suf

parole.significato: A treatise or written classification of diseases.
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin nosologia, formed as from Ancient Greek νόσος (nósos, “disease”) + Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía, “discourse, branch of knowledge”).

parole.significato: The back (upper surface) of a bird.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin, from Ancient Greek νῶτον (nôton), νῶτος (nôtos, “back”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to coins or money.
parole.testo: From Latin nummarius (“pertaining to money”), from nummus (“a coin, a piece of money”), akin to Ancient Greek νόμος (nómos, “a custom, law”).

parole.significato: A nymph.
parole.testo: From Latin nympha, from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “bride, nymph”). Doublet of nymph.

parole.significato: the European white water lily.
parole.testo: From Latin nymphaea, from Ancient Greek νυμφαῖα (numphaîa), feminine singular form of νυμφαῖος (numphaîos, “sacred to the nymphs”), from νύμφη (númphē, “nymph”). Sense 2 is a semantic loan from translingual Nymphaea, from the same Latin and Greek.

parole.significato: A shrine consecrated to water nymphs, often with a fountain.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nymphaeum, from Ancient Greek νυμφαῖον (numphaîon), a substantivisation of νυμφαῖος (numphaîos, “sacred to the nymphs”), from νύμφη (númphē, “nymph”).

parole.significato: Rapid and excessive involuntary eye movement, usually lateral.
parole.testo: First attested in 1798. From New Latin nystagmus, from Ancient Greek νυσταγμός (nustagmós, “nodding, drowsiness”), from νυστάζω (nustázō, “nod, be sleepy”).

parole.significato: A spring of fresh water, surrounded by a fertile region of vegetation, in a desert.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Oasis, from Ancient Greek Ὄασις (Óasis), from Demotic Egyptian wḥj, from Egyptian wḥꜣt (“oasis, cauldron”), G43-V28-G1-X1:N25 Compare Sahidic Coptic ⲟⲩⲁϩⲉ (ouahe) and Arabic وَاحَة (wāḥa).

parole.significato: A silver coin minted in Ancient Greece, valued at a sixth of a drachma.
parole.testo: From Latin obolus, from Ancient Greek ὀβολός (obolós), from ὀβελός (obelós). Doublet of obole and pul.

parole.significato: Any of the daughters of Oceanus and Tethys; a sea-nymph.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Oceanis, from Ancient Greek Ὠκεανίς (Ōkeanís), from Ὠκεανός (Ōkeanós) + -ις (-is), literally “sprung of Oceanus”. By surface analysis, Oceanus + -id.

parole.significato: A polygon with eight sides and eight angles.
parole.testo: From Latin octagōnon, octōgōnon (“octagon”), and from its etymon Ancient Greek ὀκτάγωνον (oktágōnon, “octagon”), probably from Koine Greek ὀκτάγωνος (oktágōnos, “having eight corners”) + -ον (-on, suffix forming nouns). ὀκτάγωνος is derived from ὀκτᾰ- (oktă-, prefix meaning ‘eight’) (from ὀκτώ (oktṓ

parole.significato: Any of several marine molluscs of the order Octopoda, having no internal or external protective shell or bone (unlike t…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin octōpūs, from Ancient Greek ὀκτώπους (oktṓpous), from ὀκτώ (oktṓ, “eight”) + πούς (poús, “foot”). Piecewise doublet of octopod and octopede.

parole.significato: toothache
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ὀδονταλγία (odontalgía, “toothache”). By surface analysis, odonto- + -algia.

parole.significato: The household common to the individuals of a compound organism.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).

parole.significato: A married priest (chiefly Orthodox Christian and Uniate usage), as opposed to a hieromonk.
parole.testo: From Latin oeconomus, from Ancient Greek οἰκονόμος (oikonómos), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + νόμος (nómos, “law, rule”).

parole.significato: An apartment, room, or hall in an ancient Roman dwelling house.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin oecus, from Ancient Greek οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).

parole.significato: A biting fly of the genus Oestrus; a botfly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin oestrus (“gadfly, sting, frenzy”), from Ancient Greek οἶστρος (oîstros), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eys-, used to form words denoting passion; see also Latin īra (“anger”), Lithuanian aistra (“violent passion”), Avestan 𐬀𐬈𐬯𐬨𐬀 (aesma, “anger”).

parole.significato: A fragile spore produced by some fungi.
parole.testo: From New Latin ōidium, equivalent to Ancient Greek ᾠόν (ōión, “egg”) + -idium.

parole.significato: A gum resin from trees of the genus Boswellia, formerly used as a medicine and now mainly as incense.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin olibanum, from Latin oleum libani, the first word meaning oil and the second from Ancient Greek λίβανος (líbanos, “frankincense (Boswellia sacra)”), from a Semitic source, compare Proto-Semitic *laban- (“white”). Cognate with Biblical Hebrew לְבוֹנָה (l'voná, “frankincen

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to oligarchy.
parole.testo: From Late Latin oligarchicus, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχικός (oligarkhikós). By surface analysis, oligarch + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Mount Olympus, the highest mountain in Greece; or (Greek mythology) the Greek gods and goddesses who…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English Olympyan, from Latin Olympius (“of or relating to Mount Olympus”) and its etymon Ancient Greek Ὀλῠ́μπῐος (Olŭ́mpĭos, “of or relating to Mount Olympus; living on Mount Olympus; Olympian”) + English -an (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘of or pertaining to’, or forming agent

parole.significato: Of or relating to the town of Olympia in Elis, Greece; Olympic.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Olympianus (“Olympic”) + English -an (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘of or pertaining to’, or forming agent nouns). Olympianus is derived from Latin Olympia (“town in Elis, Greece, where the ancient Olympic Games were held”) + -ānus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’); and Oly

parole.significato: A compound eye, found on, for example, insects and crustaceans.
parole.testo: From New Latin ommateum, from Ancient Greek ὄμμα (ómma, “eye”).

parole.significato: The central part of the hilum of a seed, through which the nutrient vessels pass into the raphe or chalaza.
parole.testo: From the post-classical Latin omphalodium from Ancient Greek ὀμφαλοειδής (omphaloeidḗs, “navel-like”) itself from Ancient Greek ὀμφαλός (omphalós, “navel”).

parole.significato: A disease caused by a worm of the genus Onchocerca, especially as transmitted to humans by flies and often causing blin…
parole.testo: From New Latin Onchocerca (a genus of parasitic worms), from Ancient Greek ὄγκος (ónkos, “barb”) + κέρκος (kérkos, “tail”) + -iasis.

parole.significato: Pertaining to tumors.
parole.testo: First attested 1857, from New Latin onco- (“tumor”). from Ancient Greek ὄγκος (ónkos, “lump, mass, bulk”).

parole.significato: Relating to osmotic pressure caused by the presence of colloids.
parole.testo: From New Latin onco- (“tumor”), from Ancient Greek ὄγκος (ónkos, “lump, mass, bulk”) + -tic.

parole.significato: The study of dreams and their interpretation.
parole.testo: From oneiro- + -logy, historically from Latin oneirologia from Ancient Greek ὄνειρος (óneiros, “dream”).

parole.significato: Being the only child of one’s parent (especially one’s father)
parole.testo: From Middle English oonlybigeten, equivalent to only + begotten. Compare also Middle English only geten, oonly geten (“only-begotten”, literally “only-gotten”) and Middle English onbygoten, oon be-gotyn, one bygeten, oon bigetun, oon bigeten (“only-begotten”, literally “one-begotten”). Calque of Lat

parole.significato: A centaur with the body of an ass, instead of a prototypical horse.
parole.testo: Late Latin onocentaurus, from Ancient Greek ὀνοκένταυρος (onokéntauros, from ὄνος (ónos, “ass”) + κένταυρος (kéntauros, “centaur”)).

parole.significato: Worship of the ass or donkey.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin onolatrīa, from the Ancient Greek ὀνολᾰτρείᾱ (onolătreíā), from ὄνος (ónos, “ass”) + λᾰτρείᾱ (lătreíā, “worship”).

parole.significato: The property of a word that sounds like what it represents.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin onomatopoeïa, from Ancient Greek ὀνοματοποιία (onomatopoiía, “the coining of a word in imitation of a sound”), from ὀνοματοποιέω (onomatopoiéō, “to coin names”), from ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”) + ποιέω (poiéō, “to make, to do, to produce”). By surface analysis, onomato- + -poeia.

parole.significato: The branch of metaphysics that addresses the nature or essential characteristics of being and of things that exist; the…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin ontologia (1606, Ogdoas Scholastica, by Jacob Lorhard (Lorhardus)), from Ancient Greek ὤν, ὄντος (ṓn, óntos, “being”), present participle of εἰμί (eimí, “being, existing, essence”) + λόγος (lógos, “account”). By surface analysis, onto- + -logy. First known English us

parole.significato: onyx
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin onychinus, from Ancient Greek ὀνῠ́χῐνος (onŭ́khĭnos).

parole.significato: Nail: Relating to fingernails, toenails, or homologous structures such as claws or hooves.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek ὄνυξ (ónux).

parole.significato: An ovicell of a bryozoan.
parole.testo: From New Latin ōoecium, from Ancient Greek ᾠόν (ōión, “egg”) + οἰκίον (oikíon, “dwelling, abode”). By surface analysis, oo- + oecium.

parole.significato: A spherical granule of which oolite is composed, formed by concentric accretion of thin layers of a mineral (usually ca…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin oolithus; the Latin word was coined by the German doctor and mineralogist Franz Ernst Brückmann (1697–1753) as a translation of German Rogenstein (“oolite”) (Rogen (“fish roe”) + Stein (“stone”)). Oolithus is derived from Ancient Greek ᾠόν (ōión, “egg; seed”) (possibly ultim

parole.significato: Any species of the suborder Serpentes; a snake or serpent.
parole.testo: From Latin ophidia (from Ancient Greek ὄφις (óphis, “snake”)) + -ian.

parole.significato: Any of various rocks having snake-like markings, such as a mottled greenish porphyry.
parole.testo: From Latin ophites, from Ancient Greek ὀφίτης (ophítēs) (Etymology 2, below). Compare Ophite.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the eyes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ophthalmicus, from Ancient Greek ὀφθᾰλμῐκός (ophthălmĭkós, “of or for the eyes”), from ὀφθᾰλμός (ophthălmós, “eye”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, “-ic”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: The middle of the posterior margin of the foramen magnum of the skull.
parole.testo: From New Latin opisthion, from Ancient Greek ὀπίσθιος (opísthios, “rear, behind”), from ὄπισθεν (ópisthen, “at the back, backwards”). By surface analysis, opisth- + -ion.

parole.significato: Sustained tetanic spasm in which the body is bent backwards and stiffened, as produced by various diseases.
parole.testo: From Latin opisthotonus, and its source, Ancient Greek ὀπισθότονος (opisthótonos), corresponding to opistho- + tonus (“muscle tension”).

parole.significato: A gum resin obtained from the root of Opopanax chironium, formerly used in medicine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin opopanax, from Hellenistic Greek ὀποπάναξ (opopánax), from Ancient Greek ὀπός (opós, “vegetable juice”) + πάναξ (pánax, “any of several plants believed to have medicinal benefits”).

parole.significato: The physics of light and vision: basic optical science.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin opticus (“optic, optical”), from Ancient Greek ὀπτικός (optikós), equivalent to optic + -ics.

parole.significato: A large group of musicians who play together on various instruments, usually including some from strings, woodwind, bra…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin orchēstra, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀρχήστρα (orkhḗstra), from ὀρχέομαι (orkhéomai, “to dance”) + -τρᾰ (-tră, “a suffix used to form instrument nouns (pl.)”).

parole.significato: A plant of the orchid family (Orchidaceae), bearing unusually-shaped flowers of beautiful colours.
parole.testo: From New Latin Orchideae, Orchidaceae, an irregular formation from Latin orchis, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis, “orchid, testicle”) (ostensibly from the shape of the roots). Supplanted Middle English ballokwort (literally “testicle plant”).

parole.significato: Synonym of orchiectomy.
parole.testo: From Latin orchis (wrongly interpreting orchid- as the stem), from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis, “orchid, testicle”) + -ectomy.

parole.significato: A procedure for fixation of a testis, often to move an undescended testicle into the scrotum and keep it there.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin orchis + -pexy, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis, “testicle”) + πῆξις (pêxis, “fixing”).

parole.significato: An orchid; now specifically, a plant of the genus Orchis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin orchis, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis, “testicle”).

parole.significato: A mountain nymph; an anthropomorphic appearance of the spirit of a mountain.
parole.testo: From Latin Orēas, Orēadis, from Ancient Greek Ὀρειάς (Oreiás), from ὄρος (óros, “mountain”).

parole.significato: The affective and conative character of mental activity as contrasted with its cognitive aspect; the appetitive aspect…
parole.testo: From Latin orexis (“longing; appetite”), from Ancient Greek ὄρεξις (órexis, “desire”), from ὀρέγω (orégō, “to reach, stretch”).

parole.significato: A type of medieval polyphony which builds upon an existing plainsong.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin organum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon, “organ, instrument, tool”). Doublet of organ, organon, and orgue.

parole.significato: A valuable yellow metal known to the Ancient Greeks and Romans; now sometimes interpreted as referring to a natural all…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin orichalcum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὀρείχαλκος (oreíkhalkos), from dative singular of ὄρος (óros, “mountain”) + χαλκός (khalkós, “copper”).

parole.significato: The branch of zoology that deals with the scientific study of birds.
parole.testo: From New Latin ornithologia, coined by Ulisse Aldrovandi from Ancient Greek ὀρνιθολόγος (ornithológos), from ὄρνις (órnis) and λόγος (lógos). See also ornitho- + -logy.

parole.significato: A person, especially a minor, both or (rarely) one of whose parents have died.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Late Latin orphanus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “without parents, fatherless”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos.  PIE word  *h₃órbʰos Cognate with Sanskrit अर्भ (árbha), Latin orbus (“orphaned”), Old Armenian որբ (orb, “orphan”), Old High German erbi, arbi (Ge

parole.significato: A kind of orphanage in ancient times.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin orphanō̆trophīum, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανοτροφεῖον (orphanotropheîon).

parole.significato: A hospital for orphans.
parole.testo: From Latin orphanō̆trophīa (cf. orphanō̆trophīum, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανοτροφεῖον (orphanotropheîon)), from Ancient Greek ὀρφᾰνός (orphănós, “orphan”) + τροφή (trophḗ, “nourishment, food; nurture, rearing, upbringing”). By surface analysis, orphan + -o- + -trophy.

parole.significato: Of a projection used in maps, architecture etc., in which the rays are parallel.
parole.testo: From ortho- + -graph + -ic. Compare French orthographique, Latin orthographus, Ancient Greek ὀρθογράφος (orthográphos).

parole.significato: Any of several antelopes, of the genus Oryx, native to Africa, which have long, straight horns
parole.testo: From Latin ory̆x, from Ancient Greek ὄρῠξ (órŭx, “a pickax; an oryx (the antelope)”).

parole.significato: One of a pair of scent organs in the larvae of certain swallowtail butterflies.
parole.testo: New Latin, from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ, “smell”), ὀσμητός (osmētós, “smelled”) + -τήριον (-tḗrion).

parole.significato: Any of the armored jawless fishes of the Paleozoic.
parole.testo: From New Latin ostracum, from Ancient Greek ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “pottery fragment; shell”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”).

parole.significato: A fragment of pottery.
parole.testo: From New Latin ostracum, from Ancient Greek ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “pottery fragment; shell”).

parole.significato: earache
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ōtalgia, from Ancient Greek ὠταλγία (ōtalgía).

parole.significato: The basal part of the ovipositor of some species of insects, typically the non-retractile sheath that remains exposed w…
parole.testo: From Latin ovum (“egg”) plus scāpus (“stem or shaft”), from Ancient Greek (Doric) σκᾶπος (skâpos).

parole.significato: Sour milk.
parole.testo: From Latin oxygala, from Ancient Greek ὀξύγαλα (oxúgala).

parole.significato: A mixture of honey, water, and vinegar, boiled to a syrup, sometimes mixed with herbs or spices.
parole.testo: From Middle English oximel, from Late Latin oxymel, oxymeli (“acid and honey”), from Ancient Greek ὀξύμελι (oxúmeli).

parole.significato: A figure of speech in which two words or phrases with opposing meanings are used together intentionally for effect.
parole.testo: First attested in the 17th century, noun use of 5th century Latin oxymōrum (adjective), neut. nom. form of oxymōrus (adjective), from Ancient Greek ὀξύμωρος (oxúmōros), compound of ὀξύς (oxús, “sharp, keen, pointed”) (English oxy-, as in oxygen) + μωρός (mōrós, “dull, stupid, foolish”) (English moro

parole.significato: a fish with a pointed snout
parole.testo: From New Latin oxyrhynchus, from Ancient Greek ὀξῠ́ρρῠγχος (oxŭ́rrhŭnkhos, “a kind of Egyptian fish”) (whence also the place name Ὀξῠ́ρρῠγχος (Oxŭ́rrhŭnkhos), from ὀξῠ́ς (oxŭ́s, “sharp”) + ῥῠ́γχος (rhŭ́nkhos, “snout”).

parole.significato: A genus, Pachysandra, of four or five species of evergreen shrubs or subshrubs, belonging to the boxwood family, Buxace…
parole.testo: From the New Latin genus name, equivalent to English pachy-, from Ancient Greek παχύς (pakhús) [Term?].

parole.significato: A public area in ancient Greece and Rome dedicated to the teaching and practice of wrestling and other sports; a wrestl…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palaestra, from Ancient Greek παλαίστρα (palaístra, “wrestling school”).

parole.significato: A Philistine.
parole.testo: From Latin Palaestinus, from Ancient Greek Παλαιστινὸς (Palaistinòs). Cognate with Middle French palestin, Palestin.

parole.significato: Emphatic repetition of a word or phrase.
parole.testo: From Late Latin palilogia (“palilogy”), from Ancient Greek παλιλογία (palilogía, “palilogy”), from πάλιν (pálin, “again”) + -λογία (-logía, “pertaining to speech, discourse”) or -λόγος (-lógos, “word, speech”).

parole.significato: A manuscript or document that has been erased or scraped clean, for reuse of the paper, parchment, vellum, or other med…
parole.testo: From Latin palimpsēstus, from Ancient Greek παλίμψηστος (palímpsēstos, “scraped again”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Pallas, an epithet of Athena, the goddess of wisdom, and potentially to other female Greek figures su…
parole.testo: From Latin Palladius (“of or relating to Pallas”) + -an (suffix forming adjectives from nouns). Palladius is derived from Pallas (from Ancient Greek Παλλάς (Pallás), genitive Παλλάδος (Palládos), an epithet of Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom) + -ius (suffix forming adjectives from nouns).

parole.significato: A safeguard.
parole.testo: The sense of "safeguard" comes from Latin Palladium (the image of Pallas that protected Troy), from Ancient Greek Παλλάδιον (Palládion), from Παλλάς (Pallás), an epithet used before Athena.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to ancient Palmyra or Palmyrena.
parole.testo: From Latin Palmȳrēnus, from Ancient Greek Παλμυρηνός (Palmurēnós). By surface analysis, Palmyra + -ene.

parole.significato: A remedy believed to cure all disease and prolong life that was originally sought by alchemists; a cure-all.
parole.testo: From Latin panacēa, from Ancient Greek πανάκεια (panákeia), from πανακής (panakḗs, “all-healing”), from πᾶν (pân, “all”) (equivalent to English pan-) + ἄκος (ákos, “cure”).

parole.significato: Synonym of pankration.
parole.testo: From Latin pancratium, from Ancient Greek παγκράτιον (pankrátion, “a complete contest”). Doublet of pankration.

parole.significato: A gland near the stomach which secretes a fluid into the duodenum to assist with food digestion.
parole.testo: Existing in English since the sixteenth century: from Latin pancreas, from Ancient Greek πάγκρεας (pánkreas), from πᾶν (pân, “all”) (equivalent to English pan-) + κρέας (kréas, “flesh”).

parole.significato: A person who furthers the illicit love affairs of others; a pimp or procurer, especially when male.
parole.testo: From Chaucer’s character Pandare (in Troilus and Criseyde), from Italian Pandaro (found in Boccaccio), from Latin Pandarus, from Ancient Greek Πάνδαρος (Pándaros). (See also Shakespeare’s Troilus and Cressida.)

parole.significato: Usually in the plural form Pandects: a compendium or digest of writings on Roman law divided in 50 books, compiled in t…
parole.testo: Sense 3 (“comprehensive treatise”) is from Latin pandectēs (“book that contains everything, encyclopedia”), from Ancient Greek πανδέκτης (pandéktēs, “encyclopedia”, literally “all-receiver”), from παν- (pan-, prefix meaning ‘all’) (from πᾶς (pâs, “all”)) + δέκτης (déktēs, “receiver, recipient”) (fro

parole.significato: An Ancient Greek stringed instrument, a kind of lute with three strings that were stopped with a fingerboard to alter t…
parole.testo: From Late Latin pandura, from Ancient Greek πανδοῦρα (pandoûra), a Pre-Greek/substrate loan. Doublet of mandola.

parole.significato: A compound raceme.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pānicula, diminutive of pānus (“ear of millet, literally 'thread wound on a bobbin'”), from Ancient Greek πῆνος (pênos, “web”), πηνίον (pēníon, “bobbin”). Doublet of panocha.

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to panmixia.
parole.testo: From New Latin panmicticus, from Ancient Greek παν- (pan-, “every, all”) + μίξις (míxis, “mixing, mingling”) + Latin -ia.

parole.significato: A situation in which an individual is just as likely to mate with a randomly chosen individual as any other in the popu…
parole.testo: From New Latin panmixia, from Ancient Greek παν- (pan-, “every, all”) + μίξις (míxis, “mixing, mingling”) + Latin -ia.

parole.significato: Panmixia.
parole.testo: From New Latin panmixis, from Ancient Greek παν- (pan-, “every, all”) + μίξις (míxis, “mixing, mingling”).

parole.significato: Uttering ominous or prophetic voices; divining.
parole.testo: From Latin panomphaeus, borrowed from Ancient Greek πανομφαῖος (panomphaîos).

parole.significato: A Classical comic actor, especially one who works mainly through gesture and mime.
parole.testo: First appears c. 1606, from Latin pantomīmus, from Ancient Greek παντόμιμος (pantómimos), from πᾶς (pâs, “each, all”) + μιμέομαι (miméomai, “to mimic”). The verbal form first appears c. 1768.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the pope or the papacy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pāpa, from Ancient Greek πάππας (páppas).

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Paphos, the mythical birthplace of the goddess of love on the island of Cyprus.
parole.testo: From Latin Paphius [from Ancient Greek Πάφιος (Páphios), from Πάφος (Páphos, “Paphos”) + -ιος (-ios)] + English -an.

parole.significato: The markedly reduced sepals of an Asteraceae floret that take the form of trichomes or scale attached to the ovary or s…
parole.testo: Via Latin pappus from Ancient Greek πάππος (páppos), an affectionate term for elderly men (referencing beards).

parole.significato: A plant (Cyperus papyrus) in the sedge family, native to the Nile river valley, paper reed.
parole.testo: From Middle English papirus, borrowed from Latin papȳrus, from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros), of unknown origin. Doublet of papyros.

parole.significato: The conic section formed by the intersection of a cone with a plane parallel to a tangent plane to the cone; the locus…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ), from παραβάλλω (parabállō, “to set side by side”), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”). Doublet of parable, parole, and palaver.

parole.significato: A pattern, a way of doing something; especially a pattern of thought, a system of beliefs, a conceptual framework.
parole.testo: From Middle English paradygme, from Late Latin paradīgma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma, “pattern”), from παραδείκνυμι (paradeíknumi, “I show [beside] or compare”) + -μα (-ma, suffix forming nouns concerning the results of actions). Doublet of paradigma.

parole.significato: A written pattern of inflection for parts of speech, especially organized into a tabular form.
parole.testo: From Late Latin paradīgma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma, “pattern”). As a loanword in both languages, paradigma typically maintains the Greek plural form in both Latin and English. Doublet of paradigm.

parole.significato: One of the two lobes forming the lower lip, or metastoma, of Crustacea.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin paragnathus, from para- + Ancient Greek γνάθος (gnáthos, “jaw”). Compare earlier paragnatha.

parole.significato: The addition of a sound, syllable or letter to the end of a word, either through natural development or as a grammatica…
parole.testo: From Late Latin paragoge, from Ancient Greek παραγωγή (paragōgḗ, “derivation, addition”).

parole.significato: A play on words; a pun.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin paragramma, from Ancient Greek παράγραμμα (parágramma).

parole.significato: coastal; native to the coast
parole.testo: From Latin paralius, from Ancient Greek παράλιος (parálios, “coastal, maritime”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to parallax
parole.testo: From New Latin parallacticus, from Ancient Greek παραλλακτικός (parallaktikós).

parole.significato: A solid figure, having six faces, all parallelograms, all opposite faces being similar and parallel.
parole.testo: From Latin parallēlepipedum, from Ancient Greek παραλληλεπίπεδος (parallēlepípedos, “with parallel surfaces”), from παράλληλος (parállēlos, “parallel”) + ἐπίπεδος (epípedos, “plane”).

parole.significato: A convex quadrilateral in which each pair of opposite edges are parallel and of equal length.
parole.testo: From Latin parallelogrammum, from Ancient Greek παράλληλος (parállēlos, “parallel”) + γραμμή (grammḗ, “line”).

parole.significato: A parallelopiped.
parole.testo: From New Latin parallelopipedon, alteration of Ancient Greek παραλληλεπίπεδος (parallēlepípedos, “with parallel surfaces”), from παράλληλος (parállēlos, “parallel”) + ἐπίπεδος (epípedos, “plane”).

parole.significato: The complete loss of voluntary control of part of a living body, such as one or more limbs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin paralysis, from Ancient Greek παράλυσις (parálusis, “palsy”), from παραλύω (paralúō, “to disable on one side”). By surface analysis, para- + -lysis. Doublet of palsy.

parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin paramesē, from Ancient Greek παραμέση (paramésē, literally “next to the middle [string]”).

parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin paranētē, from Ancient Greek παρανήτη (paranḗtē, literally “next to the lowest [string]”). parole.significato: An engraved tablet, usually of brass, set up in a public place.
parole.testo: Latin parapegma, Ancient Greek παράπηγμα (parápēgma) to fix beside: compare French parapegme.

parole.significato: A device for keeping track of cyclical events, particularly of stars, weather, seasons, and so on.
parole.testo: From Latin parapegma, from Ancient Greek παράπηγμα (parápēgma, “something fixed on or hung up”) .

parole.significato: A woman's property which was not made a part of her marriage dower, but remained her own.
parole.testo: From Late Latin parapherna, from Ancient Greek παράφερνα (parápherna, “things additional to a dowry”), from παρα- (para-, “beside”) + φερνή (phernḗ, “dowry”). parole.significato: The practice of paraphrasing: use of different words.
parole.testo: From Latin paraphrasis, from Ancient Greek παράφρασις (paráphrasis). Compare periphrasis.

parole.significato: A condition where the lower half of a patient's body is paralyzed and cannot move.
parole.testo: From New Latin paraplegia, from Ancient Greek παραπληγίη (paraplēgíē), Ionic Greek for παραπληξία (paraplēxía, “paralysis on one side”), from παραπλήσσεσθαι (paraplḗssesthai, “to be stricken on one side”), active παραπλήσσειν (paraplḗssein, “to strike on one side”), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + πλήσ

parole.significato: One of two apartments adjoining the ancient stage, probably used as dressing rooms.
parole.testo: New Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: The day of preparation before the (Jewish) Sabbath; Friday.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin parascevē, from Ancient Greek παρασκευή (paraskeuḗ, literally “preparation”).

parole.significato: A long ceremonial dagger from Roman times.
parole.testo: From Latin parazonium, from Ancient Greek παραζόνιον (parazónion).

parole.significato: A pard; a panther or leopard.
parole.testo: From Latin pardalis, from Ancient Greek πάρδαλις (párdalis), from an unattested Old Iranian word; compare Persian پلنگ (palang), Pashto پړانګ (pṙâng).

parole.significato: The study of proverbs.
parole.testo: From paremia (“proverb”) + -ology, from Latin paroemia, from Ancient Greek παροιμία (paroimía).

parole.significato: A clause, phrase or word which is inserted (usually for explanation or amplification) into a passage which is already g…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin parenthesis (“addition of a letter to a syllable in a word”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek παρένθεσις (parénthesis, “insertion”). By surface analysis, par- + en- + thesis.

parole.significato: Using, containing, or within parenthesis.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin parentheticus (from Late Latin parenthesis or Ancient Greek παρένθετος (parénthetos), + -icus) + -al. By surface analysis, par- + en- + thetical.

parole.significato: Something unimportant, incidental, or superfluous; a trifle
parole.testo: Latin parergon, Ancient Greek πάρεργον (párergon); παρά (pará, “beside”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”).

parole.significato: A paralysis which is incomplete or which occurs in isolated areas.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek πάρεσις (páresis, “letting go, paralysis”), from παρίημι (paríēmi, “relax”), from παρα- (para-) + ἵημι (híēmi, “let go”).

parole.significato: Synonym of sun dog (“a bright spot in the sky, usually one of two on the parhelic circle on both sides of the sun (or o…
parole.testo: From Latin parelion, from Ancient Greek παρήλιον (parḗlion), from παρά (pará) + ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Greek musical theory, the lower-pitched of the two movable notes in the nearer tetrachord on a lyre, pitched…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin parhypatē, from Ancient Greek παρυπάτη (parupátē, literally “next to the hypate, next-highest”). parole.significato: Of or relating to Parnassus, as the source of literary (especially poetic) inspiration; (hence) of or belonging to poet…
parole.testo: From Parnassus, from Latin Parnassus, from Ancient Greek Παρνασσός (Parnassós).

parole.significato: A work or performance that imitates another work or performance with ridicule or irony.
parole.testo: From Latin parōdia, from Ancient Greek παρῳδία (parōidía, “parody”), from παρά (pará, “besides”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).

parole.significato: A proverb.
parole.testo: From Latin paroemia (“proverb”), from Ancient Greek παροιμία (paroimía, “proverb”).

parole.significato: A pun or play on words.
parole.testo: From Latin paronomasia, from Ancient Greek παρονομασία (paronomasía, “play upon words which sound alike”), from παρα- (para-) + ὀνομασία (onomasía, “naming”).

parole.significato: The people of Paropamisus in ancient Pakistan.
parole.testo: From Latin Paropamisadae, from Ancient Greek Παροπαμισάδαι (Paropamisádai), from Old Persian *Para-uparisaina (“beyond higher than the eagle”).

parole.significato: A Parthian.
parole.testo: From Latin Parthus, from Ancient Greek Πάρθος (Párthos).

parole.significato: Passover (biblical, Israelite, Jewish, or Christian Passover; this term also includes Quartodeciman Passover, observed…
parole.testo: From Latin pascha (“Passover”), from Ancient Greek πάσχα (páskha, “Passover”), from Aramaic פַּסְחָא (paskha), from Hebrew פֶּסַח (pésakh). Doublet of Pasch, paska, paskha, and Pesach.

parole.significato: A type of lesser priest in ancient Egypt, originally serving as a doorkeeper to a temple.
parole.testo: From Latin pastophorus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek παστοφόρος (pastophóros), from παστός (pastós, “ceremonial curtain”) + -φόρος (-phóros, “bearer”), a loose calque of Demotic Egyptian jrj-ꜥꜣ, from Egyptian jrj-ꜥꜣ (“doorkeeper”), from jrj (“keeper”) + ꜥꜣ (“door”). parole.significato: The thin membrane that extends between the limbs and body of a bat or of gliding mammals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin patagīum (“gilded edging of a woman's tunic”), from an unattested Ancient Greek παταγεῖον (patageîon), perhaps from πάταγος (pátagos, “clatter”).

parole.significato: Synonym of bottom: a passive usually-male partner in homosexual anal intercourse.
parole.testo: From Latin pathicus, from Ancient Greek παθικός (pathikós), from πάθος (páthos, “suffering, feeling”), from πάσχω (páskhō, “to feel, to suffer”).

parole.significato: Related to how emotions are manifested, especially in the face.
parole.testo: From Latin pathognomicus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek παθογνωμικός (pathognōmikós), shortened form of παθογνωμονικός (pathognōmonikós, “pathognomonic”).

parole.significato: Having traits mostly inherited from the male parent
parole.testo: From Latin pātr- + -o- + Ancient Greek κλίνειν (klínein) + -ous.

parole.significato: The hiatus between prosodic units, e.g. at the end of a sentence.
parole.testo: From Latin pausa (“break”), from Ancient Greek παῦσις (paûsis). Doublet of pause.

parole.significato: Any of certain plants of the family Fabaceae: Pisum sativum and others.
parole.testo: Back-formation from pease, an original singular reinterpreted as a plural. Further from Middle English pese (“a pea”), from Old English pise, from Latin pisa, pisum, from Ancient Greek πίσον (píson).

parole.significato: Pathology of the foot.
parole.testo: Formed as pedo- (“foot”) + -pathy (“disease”); an etymological hybrid equivalent to the Latin pēs (“foot”) + the Ancient Greek πάθος (páthos, “suffering”).

parole.significato: Any winged horse; a pterippus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the open sea.
parole.testo: From Latin pelagius [from Ancient Greek πελάγιος (pelágios), from πέλαγος (pélagos) + -ιος (-ios)] + -an.

parole.significato: Living in the open sea rather than in coastal or inland waters.
parole.testo: From Latin pelagicus (and possibly pelagus); from Ancient Greek πελαγικός (pelagikós), from πέλαγος (pélagos, “sea”). By surface analysis, -pelag + -ic.

parole.significato: Any of the extinct crocodile-like animals of genus †Pelagosaurus which lived during the Jurassic period.
parole.testo: From Latin pelagus from Ancient Greek πελαγικός (pelagikós), from πέλαγος (pélagos, “sea”) + -saur.

parole.significato: Any of various seabirds of the family Pelecanidae, having a long bill with a distendable pouch.
parole.testo: From Middle English pellican, pellicane, from Old English pellican (“pelican”), from Latin pelecānus, from Ancient Greek πελεκάν (pelekán), πέλεκυς (pélekus, “hatchet”).

parole.significato: A circumscribed, elevated, livid patch on the skin.
parole.testo: From Latin pelidnoma, from Ancient Greek πελίδνωμα (pelídnōma, “dark spot”).

parole.significato: A small shield, especially one of an approximately elliptical form, or crescent-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin pelta, from Ancient Greek πέλτη (péltē, “shield”).

parole.significato: A noun having five cases.
parole.testo: From Latin pentaptōtum, from Ancient Greek πεντάπτωτος (pentáptōtos).

parole.significato: Government by five persons.
parole.testo: From Late Latin pentarchia, from Ancient Greek πενταρχίᾱ (pentarkhíā), from πεντα- (penta-, “penta-, five”) + -αρχίᾱ (-arkhíā, “-archy, rule”), perhaps via Middle French pentarchie. Equivalent to pent- + -archy.

parole.significato: The commander of a platoon of fifty men.
parole.testo: From Latin pentēcontarchus, from Ancient Greek πεντηκόνταρχος (pentēkóntarkhos, literally “commander of fifty”).

parole.significato: A military unit commanded by a pentecontarch.
parole.testo: From Latin pentēcontarchia, from Ancient Greek πεντηκονταρχία (pentēkontarkhía). By surface analysis, pentecontarch + -y.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Mount Pentelicus (Penteliko Mountain), near Athens, famous for its fine white marble quarries.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Pentelicus, from Ancient Greek Πεντελικός (Pentelikós).

parole.significato: A prosal group of two and a half feet.
parole.testo: From Latin penthēmimeris, from Ancient Greek πενθημιμερής (penthēmimerḗs, “having five half-feet”): πέντε (pénte, “five”) + ἡμι- (hēmi-) + μέρος (méros, “part, metrical foot”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Peperomia, some of which are popular houseplants.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin peperomia, from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi, “pepper”) + ὅμοιος (hómoios, “similar, like”).

parole.significato: A peplos, an Ancient Greek garment formed of a tubular piece of cloth folded back upon itself halfway down so that the…
parole.testo: From Latin peplum, from Ancient Greek πέπλον (péplon), accusative singular of πέπλος (péplos).

parole.significato: An upper garment worn by women in Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A fruit of plants of the gourd family Cucurbitaceae, possessing a hard rind and producing many seeds in a single, centr…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pepō, from Ancient Greek πέπων (pépōn, “large melon”), from πέπων (pépōn, “ripe”), from πέπτω (péptō, “ripen”). Doublet of pumpion; compare pumpkin.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, capable of, or aiding digestion.
parole.testo: From Latin pepticus, from Ancient Greek πέψις (pépsis, “digestion”), a form of πέσσω (péssō).

parole.significato: A number that is the sum of all of its divisors except itself.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin numerus perfectus, with this use of perfectus itself a semantic loan from Ancient Greek τέλειος (téleios).

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Pergamum.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Pergamēnus or its etymon Ancient Greek Περγαμηνός (Pergamēnós). By surface analysis, Pergam(um) + ene.

parole.significato: A section of text forming a coherent thought, suitable for use in a speech.
parole.testo: From Late Latin pericope, from Ancient Greek περικοπή (perikopḗ, “section”), from περι- (peri-, “across”) + κοπή (kopḗ, “cutting”), from κόπτω (kóptō, “I cut”).

parole.significato: The membrane (or periosteum) which covers the outer surface of the skull.
parole.testo: From late Latin pericranium, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek περικράνιον (perikránion), noun use of the neuter form of περικράνιος (perikránios, “around the skull”), from περί (perí, “around”) + κρανίον (kraníon, “skull”).

parole.significato: The outer layer that covers the spore-bearing organ in many fungi.
parole.testo: A New Latin form of Ancient Greek πηρίδιον (pērídion, “little pouch”).

parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin perigynium, from peri- + Ancient Greek γῠνή (gŭnḗ, “woman”) + -ium.

parole.significato: The point in the elliptical orbit of a comet, planet, etc., where it is nearest to the Sun.

parole.significato: The sum of the distance of all the lengths of the sides of an object.
parole.testo: From Latin perimetros, Ancient Greek περίμετρος (perímetros). Equivalent to peri- + meter.

parole.significato: The outer serosa layer of the uterus.
parole.testo: From peri- + Late Latin metrium (“womb”), from Ancient Greek μήτριον (mḗtrion, “of a mother”).

parole.significato: The region between the genitalia and anus.

parole.significato: Someone living on the same latitude as someone else, but on a different or opposite side of the world; one's antithesis.
parole.testo: From Late Latin perioeci, from Ancient Greek περίοικοι (períoikoi), plural of περίοικος (períoikos, “neighbour”), from περι- (peri-, “peri-”) + οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).

parole.significato: A sudden reversal of fortune as a plot point in Classical tragedy.
parole.testo: From Late Latin peripetia, and its source Ancient Greek περιπέτεια (peripéteia), from περιπίπτω (peripíptō, “to change suddenly”), from περί (perí, “round, around, about”) + the stem of πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”).

parole.significato: The use of more words than are necessary to express the idea; a roundabout, or indirect, way of speaking; circumlocutio…
parole.testo: From Latin periphrasis from Ancient Greek περίφρασις (períphrasis), from περιφράζομαι (periphrázomai, “to consider all sides of an issue”), from περί (perí, “around”) + φράζω (phrázō, “to show, point out”). See phrase.

parole.significato: An account of a voyage, particularly those of Hanno and Arrian, recording ports and coastal landmarks.
parole.testo: From Latin periplūs (“account of a voyage”) and Ancient Greek περίπλους (períplous, “voyage, naval manouver, account of a voyage”), from περί (perí, “peri-: around”) + πλοῦς (ploûs, “voyage”), from πλεῖν (pleîn, “to sail”). Cf. French périple, Spanish periplo, & Italian periplo.

parole.significato: pneumonic (of or pertaining to pneumonia (an inflammation of the lungs))

parole.significato: Superfluity of words; verbosity; long-windedness.

parole.significato: The herb vervain (Verbena officinalis).
parole.testo: From Late Latin peristerion, from Ancient Greek περιστέριον (peristérion).

parole.significato: In mammals, the serous membrane lining the cavity of the abdomen and that is folded over the viscera.

parole.significato: A mollusk of family Littorinidae.

parole.significato: A loincloth worn by men and women in ancient Greece.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin perizoma. from Ancient Greek περίζωμα (perízōma).

parole.significato: A descendant of Perseus.

parole.significato: Any of the meteors in a meteor shower that appears to come from the constellation Perseus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Persēis f, from Ancient Greek Περσηΐς f (Persēḯs), from Περσεύς (Perseús) + -ις (-is). By surface analysis, Perseus + -id.

parole.significato: Synonym of Persian.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Persicus, from Ancient Greek Περσικός (Persikós), from Πέρσης (Pérsēs, “Persian”, noun) + -ικός (-ikós, adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: One of the scales of a leaf bud.
parole.testo: From Latin pērula, diminutive of pera (“wallet”), from Ancient Greek πήρα (pḗra). Compare French pérule.

parole.significato: A petal.
parole.testo: From New Latin petalum, from Ancient Greek πέταλον (pétalon), from πέταλος (pétalos, “broad, flat”), from Proto-Hellenic *pétalos, from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to spread out”). Doublet of petal.

parole.significato: A large broad-rimmed bell used for summoning monks.
parole.testo: From Latin petasius, from Ancient Greek πέτασος (pétasos, “petasus: a broad-brimmed hat”).

parole.significato: Any flying marsupial of the order Phalangeriformes, such as those in genera Petaurista, Phalanger, Acrobates.
parole.testo: From Latin petaurista (“a ropedancer, acrobat”), from Ancient Greek πετευριστής (peteuristḗs), from πετευρίζομαι (peteurízomai, “dance on a rope”), from πέτευρον (péteuron, “a pole, a stage for ropedancers”).

parole.significato: radiotelephony clear-code word for the letter P.
parole.testo: From Middle English Peter, from Old English Petrus, from Latin Petrus, from Ancient Greek Πέτρος (Pétros), from πέτρος (pétros, “stone, rock”). Doublet of Pedro, Piers, and Boutros.

parole.significato: The logical fallacy of begging the question (i.e., "assuming the conclusion").
parole.testo: From Latin petītiō prīncipiī (literally “an assumption from the beginning”), calque of Ancient Greek τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ αἰτεῖσθαι (tò en arkhēî aiteîsthai, “to assume from the beginning”).

parole.significato: Petrifying; converting into stone.
parole.testo: Latin petra (“rock, stone”), from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: stone
parole.testo: * From Latin petra (“stone, rock”), from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, “stone, rock”). * Clipping of petroleum.

parole.significato: Spreading, obstinate ulceration.
parole.testo: From Latin phagedaena, from Ancient Greek φᾰγέδαινα (phăgédaina, “cancerous sore, canker”).

parole.significato: An ancient Greek and Macedonian military unit that consisted of several ranks and files (lines) of soldiers in close ar…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phalanx or Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx, “battle order; array”). Doublet of phalange, planch, plancha, planche, and plank.

parole.significato: Any of three small wading birds in the genus Phalaropus, of the family Scolopacidae, that have lobed toes.
parole.testo: From New Latin Phalaropus, formed irregularly from Ancient Greek φαλαρίς (phalarís, “coot”) + πούς (poús, “foot”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Greece, a metal medallion worn by men or used to ornament the harness of a horse.
parole.testo: From Latin phalerae, from Ancient Greek φάλαρα (phálara) (plural of φάλαρον (phálaron)).

parole.significato: Phallic priest thought to have been a precursor of the Christian stylite.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phallobatēs, from Ancient Greek φαλλοβάτης (phallobátēs, literally “phallus-climber”). Doublet of phallobate (derived via the Latin adapted form phallobata; compare English stylobate).

parole.significato: The person who carries the phallus in a phallophoria
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phallophorus, from Ancient Greek φαλλοφόρος (phallophóros). By surface analysis, phallo- + -phorus.

parole.significato: A penis, especially when erect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phallus (“membrum virile, phallus, or a figure thereof”), from Ancient Greek φαλλός (phallós).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Pharisees.
parole.testo: From Latin Pharisaicus, from Ancient Greek Φαρισαϊκός (Pharisaïkós). By surface analysis, Pharisee + -ic.

parole.significato: A member of an ancient Jewish political party, a social movement, and a school of thought among Jews that flourished du…
parole.testo: From Latin Pharisaeus, from Ancient Greek Φαρισαῖος (Pharisaîos), a transliteration of Aramaic פְּרִישַׁיָּא (pərîšayyâ’), emphatic plural of פְּרִישׁ (pərîš, “separatist”, literally “separated”), related to Hebrew פרוש (parush), qal passive participle of the verb פָּרַשׁ (pāraš), meaning one who is

parole.significato: pharmaceutical
parole.testo: From Latin pharmaceuticus (“of drugs”), from Ancient Greek φαρμακευτικός (pharmakeutikós, “drug maker”).

parole.significato: Synonym of quack: a peddler of fraudulent medicines and cures.
parole.testo: From Latin pharmacopola, from Ancient Greek φαρμακοπώλης (pharmakopṓlēs), from φάρμακον (phármakon, “drug, charm, enchantment”) + -πώλης (-pṓlēs, “-seller, -monger”). Doublet of pharmacopolist.

parole.significato: Synonym of pharmacist: a person who sells medicine, an apothecary.
parole.testo: From Latin pharmacopola + -ist, from Ancient Greek φαρμακοπώλης (pharmakopṓlēs), from φάρμακον (phármakon, “drug, charm, enchantment”) + -πώλης (-pṓlēs, “-seller, -monger”). Cf. papyropolist. Doublet of pharmacopole.

parole.significato: The study of lighthouses or other forms of light-signalling.
parole.testo: From Latin Pharos or its source Ancient Greek Φάρος (Pháros) + -logy.

parole.significato: Forms terms relating to the pharynx.
parole.testo: From New Latin pharynx, from Ancient Greek φάρυγξ (phárunx, “throat”), akin to modern Greek φάρυγγας (fáryngas, “pharynx”).

parole.significato: The part of the alimentary canal and respiratory tract that extends from the back of the mouth and nasal cavity to the…
parole.testo: Borrowing from New Latin pharynx, from Ancient Greek φᾰ́ρῠγξ (phắrŭnx, “throat”).

parole.significato: A distinguishable part of a sequence or cycle occurring over time.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin phasis, borrowed from Ancient Greek φάσις (phásis, “appearance”), from φᾰ(ν)- (phă(n)-, root of φαίνω (phaínō, “to bring to light; to appear”)) + -σῐς (-sĭs). Compare phantasm and see face.

parole.significato: The French bean, or kidney bean.
parole.testo: From Latin phaselus, phaseolus, from Ancient Greek φάσηλος (phásēlos, “a kind of bean”). Compare French phaséole, faséole, English fesels.

parole.significato: any of several domesticated beans, of the genus Phaseolus, native to the Americas
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phaseolus.

parole.significato: A phase (of the moon, a planet etc.).
parole.testo: From Late Latin phasis, or its source, Ancient Greek φάσις (phásis, “appearance”).

parole.significato: An apparition; a phantom.
parole.testo: From Latin phasma or Ancient Greek φάσμα (phásma). See phase.

parole.significato: Any of a series of dioctahedral micas of composition K(AlMg)₂(OH)₂(SiAl)₄O₁₀, similar to muscovite but with addition of…
parole.testo: From Latin phengites, from Ancient Greek φέγγος (phéngos). Doublet of fengite.

parole.significato: A thing or being, event or process, perceptible through senses; or a fact or occurrence thereof.
parole.testo: From Late Latin phaenomenon (“appearance”), from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, “thing appearing to view”), neuter present middle participle of φαίνω (phaínō, “I show”).

parole.significato: Consisting of three prosodic feet, normally a spondee, dactyl, and spondee (or trochee), but admitting of some variatio…
parole.testo: From Latin Pherecratēus, by-form of Pherecratīus, from Ancient Greek Φερεκρᾰ́τειος (Pherekrắteios), from Φερεκρᾰ́της (Pherekrắtēs, “Pherecrates”), the name of the metre’s inventor.

parole.significato: Φ, the 21st letter of the Euclidean and modern Greek alphabet, usually romanized as "ph".
parole.testo: From Late Latin phi, from Ancient Greek φεῖ (pheî).

parole.significato: Benevolent altruism with the intention of increasing the well-being of humankind.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin philanthrōpia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpía). By surface analysis, phil- + -anthropy.

parole.significato: Any of the discourses of Demosthenes against Philip II of Macedon, defending the liberty of Athens.
parole.testo: From Latin philippicus, from Ancient Greek φιλιππικός (philippikós), from Φίλιππος (Phílippos, “lover of horses”), from φίλος (phílos, “loving”) + ἵππος (híppos, “horse”).

parole.significato: Any of several climbing plants, of the genus Philodendron, native to America and the West Indies that are often grown a…
parole.testo: From New Latin philodendron, from Ancient Greek φῐλόδενδρον (phĭlódendron), neuter of φῐλόδενδρος (phĭlódendros, “loving trees”). First known use: 1877.

parole.significato: The humanistic study of texts and their languages, especially ancient or classical languages.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Philologie, from Latin philologia, from Ancient Greek φιλολογίᾱ (philologíā, “love of argument or reasoning, love of learning and literature”).

parole.significato: The shallow vertical groove running from the nasal septum to the center of the upper lip.
parole.testo: Borrowed from the Latin philtrum (“a love potion”), from Ancient Greek φῐ́λτρον (phĭ́ltron, “a love charm; the dimple in the upper lip”). Doublet of philter.

parole.significato: An inflammation, especially of the internal organs.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek φλεγμᾰσία (phlegmăsía, “inflammation”), from φλέγμα (phlégma, “flame”) (whence also phlegm).

parole.significato: A solid mass formed by inflamed connective tissue, such as forms around an appendix in appendicitis.
parole.testo: From Latin phlegmōn, phlegmonē (“inflammation beneath the skin”), from Ancient Greek φλεγμονή (phlegmonḗ, “inflammation, fiery heat”), from φλέγω (phlégō, “burn”).

parole.significato: The hypothetical fiery principle formerly assumed to be a necessary constituent of combustible bodies and to be given u…
parole.testo: From New Latin phlogiston, coined by Georg Ernst Stahl in 1702, from Ancient Greek φλογιστόν (phlogistón), neuter of φλογιστός (phlogistós, “burnt up, inflammable”), from φλογίζω (phlogízō, “to set fire to”), from φλόξ (phlóx, “flame”).

parole.significato: Any flowering plant of the genus Phlox.
parole.testo: From New Latin Phlox, from Ancient Greek φλόξ (phlóx, “flame”).

parole.significato: An irrational, abnormal, or obsessive fear (of something).
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1790, from words ending in -phobia, ultimately from Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”). Compare ism, from -ism, itis, from -itis, and ana, from -ana.

parole.significato: A seal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phōca, from Ancient Greek φώκη (phṓkē).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the ancient Greek region of Phocis.
parole.testo: From Latin Phōcis (itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Φωκίς (Phōkís)) + -an.

parole.significato: Pertaining to true seals (also known as earless seals, as opposed to eared seals such as sea lions); seallike.
parole.testo: From Latin phōca (“seal”) (from Ancient Greek φώκη (phṓkē)) + -ine.

parole.significato: Relating to the sounds of spoken language.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phōnēticus, from Ancient Greek φωνητῐκός (phōnētĭkós). By surface analysis, phone + -etic.

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol P) with an atomic number of 15, that exists in several allotropic forms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phōsphorus, from Ancient Greek φωσφόρος (phōsphóros, “the bearer of light”), from φῶς (phôs, “light”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry”).

parole.significato: divination using light
parole.testo: From photo- (“light”) + -mancy (“divination of”), from Latin -mantia, ultimately from Ancient Greek μᾰντείᾱ (mănteíā, “divination”).

parole.significato: Any of several perennial reeds, of the genus Phragmites, found in wetlands.
parole.testo: From Latin phragmītēs, from Ancient Greek φραγμίτης (phragmítēs).

parole.significato: A short written or spoken expression.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”), from φράζω (phrázō, “to tell, express”).

parole.significato: A clan or kinship group consisting of a number of families claiming descent from a common ancestor and having certain c…
parole.testo: PIE word  *bʰréh₂tēr From Latin phrātria, from Ancient Greek φρατρία (phratría, “tribe, clan”), from φράτηρ (phrátēr) + -ία (-ía).

parole.significato: phrenitis
parole.testo: From Latin phrenesis, from Ancient Greek *φρένησις (*phrénēsis), a later equivalent of φρενῖτις (phrenîtis, “inflammation of the brain”). Doublet of frenzy.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the diaphragm
parole.testo: From New Latin phrenicus, from Ancient Greek φρήν (phrḗn, “diaphragm”).

parole.significato: Madness, especially as caused by inflammation of the brain; encephalitis, encephalomeningitis, or meningitis.
parole.testo: From Latin phrenītis, from Ancient Greek φρενῖτις (phrenîtis), from φρήν (phrḗn, “mind”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Phrygia, its people, or their culture.
