parole.testo: From Latin Phrygiānus + English -an (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Phrygianus is derived from Phrygia + -ānus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’); and Phrygia is from Ancient Greek Φρῠγῐ́ᾱ (Phrŭgĭ́ā, “region in Anatolia”), from Φρῠ́ξ (Phrŭ́x, “person from Phrygia”) (fu

parole.significato: An infestation by pubic lice (Pthirus pubis).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin phthīriāsis, from Ancient Greek φθειρίασις (phtheiríasis).

parole.significato: phthisic
parole.testo: From Latin phthisicus, from Ancient Greek: compare French phthisique. See phthisis.

parole.significato: An atrophy of the body or part of the body, especially pulmonary tuberculosis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phthisis, from Ancient Greek φθίσις (phthísis, “consumption, decline, wasting away”), from φθίω (phthíō, “to waste away”).

parole.significato: The ruler of a phyle in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Latin phylarchus, from Ancient Greek φύλαρχος (phúlarkhos), from φῡλή (phūlḗ, “large clan or tribe of ancient Greece”).

parole.significato: A local division of the people; a clan or tribe.
parole.testo: From New Latin phȳlē, from Ancient Greek φῡλή (phūlḗ, “a union of individuals into a community”).

parole.significato: A flattened petiole or leaf rachis that resembles and functions as a leaf, and may or may not be combined with an actua…
parole.testo: From Latin phyllodium, from Ancient Greek φυλλώδης (phullṓdēs, “resembling a leaf”).

parole.significato: phyllode
parole.testo: From New Latin phyllōdium, from Ancient Greek φυλλώδης (phullṓdēs, “leaflike”).

parole.significato: A leaf, or something (flat) resembling a leaf.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phyllon, from Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”). Doublet of phyllo, distantly also with foil, folio, and folium.

parole.significato: All of the organisms descending from a given common ancestor, regarded as a race, tribe, vel sim.; a clade.
parole.testo: From Late Latin phȳlon (a synonym of tribus, whence the English tribe), from Ancient Greek φῦλον (phûlon, “race, tribe”), whence the English phylum.

parole.significato: A rank in the classification of organisms, below kingdom and above class; also called a divisio or a division, especial…
parole.testo: From Latin phylum, from Ancient Greek φῦλον (phûlon, “tribe, race”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Physalis.
parole.testo: From New Latin Physalis, coined by Linnaeus from Ancient Greek φυσαλλίς (phusallís, “bladder, wind instrument”), from φυσιόω (phusióō, “to puff up, blow up”), φυσώ (phusṓ).

parole.significato: Relating to or concerning existent materials; physical.
parole.testo: From Middle English phisik, from Latin physicus, from Ancient Greek φῠσῐκός (phŭsĭkós, “natural; physical”), from φύσις (phúsis, “origin, birth; nature, quality; form, shape; type, kind”), from φῠ́ω (phŭ́ō, “grow”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to appear, become, rise up”).

parole.significato: Of medicine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin physicālis, from Latin physica (“study of nature”), from Ancient Greek φυσική (phusikḗ), feminine singular of φυσικός (phusikós, “natural; physical”), from φύσις (phúsis, “origin, birth; nature, quality; form, shape; type, kind”), from φῠ́ω (phŭ́ō, “grow”), ultimately from P

parole.significato: Any of the genus Phytolacca of herbaceous plants; the poke or pokeweed.
parole.testo: From New Latin phytolacca, from Ancient Greek φῠτόν (phŭtón, “plant”) + Italian lacca (“crimson lake”).

parole.significato: A plant-like animal; a zoophyte.
parole.testo: From phyto- + zoon, from New Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: The powder of aloes with canella, formerly officinal, employed as a cathartic.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin picra, from Ancient Greek πίκρα (píkra, “a kind of antidote”), from πικρός (pikrós, “sharp, bitter”).

parole.significato: The symbol ¶.
parole.testo: Probably an alteration of Middle English pylcrafte, modification of Late Latin paragraphus, itself from the Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos).

parole.significato: An art gallery, especially one exhibiting pictures.
parole.testo: From Latin pinacotheca, from Ancient Greek πινακοθήκη (pinakothḗkē).

parole.significato: A tablet or register.
parole.testo: From Latin pinax, from Ancient Greek πίναξ (pínax, “tablet”).

parole.significato: A small crab of the genus Pinnotheres, which live symbiotically in the shells of certain molluscs.
parole.testo: From Latin pīnotērēs, from Ancient Greek πινοτήρης (pinotḗrēs), from Ancient Greek πίνη (pínē, “pen shell”) + Ancient Greek τηρέω (tēréō, “to guard”).

parole.significato: Robbery at sea, a violation of international law; taking a ship away from the control of those who are legally entitled…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pīrātia, from Classical Latin pīrāta + ia, or Ancient Greek πειρατεία (peirateía). The sense of “unauthorized duplication” developed in England between 1660 and 1710. The English Crown granted strict monopolies over book printing to specific guilds, such as the Stationers’ Compan

parole.significato: Babesia, a genus of hematozoa that invades the red blood cells of humans and domesticated animals such as dogs and sheep
parole.testo: From Latin pirum (“pear”) + Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma, “image, formation”).

parole.significato: Someone with a Pisces astrological sign.
parole.testo: From Latin piscēs, the nominative plural of piscis (“fish”), calque of Ancient Greek ἰχθύες (ikhthúes, “fish (pl); name of constellation”). Compare Akkadian 𒁺𒉺𒉺 (DU.NU.NU, “fish-cord”); the constellation is often depicted as two fish tied by a ribbon.

parole.significato: A soft, black, tarry bitumen, intermediate between petroleum and asphalt.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pissasphaltus, from Ancient Greek πισσάσφαλτος (pissásphaltos), from πίσσα (píssa, “pitch”) + ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos, “asphalt”).

parole.significato: Having faith; trusting
parole.testo: From Latin pisticus (“pure; genuine”), from Ancient Greek πιστικός (pistikós).

parole.significato: Designating a mode lying a perfect fourth below the authentic form.
parole.testo: From Late Latin plagalis, from plaga, from plagius, from Byzantine Ancient Greek πλάγιος (plágios, “plagal”), πλάγιος (plágios, “oblique”).

parole.significato: Slanted, oblique.
parole.testo: From Late Latin plagio-, from Ancient Greek πλάγιος (plágios, “oblique”).

parole.significato: Membership of a particular planet or moon, by origin, birth, naturalization, ownership, allegiance or otherwise.
parole.testo: From planet + -ality from Latin planeta, planetes, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to planets; planetary.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin planeticus, from Ancient Greek πλανητικός (planētikós), from πλανητός (planētós, “wandering; planetary”), from πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer, planet”), from πλανάω (planáō, “to wander”) + -της (-tēs, masculine agent noun suffix).

parole.significato: Protoplasm.
parole.testo: From Late Latin plasma (“mold”) or Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma, “something formed”), in some cases via German Plasma or French plasme, like English plasma.

parole.significato: A state of matter consisting of partially ionized gas and electrons.
parole.testo: From Late Latin plasma (“mold”), from Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma, “something formed”).

parole.significato: A procedure in which whole blood is removed from a donor or patient and centrifuged to isolate blood cells that are res…
parole.testo: From New Latin plasma + Ancient Greek ἀφαίρεσις (aphaíresis, “removal”).

parole.significato: A synthetic, solid, hydrocarbon-based polymer, whether thermoplastic or thermosetting.
parole.testo: From Latin plasticus (“of molding”), from Ancient Greek πλαστικός (plastikós), from πλάσσω (plássō, “to mold, form”). Doublet of plastique.

parole.significato: A semiaquatic monotreme from eastern Australia with a bill resembling that of a duck, that has a mole-like body, a tail…
parole.testo: From New Latin Platypus (originally a genus name already in use for a type of beetle), from Ancient Greek πλατύπους (platúpous, “flat-footed”), from πλατύς (platús, “flat”) + πούς (poús, “foot”). Piecewise doublet of flatfoot.

parole.significato: A superficial muscle of the human neck that overlaps the sternocleidomastoid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin platysma, from Ancient Greek πλᾰ́τῠσμᾰ (plắtŭsmă, “flat object”), from πλᾰτῠ́νω (plătŭ́nō, “widen”) + -μᾰ (-mă, “nominal suffix”).

parole.significato: A small piece of plastic, metal, ivory, etc., for plucking the strings of a guitar, lyre, mandolin, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin plēctrum, from Ancient Greek πλῆκτρον (plêktron, “anything to strike with, an instrument for striking the lyre, a spear point”), from πλήσσειν (plḗssein, “to strike, to smite, to sting”). Displaced native Old English sleġel.

parole.significato: Redundancy in wording.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin pleonasmus, from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós), from πλεονάζω (pleonázō, “to be superfluous”), from πλείων (pleíōn, “more”).

parole.significato: An excessive amount or number; an abundance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin plēthōra, from Ancient Greek πληθώρα (plēthṓra, “fullness, satiety”), from πλήθω (plḗthō, “to be full”) + -η (-ē, nominal suffix).

parole.significato: Suffering from plethora; ruddy in complexion, congested or swollen with blood.
parole.testo: From Late Latin plethoricus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πληθωρικός (plēthōrikós), from πληθώρα (plēthṓra, “plethora”). By surface analysis, plethora + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the pleura; pleural.
parole.testo: From Latin pleura. By surface analysis, pleur- + -o-.

parole.significato: A figure of speech in which a word is repeated so as not only to signify the individual thing denoted by it, but also i…
parole.testo: From Latin plŏcē, from Ancient Greek πλοκή (plokḗ, “complication”).

parole.significato: Any specific edition of a work by Plutarch, often specifically Plutarch's Lives
parole.testo: Via Latin Plūtarchus from Ancient Greek Πλούτᾰρχος (Ploútărkhos).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Pluto, the Greek and Roman god of the underworld; demonic, infernal.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Latin Plūtōnius (“of or relating to Pluto, Greek and Roman god of the underworld”) + -an (suffix forming adjectives). Plūtōnius is from Ancient Greek Πλουτώνιος (Ploutṓnios, “of or relating to Pluto”), from Πλούτων (Ploútōn, “Pluto”) (from πλοῦτος (ploûtos, “riches, wea

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or resembling air or other gases
parole.testo: From Latin pneumaticus, from Ancient Greek πνευματικός (pneumatikós, “relating to wind or air”), from πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, air, breath, spirit”), from πνέω (pnéō, “to blow, breath”).

parole.significato: The study of the respiratory system and organs.
parole.testo: From New Latin pneumologia, from Ancient Greek πνεύμων (pneúmōn, “lung”) + -logia (“-logy”). By surface analysis, pneumo- + -logy.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to the lungs; pulmonary.
parole.testo: From the post-Classical Latin pneumonicus and its etymon, the Ancient Greek πνευμονικός (pneumonikós).

parole.significato: A nocturnal monster in Ancient Greece that would choke its victims; incubus; nightmare.
parole.testo: From New Latin pnīgalion, from Ancient Greek πνῑγαλίων (pnīgalíōn, “nightmare”), from πνῑ́γω (pnī́gō, “to throttle, strangle”).

parole.significato: Any grass of the genus Poa, especially Poa annua.
parole.testo: From scientific Latin Poa (genus name), from Ancient Greek πόα (póa, “fodder”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to gout.
parole.testo: From Latin podagricus, from Ancient Greek ποδαγρικός (podagrikós, “gouty”).

parole.significato: A stalk which bears the fructification in some lichens, such as the reindeer moss.
parole.testo: From New Latin podetium, from Ancient Greek πούς (poús, “foot”).

parole.significato: A platform on which to stand, as when conducting an orchestra or preaching at a pulpit; any low platform or dais.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin podium, from Ancient Greek πόδιον (pódion, “base”), a diminutive of πούς (poús, “foot”). Doublet of pew.

parole.significato: The study of poesy or poetry.
parole.testo: From Latin poēsis [itself from Ancient Greek ποίησις (poíēsis)] + -logy.

parole.significato: The military commander-in-chief in Athens, one of the nine archonts.
parole.testo: From Latin polemarchus, from Ancient Greek πολέμαρχος (polémarkhos). By surface analysis, polem- + -arch.

parole.significato: Government that is in some manner chosen by the governed citizens.
parole.testo: From Latin politicus, from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós), from πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”) + -cracy.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the role of citizens in the organization and choice of government.
parole.testo: From Latin politicus, from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós), from πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”) + -cratic.

parole.significato: A state of many rulers, many leaders.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “many”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “beginning”).

parole.significato: long-lasting; chronic.
parole.testo: From Late Latin polychronius (“long-lived”), from Ancient Greek πολῠχρόνῐος (polŭkhrónĭos, “long-lived”).

parole.significato: The condition of having more than one spouse or marriage partner at one time.
parole.testo: Recorded since 1591, from Late Latin polygamia, from Ancient Greek πολυγαμία (polugamía), itself from πολύγαμος (polúgamos, “married to many”), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + γάμος (gámos, “marriage”). Relates to modern prefix and suffix poly- + -gamy.

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Polygonum, especially knotgrass.
parole.testo: From Latin polygonium, from Ancient Greek πολύγονον (polúgonon). More at polygonum.

parole.significato: A solid figure with many flat faces and straight edges.
parole.testo: From New Latin polyedron, from Ancient Greek πολύεδρος (polúedros, “having many seats”), from πολυ- (polu-, “many”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”); compare French polyèdre. By surface analysis, poly- + -hedron.

parole.significato: Someone gifted or learned to a great extent or in multiple disciplines; a great scholar.
parole.testo: From Latin polyhistor (“very learned”), from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πολυΐστωρ (poluḯstōr, “greatly learned”).

parole.significato: Having, or assuming, a variety of forms, characters, or styles
parole.testo: From New Latin polymorphus, from Ancient Greek πολύμορφος (polúmorphos, “multiform, manifold”), from πολυ- (polu-, “many, much”) + μορφή (morphḗ, “form, shape”). By surface analysis, poly- + -morphous.

parole.significato: A cylindrical coelenterate, such as the hydra, having a mouth surrounded with tentacles.
parole.testo: From Latin polypus (“a polyp, a polypus in the nose”), from Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous, from πολύς (polús, “many”) + πούς (poús, “foot”)). Doublet of polypus.

parole.significato: Synonym of polypody: any fern of the genus Polypodium.
parole.testo: From Late Latin polypodium, from Ancient Greek πολυπόδιον (polupódion), from πολυ- (polu-, “poly-, many”) + πούς (poús, “-pod, foot”) + -ιον (-ion, “-ium”). Later reinforced by the translingual scientific use of Polypodium.

parole.significato: A stylistic scheme in which words from the same root are used together, or a word is repeated in a different inflection…
parole.testo: Via Latin, from Ancient Greek πολύπτωτον (polúptōton), neuter of πολύπτωτος (polúptōtos, “having many cases”), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”).

parole.significato: A medical phenomenon.
parole.testo: From Latin polypus, from Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous). Doublet of polyp.

parole.significato: Synonym of polysemic.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin polysēmus, from Ancient Greek πολύσημος (polúsēmos), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + σημαίνω (sēmaínō, “I signify, mean”).

parole.significato: A machine consisting of many pulleys
parole.testo: From Latin polyspaston (“hoisting-tackle with many pulleys”), from Ancient Greek πολύσπαστον (polúspaston, “compound pulley”).

parole.significato: dyshidrosis eczema
parole.testo: From Latin pompholyx, from Ancient Greek πομφόλυξ (pomphólux, “a bubble; the slag on the surface of smelted ore”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to kingdom of Pontus.
parole.testo: From Latin ponticus, from Ancient Greek Ποντῐκός (Pontĭkós), from Πόντος (Póntos, “Black Sea, Pontus”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic: forming adjectives”). Equivalent to Pontus + -ic. Doublet of bonduc and bundook.

parole.significato: An honorific title given to a son of a reigning emperor in the Byzantine Empire, notably borne by Constantine VII Porph…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin porphyrogenitus, from Ancient Greek πορφυρογέννητος (porphurogénnētos, literally “born in the purple”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a type of Ancient Greek wine.
parole.testo: Latin Pramnium, from Ancient Greek Πράμνιος (Prámnios).

parole.significato: A variety of cryptocrystalline of a green colour.
parole.testo: From Latin prasius, from Ancient Greek πράσιος (prásios, “of a green colour”), from πράσον (práson, “leek”).

parole.significato: Of a clear, light green color.
parole.testo: From Latin prasinus, from Ancient Greek πρᾰ́σῐνος (prắsĭnos, “leek-green, light green”).

parole.significato: The practical application of any branch of learning.
parole.testo: Partly from Latin prāxis and partly from its etymon Ancient Greek πρᾶξις (prâxis, “action, activity, practice”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or of the nature of a preposition.
parole.testo: From Latin praepositiō (“a setting before, a preposition”), a calque of Ancient Greek πρόθεσις (próthesis, “a setting before, preposition (grammar)”) + -al.

parole.significato: Inability of the eye, due to ageing, to focus on nearby objects.
parole.testo: From New Latin presbyōpia, from Ancient Greek πρέσβυς (présbus, “old man”), and New Latin -ōpia (“vision problem”), from Ancient Greek ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”). By surface analysis, presby- + -opia.

parole.significato: An elder, priest, pastor, or minister in various Christian churches.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros), from πρέσβυς (présbus, “elder, older”). Doublet of prester and priest.

parole.significato: The home of a Roman Catholic parish priest.
parole.testo: From Middle English presbetory, presbytory (“part of church reserved for clergy”), from Late Latin presbyterium (“group of presbyters, part of church reserved for clergy”), from Ancient Greek πρεσβῠτέρῐον (presbŭtérĭon, “group of presbyters”), from πρεσβῠ́τερος (presbŭ́teros, “elder, priest”) + -ῐον

parole.significato: A waterspout.
parole.testo: From New Latin prēstēr, from Ancient Greek πρηστήρ (prēstḗr, “hurricane or waterspout attended with lightning; (in plural) veins of the neck when swollen by anger”).

parole.significato: A potentially painful or harmful medical condition in which the erect penis does not return to its flaccid state (despi…
parole.testo: From Latin priapismus, from Priapus (“the god of procreation, the penis”) + -ism, from Ancient Greek πριαπισμός (priapismós).

parole.significato: A religious clergyman (clergywoman, clergyperson) who is trained to perform services or sacrifices at a church or templ…
parole.testo: From Middle English prest, preest, from Old English prēost (“priest”), from Late Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros), from πρέσβυς (présbus, “elder, older”). Reinforced in Middle English by Old French prestre, also from Latin presbyter. Doublet of presbyter and prester. * T

parole.significato: A polyhedron with parallel ends of the same polygonal shape and size, the other faces being parallelogram-shaped sides.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin prisma (“(geometry) prism”), from Ancient Greek πρίσμᾰ (prísmă, “anything sawn; sawdust; (Koine, geometry) prism”), from πρῐ́ζω (prĭ́zō) (a variant of πρῑ́ω (prī́ō, “to saw”), further etymology unknown) + -μᾰ (-mă, suffix forming neuter nouns denoting the effect or

parole.significato: An elongated tube from the head or connected to the mouth, of an animal.
parole.testo: From Latin proboscis, from Ancient Greek προβοσκίς (proboskís, “elephant's trunk”) literally "means for taking food," from προ- (pro-, “before”) + βόσκω (bóskō, “to nourish, feed”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *gʷeh₃- from which also comes βοτάνη (botánē, “grass, fodder”).

parole.significato: A rhetorical exercise in which the speaker raises an objection to his own argument and then immediately answers it, in…
parole.testo: From Latin procatalepsis (“anticipating and answering an objection”), from Ancient Greek προκατάληψις (prokatálēpsis, “seizing in advance”).

parole.significato: A metrical foot consisting of four short syllables.
parole.testo: From Latin proceleusmaticus, from Ancient Greek προκελευσματικός (prokeleusmatikós), to rouse to action beforehand, to incite.

parole.significato: Synonym of apheresis.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin procopē, via Ancient Greek προκοπή (prokopḗ) from verb προκόπτω (prokóptō, “to cut away in front; forward, advance”), προ- (pro-, “before; in front”) + κόπτω (kóptō, “to cut”).

parole.significato: Synonym of proem.
parole.testo: From Latin prooemium, from Ancient Greek προοίμιον (prooímion).

parole.significato: The addition of a leap day to the lunar calendar.
parole.testo: From New Latin proemptōsis, from Ancient Greek προ- (pro-, “before”) + ἔμπτωσις (émptōsis, “falling”).

parole.significato: A forecast of the future course or outcome of a situation based on what is presently known; a prediction.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin prognōsis (“forecast, prediction; forecast of the course and outcome of a disease”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πρόγνωσις (prógnōsis, “forecast of the course and outcome of a disease; (Koine) foreknowledge, perceiving beforehand, prediction”), from προ- (pro

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to or characterized by prognosis or prediction.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prognosticus, from Ancient Greek προγνωστικός (prognōstikós, “foreknowing”), from πρό (pró) + γνωστικός (gnōstikós, “of or for knowing, good at knowing”), from γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to learn to know, to perceive, to mark, to learn”).

parole.significato: To predict or forecast, especially through the application of skill.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prognosticare; see prognostic for more.

parole.significato: The assignment of something to a period of time that precedes it.
parole.testo: From Latin prolepsis, from Ancient Greek πρόληψις (prólēpsis, “preconception, anticipation”), from προλαμβάνω (prolambánō, “take beforehand, anticipate”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Prometheus, a demigod in Greek mythology who created mortals from clay and stole fire from Zeus to…
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Prometheus (“demigod in Greek mythology”) + -an (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives; and forming agent nouns). Prometheus is a learned borrowing from Latin Promētheus, and from its etymon Ancient Greek Προμηθεύς (Promētheús), from προμηθής (promēthḗ

parole.significato: Being the product of two consecutive integers.
parole.testo: Apparently from New Latin pronicus, a misspelling of Latin promicus, from Ancient Greek προμήκης (promḗkēs, “elongated, oblong”), but the spelling has been pronic from its earliest known occurrence in English (Leonhard Euler, Opera Omnia, series 1, volume 15).

parole.significato: A medicine which preserves or defends against disease; a preventive.
parole.testo: From Latin prophylacticus, from Ancient Greek προφυλακτικός (prophulaktikós, “prophylactic”).

parole.significato: The prevention of, or the protective treatment for, disease.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek πρό (pró, “before”) + φύλαξις (phúlaxis, “a watching, guarding”).

parole.significato: To pledge; to offer as a toast in the manner of drinking, that is, by drinking first and passing the cup.
parole.testo: From Latin propinō, from Ancient Greek προπῑ́νω (propī́nō, “to drink to someone's health”).

parole.significato: An aromatic glue-like substance produced by honeybees from tree resin, waxes, and their own secretions, used in the con…
parole.testo: From Latin propolis, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πρόπολις (própolis, “suburb; propolis”) (apparently because the material was used by bees to extend their hives), from Ancient Greek προ- (pro-, “pro-”) + πόλις (pólis, “city”).

parole.significato: A vestibule or entrance, (especially) to a temple.
parole.testo: From Latin propylaeum, from Ancient Greek προπύλαιον (propúlaion), from προ- (pro-, “before”, “in front of”) + πύλη (púlē, “gate”).

parole.significato: The stage area between the curtain and the orchestra.
parole.testo: From Latin proscaenium (“in front of the scenery”), from Ancient Greek προσκήνιον (proskḗnion), from πρό (pró, “before”) + σκηνή (skēnḗ, “scene building”).

parole.significato: An early larval form of a trematode worm; a redia.
parole.testo: From New Latin proscōlēx, from Ancient Greek προ- (pro-) + σκώληξ (skṓlēx).

parole.significato: A study of the individuals in a group of people within a specific context and their relationships.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting New Latin combining forms: prosopo- + -graphy; from the Latin prosōpographia (“description of a person’s appearance; description of an individual’s life”), from the Ancient Greek πρόσωπον (prósōpon, “face, person”) + -γρᾰφῐ́ᾱ (-grăphĭ́ā, “writing,

parole.significato: An artificial replacement for a body part, either internal or external.
parole.testo: Via Latin, from Ancient Greek πρόσθεσις (prósthesis, “addition”), from προστίθημι (prostíthēmi, “to add”), from πρός (prós, “towards”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to place”), from Proto-Indo-European *próti, *préti + *dʰédʰeh₁ti (“to be putting, to be placing”). By surface analysis, prosth- + -esis.

parole.significato: Artificial, acting as a substitute for part of the body; relating to prosthesis.
parole.testo: From New Latin prostheticus, from Ancient Greek προσθετικός (prosthetikós, “adding; repletive; giving additional power”), from πρόσθεσις (prósthesis, “addition”), from προστίθημι (prostíthēmi, “I add”), from πρός (prós, “towards”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “I place”). By surface analysis, prosth- + -etic.

parole.significato: The first part of a play, in which the setting and characters are introduced.
parole.testo: From Late Latin protasis, from Ancient Greek πρότασις (prótasis), from προτείνω (proteínō, “put forward, tender, propose”), from πρό (pró) + τείνω (teínō, “stretch”).

parole.significato: A plant, usually a pteridophyte, in gametophyte stage in the metagenesis cycle.
parole.testo: From Latin pro (“forwards”) + Ancient Greek θᾰλλός (thăllós, “young branch, twig”).

parole.significato: The prepending of phonemes at the beginning of a word without changing its morphological structure, as in Spanish esfer…
parole.testo: From Late Latin prothesis, prosthesis, alteration (dropping the ‘s’) from Ancient Greek πρόσθεσις (prósthesis, “addition, augmentation”), (English prosthesis) from προστίθημι (prostíthēmi, “to add”), from πρός (prós, “towards”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to place”), from Proto-Indo-European *próti, *préti

parole.significato: A negotiator; a factor, especially one who negotiates marriages.
parole.testo: Latin proxeneta, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: The town hall in an Ancient Greek city.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prytanēum, from Ancient Greek πρυτανεῖον (prutaneîon), from πρύτανις (prútanis, “prytanis”) + -εῖον (-eîon, noun-forming suffix meaning “place or building associated with a specific purpose or person”). By surface analysis, prytanis + -eum.

parole.significato: An official in ancient Athens
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prytanis, from Ancient Greek πρύτανις (prútanis).

parole.significato: An omasum.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin psalterium, from Ancient Greek ψαλτήριον (psaltḗrion). Doublet of psalter, psalterion, and psaltery.

parole.significato: A psephism.
parole.testo: From Latin psēphisma, and its source, Ancient Greek ψήφισμα (psḗphisma).

parole.significato: Divination by drawing pebbles from a pile.
parole.testo: From New Latin psēphomantia, from Ancient Greek ψῆφος (psêphos, “pebble used for casting a vote”), + -mancy.

parole.significato: A false pregnancy: the appearance of signs and symptoms associated with pregnancy when the person or animal is not preg…
parole.testo: From pseudo- + cyesis, from Latin pseudo- + Ancient Greek κύησις (kúēsis).

parole.significato: A pathological liar
parole.testo: From Latin pseudologus (“liar”), from Ancient Greek ψευδολόγος (pseudológos, “speaking falsely, lying”). Equivalent to pseudo- + -logue.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a pseudonym.
parole.testo: From Latin pseudōnymus, from Ancient Greek ψευδώνῠμος (pseudṓnŭmos). By surface analysis, pseudonym + -ous.

parole.significato: The twenty-third letter of Classical and Modern Greek and the twenty-fifth letter of Old and Ancient Greek.
parole.testo: From Middle English psi, from Latin psī, from Ancient Greek ψεῖ (pseî), the name for the twenty-third letter of the alphabet (Ψ, ψ).

parole.significato: Parrot.
parole.testo: From Latin psittacus (“parrot”), from Ancient Greek ψιττακός (psittakós).

parole.significato: A cutaneous disease, especially psoriasis, scabies, or mange.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin psōra, from Ancient Greek ψώρα (psṓra).

parole.significato: The human soul, mind, or spirit.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin psychē, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”).

parole.significato: A spirit, deity, person, etc., who guides the souls of the dead to the afterlife.
parole.testo: From Latin psȳchopompus, from Ancient Greek ψῡχοπομπός (psūkhopompós), from ψῡχή (psūkhḗ, “soul”) + πομπός (pompós, “conductor”).

parole.significato: Any of several plants of Plantago subg. Psyllium.
parole.testo: From Latin psyllium, from Ancient Greek ψύλλιον (psúllion, “fleawort”), from ψύλλα (psúlla, “flea”) + -ιον (-ion, forming neuter diminutives).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to or lying in the region of the inferior part of the sphenoid bone of the vertebrate skull.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin pterygoīdēs, from Ancient Greek πτερῠγοειδής (pterŭgoeidḗs, “like a wing”), from πτέρῠξ (ptérŭx, “a wing”) + -ο- (-o-) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-like, -oid”).

parole.significato: The appearance or study of feathers on a bird, including factors such as their texture or shape.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin ptilōsis, from the Ancient Greek πτῐ́λωσῐς (ptĭ́lōsĭs).

parole.significato: The way in which an individual leaf is folded in the bud.
parole.testo: From New Latin ptyxis, from Ancient Greek πτύξις (ptúxis, “a folding”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to ancient Carthage, its inhabitants, or their language.
parole.testo: From Latin Pūnicus, variant of Poenicus, from Poenus + -icus, from Ancient Greek Φοῖνιξ (Phoînix), from Mycenaean Greek 𐀡𐀛𐀑𐀍 (po-ni-ki-jo) under influence from φοινός (phoinós, “crimson red”) owing to its relation to Tyrian purple, apparently from or cognate with Egyptian fnḫw (“Asiatics, Semites”),

parole.significato: Of a purple hue.
parole.testo: From Middle English purple, purpel, from Old English purpul (“purple”, adjective), taken from Old English purpure (“purple colour”, noun), from Latin purpura (“purple dye, shellfish”), from Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra, “purple-fish”), perhaps of Semitic origin. Doublet of purpura and purpure. Th

parole.significato: Pertaining to or affected with purpura (skin discoloration from blood inside it).
parole.testo: From Latin purpura (“purple”), from Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra). The medical sense is from the English purpura (“the appearance of purple discolorations on the skin”). By surface analysis, purpura + -ic.

parole.significato: An unidentified large animal with horns, possibly the addax, mentioned in the Bible (Deuteronomy 14:5) as one of the an…
parole.testo: From Latin pygargus from Ancient Greek πύγαργος (púgargos), a compound of Ancient Greek πῡγή (pūgḗ, “rump”) + ἀργός (argós, “white”).

parole.significato: A member of various legendary races of dwarfs, or supernatural peoples of diminutive stature.
parole.testo: From Latin Pygmaeī, from Ancient Greek πυγμαῖος (pugmaîos, “a member of a legendary race of dwarves”), from πυγμή (pugmḗ, “fist (as small as a fist)”). In Ancient Greek, first mentioned by Homer; only applied to actual human races in the 19th century.

parole.significato: The passage between the iter and optocoele in the brain.
parole.testo: From New Latin pyla, from Ancient Greek πύλη (púlē, “gate, entrance”).

parole.significato: pylorus
parole.testo: From Latin pylōrus, from Ancient Greek πυλωρός (pulōrós, “gatekeeper”), from πύλη (púlē, “door, gate”) + οὖρος (oûros, “guard”) + -o-.

parole.significato: In vertebrates, including humans, a zone at the lower end of the stomach that leads to and opens into the duodenum.
parole.testo: From Latin pylōrus, from Ancient Greek πυλωρός (pulōrós, “gatekeeper”).

parole.significato: pus
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek πύον (púon, “pus”), from Proto-Indo-European *puH-; compare Sanskrit पूयति (pūyati, “stinks, rots”), Ancient Greek πύθω (púthō, “to rot”), Gothic 𐍆𐌿𐌻𐍃 (fuls, “foul”), Old English ful (“foul”).

parole.significato: A pyramid.
parole.testo: From Middle English piramis, from Latin pȳramis, from Ancient Greek πυραμίς (puramís).

parole.significato: A funeral pile; a combustible heap on which corpses are burned.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pyra (“pyre, funeral pile”), from Ancient Greek πυρά (purá), from πῦρ (pûr, “fire”). Doublet of fire.

parole.significato: An ancient Persian temple devoted to fire.
parole.testo: From Late Latin pyreum, from Ancient Greek πυρεῖον (pureîon).

parole.significato: A nutlet resembling a seed, or the stone of a drupe, comprising the endocarp and the kernel.
parole.testo: From New Latin pyrēna, from Ancient Greek πῡρήν (pūrḗn, “fruit-stone”).

parole.significato: Any of several daisy-like perennial African plants of the genus Tanacetum, especially Tanacetum cinerariifolium.
parole.testo: From Old English pyretre, from (and later reformed after) Latin pyrethrum (in Pliny), from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πύρεθρον (púrethron).

parole.significato: Caused by, pertaining to or resulting in fever.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin pyreticus, from Ancient Greek πυρετικός (puretikós, “febrile”), from πυρετός (puretós, “fever”), from πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).

parole.significato: Fever.
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin pyrexia, from Ancient Greek πυρεξία (purexía, “feverishness”), from πυρετός (puretós, “fever”).

parole.significato: Fire, heat.
parole.testo: From Latin pyr, from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).

parole.significato: A variety of garnet, of a poppy or blood-red color, frequently with a tinge of orange. It is used as a gemstone.
parole.testo: From Latin pyrōpus, from Ancient Greek πυρωπός (purōpós, “fiery-eyed, fire-colored”), from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”); compare French pyrope.

parole.significato: Of or relating to fireworks.
parole.testo: From Latin pyrotechnica, from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) + τεχνικός (tekhnikós, “skillful, workmanlike”). Analyzable as pyro- + technic.

parole.significato: A yellowish organic keto acid, 2-oxopropanoic acid, which occurs as an intermediate in many metabolic processes, especi…
parole.testo: From New Latin acidum pyruvicum, from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) + ūva (“grape”) + -icum (neuter singular of -icus), from its being produced by the dry distillation of racemic acid, originally derived from grapes. By surface analysis, pyr(e) + Latin uv(a) + -ic.

parole.significato: Pythagorean.
parole.testo: From Latin Pȳthagoricus, from Ancient Greek Πυθαγορικός (Puthagorikós), from Πυθαγόρας (Puthagóras, “Pythagoras”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Delphi or to its priestess, Pythia.
parole.testo: From Latin Pythius, from Ancient Greek πύθιος (púthios, “belonging to Pytho, the older name of Delphi and its environs”): compare French pythien.

parole.significato: Any of the family Pythonidae of nonvenomous constrictor snakes.
parole.testo: From Latin pȳthon, from Ancient Greek Πύθων (Púthōn), the name of the mythological enormous serpent at Delphi slain by Apollo, probably from Πυθώ (Puthṓ), older name of Delphi.

parole.significato: The priestess of the oracle of Apollo at Delphi.
parole.testo: From Late Latin pythonissa, from Ancient Greek Πυθία (Puthía). Compare Pythia.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to, or resembling, a python (“large constricting snake of the family Pythonidae”); pythonlike.
parole.testo: From python (“snake of the family Pythonidae”) + -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives from nouns). Python is derived from Latin Pȳthōn, from Ancient Greek Πῡ́θων (Pū́thōn, “Python, mythical serpent which lived at Delphi”), from Πῡθώ (Pūthṓ, “Pytho, ancient name of Delphi; Pyt

parole.significato: A seed capsule in the form of a box, the seeds being released when the top splits off.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek πυξίδιον (puxídion), diminutive of πῠξῐ́ς (pŭxĭ́s, “box”).

parole.significato: “quod erat faciendum”, “what was to have been done” – used to end a mathematical passage other than a proof.
parole.testo: From Latin quod erat faciendum (“what was to have been done”), from Ancient Greek ὅπερ ἔδει ποιῆσαι (hóper édei poiêsai).

parole.significato: Of, related to, or suffering from quadriplegia.
parole.testo: From quadri- (of Latin origins) and -plegic, from Ancient Greek πλήσσειν (plḗssein, “to strike”); probably patterned after paraplegic from the Ancient Greek παραπληγή (paraplēgḗ, “the paralysis of half of the body”).

parole.significato: which was to be proved; which was to be demonstrated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin quod erat dēmōnstrandum (“that which was to be proved”), calqued from Ancient Greek ὅπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι (hóper édei deîxai, “precisely what was required to be proved”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Rachel sandwich.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin Rāchēl, from Ancient Greek Ῥαχήλ (Rhakhḗl), from Biblical Hebrew רָחֵל (rāḫēl, “ewe”). Doublet of Raquel.

parole.significato: The spinal column, or the vertebrae of the spine.
parole.testo: From New Latin rhachis/rachis, from Ancient Greek ῥάχις (rhákhis, “spine, ridge”).

parole.significato: radish (especially the root of the plant)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin raphanus, from Ancient Greek ῥάφανος (rháphanos).

parole.significato: A seamlike ridge or furrow on an organ, bodily tissue, or other structure, typically marking the line where two halves…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin raphē, from Ancient Greek ῥᾰφή (rhăphḗ, “seam; suture”).

parole.significato: “Right reason”, which regards virtue as desirable in itself.
parole.testo: First attested in an English text in 1677; borrowed from Latin rēcta ratiō (“right reason”), a calque of Ancient Greek ὀρθὸς λόγος (orthòs lógos). Cf. Cicero, De leg. I, 7, I, 2: “Recta ratio - quae cum sit lex, lege quoque consociati homines cum diis putandi sumus.” Term used in a letter to "Tom" b

parole.significato: A great quantity of blood.
parole.testo: From Middle English Red See, Reede See, Rede See, reade sea, from Old English Rēad Sǣ, a calque of Latin Mare Rubrum, itself a calque of Ancient Greek Ἐρυθρᾱ̀ θάλασσα (Eruthrā̀ thálassa); equivalent to red + sea.

parole.significato: A fear or hatred of religion, religious faith, religious people or religious organizations.
parole.testo: From Latin religiō (“moral obligation, worship”) and Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: Divination with wands or rods, especially to use a divining rod to find things below the ground.
parole.testo: From rhabdo- + -mancy, first attested in 1646. From Latin rhabdomantīa, from Ancient Greek ῥαβδομαντεία (rhabdomanteía), from ῥάβδος (rhábdos, “rod”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”).

parole.significato: A simple, straight spicule.
parole.testo: From a New Latin form of Ancient Greek ῥάβδος (rhábdos, “rod”).

parole.significato: A strict and just judge.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek Ῥαδάμανθυς (Rhadámanthus).

parole.significato: The false rhubarb (Rheum rhaponticum)
parole.testo: From Latin rhaponticum, literally rha (“rhubarb”) ponticum (“Pontic; of the Black Sea”), from Ancient Greek ῥῆον (rhêon, “rhubarb”) and Ancient Greek Πόντος (Póntos, “Black Sea”).

parole.significato: Part of or similar to rhetoric, the use of language as a means to persuade.
parole.testo: From Middle English rethorycal, rethoricalle, rethorycall, from rethorik, rhetoric (noun) or Latin rēthoricus, rhētoricus, from Ancient Greek ῥητορικός (rhētorikós, “concerning public speaking”). By surface analysis, rhetoric + -al.

parole.significato: A type of discourse that has a characteristic configuration of topics, themes, and arguments.
parole.testo: From Latin rhētorica from Ancient Greek ῥήτωρ (rhḗtōr, “public speaker”) + from Latin lectus, form of Latin legō (“to read”).

parole.significato: Any disorder of the muscles, tendons, joints, bones, nerves, characterized by pain, discomfort and disability.
parole.testo: First attested 1601, from Latin rheumatismus (“rheum”), from Ancient Greek ῥευματισμός (rheumatismós, “humour, discharge, rheum”) from ῥευματίζομαι (rheumatízomai, “to suffer from a rheum”) from ῥεῦμα (rheûma, “stream, flow”) from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”)

parole.significato: Any large herbivorous ungulate mammal native to Africa and Asia of the family Rhinocerotidae, with thick, gray skin and…
parole.testo: From Latin rhīnocerōs, from Ancient Greek ῥῑνόκερως (rhīnókerōs, “nose-horned”), composed of ῥῑ́ς, ῥῑνός (rhī́s, rhīnós, “nose, of (the) nose”) + κέρας (kéras, “horn”).

parole.significato: Compulsive nose-picking; the insertion of a finger into one's nose.
parole.testo: From rhino- (“nose, nasal”) + Latin tillexis (“habit of plucking”, see below) + -o- + -mania (“obsession”). The tillexis stem is seemingly a New Latin borrowing from Ancient Greek τίλλω (tíllō, “to pluck or pull”). There is a divergence regarding the exo affix. It is suggested it may derive from ἔξω

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Rhipsalis, epiphytic flowering plants in the cactus family, often known as mistletoe cacti.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek ῥίψ (rhíps, “wickerwork”) + Latin -alis (“-al”).

parole.significato: Oleander (Nerium oleander).
parole.testo: The obsolete sense derives from Latin rhododendron (“oleander”), from Ancient Greek ῥοδόδενδρον (rhodódendron, “oleander”), from ῥόδον (rhódon, “rose”) + δένδρον (déndron, “tree”). The modern sense comes through the intermediary of the genus name Rhododendron, not closely related taxonomically, but

parole.significato: A parallelogram having all sides of equal length.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rhombus, from Ancient Greek ῥόμβος (rhómbos, “rhombus, spinning top”). Doublet of rhomb and rhumb.

parole.significato: A dry rattling sound heard during breathing, due to deposits in the bronchial tubes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rhonchus (“snoring”), from Ancient Greek ῥόγχος (rhónkhos) (Caelius Aurelianus), of imitative origin.

parole.significato: Having each successive word longer by a letter or syllable.
parole.testo: From Latin rhopalicus, from Ancient Greek ῥόπαλον (rhópalon, “club, bat”).

parole.significato: One of the small sensory tentacular structures of various jellyfish species.
parole.testo: From New Latin rhopalium, from Ancient Greek ῥοπαλιον (rhopalion), diminutive of ῥόπαλον (rhópalon, “club”).

parole.significato: Having a series of fleshy lobes or filaments.
parole.testo: From New Latin rhopalium, from Ancient Greek ῥοπαλιον (rhopalion), diminutive of ῥόπαλον (rhópalon, “club”) + -cercous.

parole.significato: An exaggerated use of the sound of the letter R.
parole.testo: From New Latin rhōtacismus, from Ancient Greek *ῥωτακισμός (*rhōtakismós), from ῥωτακίζω (rhōtakízō, “to incorrectly use rho”), from ῥῶ (rhô, “rho (the Greek equivalent of r)”) in analogy with ἰωτακίζω (iōtakízō, “to incorrectly use iota”); itself from ἰῶτα (iôta) in analogy with ἀττικίζω (attikízō,

parole.significato: The variation of strong and weak elements (such as duration, accent) of sounds, notably in speech or music, over time;…
parole.testo: First coined in 1557, from Latin rhythmus, from Ancient Greek ῥυθμός (rhuthmós, “any measured flow or movement, symmetry, rhythm”), from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow, run, stream, gush”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Eastern Roman Empire, that is, to the Byzantine Empire.
parole.testo: From post-Classical Latin Rōmaeus [calque of Ancient Greek Ῥωμαῖος (Rhōmaîos)] + -an. By surface analysis, Rome + -ean.

parole.significato: Aspiration on a vowel or semivowel in Ancient Greek.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin spīritus asper, from Ancient Greek δασὺ πνεῦμα (dasù pneûma).

parole.significato: One of the red dye products extracted from madder root, probably identical with ruberythrinic acid.
parole.testo: From Latin rubeus (“red”) + Ancient Greek ῥητίνη (rhētínē, “resin”).

parole.significato: An epithet of God in His role as protector of the Israelite army, usually translated (alongside YHWH or Elohim) as "Lor…
parole.testo: From Latin Sabaoth, from Ancient Greek Σαβαώθ (Sabaṓth), from Biblical Hebrew צְבָאוֹת (ts'vaót), plural of צָבָא (tsaváʾ, “army”).

parole.significato: A person who regards and keeps the seventh day of the week ("Saturday", the Israelite or Jewish Sabbath) as holy in con…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin sabbatarius, from Latin sabbatum, from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton), from Hebrew שבת (shabát) + -an. In use from c. 1610.

parole.significato: Strict observance of the Sabbath.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sabbatismus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Of or relating to sugar; sugary.
parole.testo: From New Latin saccharum (“sugar”) + English -ine (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Saccharum is derived from saccharon (“syrupy liquid from bamboo or reeds”), from Ancient Greek σάκχαρον (sákkharon), from Pali sakkharā (“sugar; gravel; granule, grain; crystal; potsherd”), f

parole.significato: sugar
parole.testo: From Latin saccharum, ultimately from the same source as sugar.

parole.significato: Someone with a Sagittarius star sign.
parole.testo: From Latin sagittārius (“archer”), calque of Ancient Greek τοξότης (toxótēs); possibly adapted from Akkadian 𒀯𒉺𒉋𒊕 (pabilsaĝ, “the bow-armed god Pabilsaĝ”) (see Pabilsaĝ), from Sumerian 𒀯𒉺𒉋𒊕 (ᴹᵁᴸPA.BIL₂.SAG).

parole.significato: A rare mineral composed of ammonium chloride found around volcanic fumaroles and guano deposits.
parole.testo: From Middle English sal armenak, sal armoniac, salarmoniac, sal armoniacum, sal armoniak, sal armonyak, salarmonyak, salle armonyacke, salt armoniake, salt armonyac, from Latin sal ammōniacus, sal armōniacus (“salt of Amun, ammonium chloride”), named so because it was found near the temple of (Jupit

parole.significato: A trumpet-shaped tube.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin salpinx.

parole.significato: A native, or inhabitant of Samaria; especially one practising certain ethnoreligious traditions indigenous to that regi…
parole.testo: From Latin Samarītānus, from Ancient Greek Σαμαρείτης (Samareítēs), from Σαμαρεία (Samareía, “Samaria”), derived from Biblical Hebrew שֹׁמְרוֹנִים (Šōmərôním) and שֹׁמְרוֹן (Šōmərôn) respectively. Attested in Old English.

parole.significato: An ancient form of triangular harp having a very sharp, shrill tone.
parole.testo: From Latin sambūca, from Ancient Greek σαμβύκη (sambúkē), ultimately from Aramaic סַבְּכָא (sabbəḵā).

parole.significato: Realgar; red sulphide of arsenic.
parole.testo: From Latin sandaraca, from Ancient Greek σανδαράκη (sandarákē, “realgar”).

parole.significato: A kind of minium, or red lead, made by calcining lead carbonate, but inferior to true minium.
parole.testo: From Latin sandix, sandyx (“vermilion, or a colour like vermilion”), from Ancient Greek σάνδυξ (sándux).

parole.significato: A member of a nomadic people from the Sinai near the Roman province of Arabia in the early centuries AD, who were speci…
parole.testo: From Late Latin Saracenus, from Ancient Greek Σαρακηνός (Sarakēnós) - *Saraka[?] + -ινος. The source of the Greek has long been debated. * In the 17th-19th centuries, the most widely accepted theory derived it from Arabic شَرْقِيِّين (šarqiyyin, “easterners”), as the Sarakenoi lived to the east of m

parole.significato: Either of two species of osteoglossid fish of the genus Scleropages, native to northeastern Australia.
parole.testo: Origin unknown. Perhaps a mispronunciation of New Latin Ceratodus (“an extinct genus of lungfish”), which is from Ancient Greek κέρας (kéras, “horn”) + ὀδούς (odoús, “tooth”).

parole.significato: Use of acerbic language to mock or convey contempt, often using verbal irony and (in speech) often marked by overemphas…
parole.testo: From Late Latin sarcasmus, from Ancient Greek σαρκασμός (sarkasmós, “a sneer”), from σαρκάζω (sarkázō, “to gnash the teeth (in anger)”, literally “to strip off the flesh”), from σάρξ (sárx, “flesh”).

parole.significato: A shrub of species Astragalus sarcocolla, native to Iran.
parole.testo: From Latin sarcocolla, from Ancient Greek σαρκοκόλλα (sarkokólla), from σάρξ (sárx, “flesh”) + κόλλα (kólla, “glue, adhesive”).

parole.significato: A stonen coffin, often with its exterior inscribed, or decorated with sculpture.
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Latin sarcophagus (“grave; sarcophagus; flesh-eating, carnivorous”), from Ancient Greek σᾰρκοφᾰ́γος (sărkophắgos, “sarcophagus; flesh-eating, carnivorous”) (so named from λῐ́θος σᾰρκοφᾰ́γος (lĭ́thos sărkophắgos, literally “flesh-eating stone”) a type of limestone found at A

parole.significato: Sardonic.
parole.testo: From Latin sardonius, from Ancient Greek Σαρδόνιος (Sardónios, “Sardinian”), earlier σαρδάνιος (sardánios).

parole.significato: A gemstone having bands of red sard; a variety of onyx or chalcedony.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English sardonix, sardonyx (c. 1382), from Latin sardonyx, from Ancient Greek σᾰρδόνῠξ (sărdónŭx). Doublet of sardoin.

parole.significato: A demon follower of Satan (principal evil spirit); a fallen angel.
parole.testo: From Middle English Sathan, Satan, from Old English Satan, from Latin Satan, from Ancient Greek Σατάν (Satán), from Hebrew שָׂטָן (satán, “adversary, accuser”). Compare Arabic شَيْطَان (šayṭān, “satan, devil”). Doublet of shaitan and shetani.

parole.significato: A governor of a Persian province.
parole.testo: From Middle English satrape, from Latin satrapēs (“governor”), from Ancient Greek σατράπης (satrápēs), from Old Median *xšaθrapāvan (literally “kingdom-protector”), which is cognate with Old Persian 𐎧𐏁𐏂𐎱𐎠𐎺𐎠 (xšaçapāvā); see there for more.

parole.significato: Excessive sexual desire, found in a man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin satyriasis, from Ancient Greek σατυρίασις (saturíasis).

parole.significato: Any of various kinds of orchids.
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek σατύριον (satúrion, “a kind of orchid”) from Σάτυρος (Sáturos, “a Satyr”).

parole.significato: Having sides all unequal in length.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin scalēnus (“of unequal sides”), from Ancient Greek σκᾰληνός (skălēnós, “uneven, unequal”).

parole.significato: To cause great offense to (someone); to shock with something scandalous.
parole.testo: From Latin scandalizō, from Ancient Greek σκανδαλίζω (skandalízō). By surface analysis, scandal + -ize.

parole.significato: The carina or keel of papilionaceous flowers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scaphium, from Ancient Greek σκάφιον (skáphion).

parole.significato: Shaped like a boat.
parole.testo: From Latin scaphoides, from Ancient Greek σκᾰφοειδής (skăphoeidḗs, “like a bowl, hollow”), from σκᾰ́φη (skắphē, “boat, trough, bowl”).

parole.significato: A marine food fish, the scarus or parrotfish (family Scaridae).
parole.testo: From Latin scarus (“a kind of fish”), from Ancient Greek σκάρος (skáros, “parrot wrasse, Sparisoma cretense, syn. Scarus cretensis”).

parole.significato: A shiteater: a human or animal that consumes excrement.
parole.testo: From New Latin scatophagus, from Ancient Greek σκατοφάγος (skatophágos), from σκατο- (skato-, “shit”) and φάγος (phágos, “eater; glutton”), from φᾰγεῖν (phăgeîn, “to eat”) + -ος (-os, “-er”, forming agent nouns). Equivalent to scato- + -phage. In particular reference to dungflies, an anglicization o

parole.significato: Synonym of coprophagous: typified by consuming shit or other excrement.
parole.testo: From New Latin scatophagus, from Ancient Greek σκατοφάγος (skatophágos), from σκατο- (skato-, “shit”) and φάγος (phágos, “eating”), from φᾰγεῖν (phăgeîn, “to eat”) + -ος (-os, “-ous”, forming adjectives). Equivalent to scato- + -phagous.

parole.significato: A limping satiric meter in classical verse.
parole.testo: From Latin scāzon, from Ancient Greek σκάζων (skázōn), from σκάζω (skázō, “to limp”).

parole.significato: An outline or image universally applicable to a general conception, under which it is likely to be presented to the min…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin schēma, from Ancient Greek σχῆμα (skhêma, “form, shape”). Doublet of scheme.

parole.significato: An artful deviation from the ordinary arrangement of words.
parole.testo: From late Middle English scheame, from Medieval Latin schēma (“figure, form”), from Ancient Greek σχῆμα (skhêma, “form, shape”), from ἔχω (ékhō, “to hold”). Doublet of schema. Compare sketch.

parole.significato: An Egyptian or Persian measure of length, varying from thirty-two to sixty stadia.
parole.testo: From Latin schoenus, from Ancient Greek σχοῖνος (skhoînos, “a rush, a reed, a land measure”).

parole.significato: A very small interval equal to half a comma.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin schisma, from Ancient Greek σχίσμα (skhísma, “cleft, division”), whence the orthographic borrowing skhisma. Doublet of schism.

parole.significato: A scholium.
parole.testo: From New Latin scholion, from Ancient Greek σχόλῐον (skhólĭon, “interpretation, comment”).

parole.significato: A note added to a text as an explanation, criticism or commentary.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek σχόλιον (skhólion, “comment”), from σχολή (skholḗ, “discussion”).

parole.significato: Any of several nocturnal fish, of the genus Sciaena, from the Eastern Atlantic, Mediterranean Sea and Black Sea; a croa…
parole.testo: From Latin sciaena, from Ancient Greek σκίαινα (skíaina, “a sea-fish”, perhaps “a kind of grayling” or “ombre”), from σκιά (skiá, “shadow, shade”) and -ινα (-ina, suffix forming related feminine nouns).

parole.significato: shadow-boxing; fighting that is futile or make-believe
parole.testo: From Late Latin sciamachia, and its source, Hellenistic Ancient Greek σκιαμαχία (skiamakhía), from σκιά (skiá, “shadow”) + μάχη (mákhē, “battle”).

parole.significato: Neuralgia of the sciatic nerve, characterised by pain radiating down through the buttocks and the back of the thigh.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Late Latin sciatica, feminine of sciaticus, from Ancient Greek ἰσχιαδικός (iskhiadikós), the adjective of ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip”).

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Scilla; a squill.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scilla, from Ancient Greek σκίλλα (skílla). Doublet of squill.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the family Scincidae, or skinks.
parole.testo: Latin scincus a kind of lizard, from Ancient Greek σκίγγος (skíngos), σκίγκος (skínkos), + -oid. Compare skink.

parole.significato: A kind of stinging or biting insect; a flea, gnat, sandfly, or the like.
parole.testo: From Latin scinifes, cinifes or ciniphes, plural, from Ancient Greek σκνίψ (skníps, “gnat, small fly(, flea?)”), plural σκνῖφες (sknîphes) or σκνῖπες (sknîpes).

parole.significato: divination using shadows
parole.testo: From Late Latin sciomantia, from Ancient Greek σκιά (skiá, “shadow”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to or characteristic of squirrels.
parole.testo: From Latin sciūrus (“squirrel”), from Ancient Greek σκίουρος (skíouros, “squirrel”), from σκιά (skiá, “shadow”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”), + -ine.

parole.significato: The white of the eye; the tough outer coat of the eye that covers the eyeball except for the cornea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin sclera, from Ancient Greek σκληρός (sklērós, “hard”).

parole.significato: A chronic systemic autoimmune disease characterized by hardening the skin or other organs through excessive deposits of…
parole.testo: From New Latin sclēroderma, from Ancient Greek σκληρός (sklērós, “hard”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin, hide”). By surface analysis, sclero- + -derma.

parole.significato: A compact mass of hardened mycelium stored with reserve food material that, in some higher fungi such as ergot, becomes…
parole.testo: From New Latin sclerotium, from Ancient Greek σκληρός (sklērós, “hard”).

parole.significato: The abnormal lateral curvature of the spine.
parole.testo: From Latin scoliosis, from Ancient Greek σκολίωσις (skolíōsis, “twisting; torsion”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Scolopacidae, or sandpipers.
parole.testo: From Latin scolopax (“a snipe”), from Ancient Greek σκολόπαξ (skolópax).

parole.significato: A mythical sea-creature, reputed to be able to disgorge its bowels to dislodge any fishing-hook.
parole.testo: From Latin scolopendra, from Ancient Greek σκολόπενδρα (skolópendra).

parole.significato: An idiot: a buffoon.
parole.testo: Latin scomma (“a taunt, jeer, scoff”), from Ancient Greek σκῶμμα (skômma, “jest, gibe”).

parole.significato: A small European migratory owl, Otus scops, that winters in sub-Saharran Africa.
parole.testo: From Latin scops, from Ancient Greek σκώψ (skṓps, “a type of small owl”), from σκοπός (skopós, “watcher”), from σκέπτομαι (sképtomai, “to look at”).

parole.significato: Full of rocks; rocky.
parole.testo: From Latin scopulosus, from scopulus (“a rock”), from Ancient Greek σκόπελος (skópelos).

parole.significato: The slag or dross that remains after the smelting of metal from an ore.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English, from Latin scōria, from Ancient Greek σκωρία (skōría), from σκῶρ (skôr, “dung”).

parole.significato: Someone with a Scorpio star sign
parole.testo: From Latin scorpiō (“scorpion”), from Ancient Greek σκορπίος (skorpíos), calque of Akkadian 𒀯𒄈𒋰 (zuqaqīpu, “scorpion; constellation name”), calque of Sumerian 𒀯𒄈𒋰 (ᴹᵁᴸGIR₂.TAB). Doublet of scorpion.

parole.significato: Any of the order Scorpiones of arachnids related to spiders, characterised by two large front pincers and a curved tail…
parole.testo: From Middle English scorpioun, skorpioun, schorpion, schorpiun, partly from Old English sċorpio and partly from Anglo-Norman scorpïun, Old French scorpïon, escorpïon; all from Latin scorpiō, ultimately from Ancient Greek σκορπίος (skorpíos). The cheerleading move is so called because of the resembla

parole.significato: A concave molding with a lower edge projecting beyond the top.
parole.testo: From Latin scotia, from Ancient Greek σκοτία (skotía, “dark, shadowy”).

parole.significato: An area of impaired or lost vision within a visual field otherwise in a good (or at least healthy) state.
parole.testo: From Late Latin scotoma, from Ancient Greek σκότωμα (skótōma), from σκότος (skótos, “darkness”). By surface analysis, scot- + -oma. The figurative sense is an extension from the literal sense, as if the mind, like an eye, cannot "see" certain things.

parole.significato: A small fish of the family Cottidae, usually lacking scales. Often found on river bottoms and in tidal pools.
parole.testo: From earlier scorpene, from Latin scorpaena, from Ancient Greek σκόρπαινα (skórpaina, “kind of fish”), diminutive of σκορπίος (skorpíos). Compare scorpionfish.

parole.significato: A kind of large drinking cup used in Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome, especially by poor people.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scyphus (“cup”), from Ancient Greek σκῠ́φος (skŭ́phos).

parole.significato: A cylinder with a strip of parchment wound around it on which a message is written, used for cryptography by the ancien…
parole.testo: From Latin scytale (“cylinder used for encoding and decoding”), from Ancient Greek σκυτάλη (skutálē, “club, baton, cylinder used for encoding and decoding”).

parole.significato: Any member of the family Scytalinidae of very slender burrowing fish called graveldivers.
parole.testo: From Latin Scytalinidae, from Ancient Greek σκυτάλη (skutálē, “club”) + -ινος (-inos, “-ine”) + -ίδης (-ídēs, “-id”). Equivalent to scytale + -ine + -id.

parole.significato: A tetralone derivative involved in certain redox reactions.
parole.testo: From scytale + -one, from Latin scytale, from Ancient Greek σκυτάλη (skutálē, “club”).

parole.significato: A Scythian.
parole.testo: From Latin Scytha, from Ancient Greek Σκύθης (Skúthēs). Doublet of Saca, Saka, and Shaka.

parole.significato: Pertaining to (what is now classified as) the superorder Selachimorpha or division Selachii, comprising the sharks; or,…
parole.testo: From the (disused) genus name Selache, from Latin selachē, from the plural of Ancient Greek σέλαχος (sélakhos, “shark”).

parole.significato: Relating to the Greek-Macedonian dynasty which ruled (312–63 BCE) an empire created by Seleucus out of the eastern conq…
parole.testo: From Latin Seleucides, from Ancient Greek Σελευκίδης (Seleukídēs), named after Seleucus I Nicator. Equivalent to Seleucus + -id.

parole.significato: Semiotics, the study of signs.
parole.testo: From New Latin semaeologia, from Ancient Greek σημεῖον (sēmeîon, “sign”) + -logia (“-logy”). By surface analysis, semio- + -logy.

parole.significato: A member of a modern people that speak a Semitic language.
parole.testo: From Sem, Shem + -ite, from Late Latin Sēm, from Ancient Greek Σήμ (Sḗm), from Biblical Hebrew שם (šēm). Compare German Semit, New Latin Sēmīta, French sémite.

parole.significato: A Gaulish tribe in the Roman period.
parole.testo: Via Latin from Ancient Greek Σήνωνες (Sḗnōnes), originally the capital of the Gaulish people of the same name.

parole.significato: A dark brown pigment made from the secretions of the cuttlefish.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sēpia (“cuttlefish”), from Ancient Greek σηπία (sēpía). Cognate with Italian seppia, Portuguese siba, and Spanish sepia.

parole.significato: Synonym of septicemia.
parole.testo: From New Latin septaemia, from Ancient Greek σηπτός (sēptós), verbal adjective of σήπω (sḗpō, “make rotten”), + αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) + -ia.

parole.significato: A temple or other religious institution dedicated to the syncretic Greco-Egyptian deity Serapis.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek Σεραπεῖον (Serapeîon).

parole.significato: Synonym of Chinese or Northern Chinese, chiefly in the context of ancient Greco-Roman knowledge of China and its role a…
parole.testo: From Seres + -ian, from Latin Seres (“the ancient northern Chinese”), from Ancient Greek, possibly from the Old Chinese word for silk.

parole.significato: Synonym of Chinese or Northern Chinese, in the context of ancient Greco-Roman knowledge of China.
parole.testo: From Latin Sēricus, from Ancient Greek Σηρικός (Sērikós), from Σῆρες (Sêres, “Seres”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”), from σήρ (sḗr, “silkworm”), possibly from Old Chinese 絲 (*sə, “silk”). Equivalent to Seres + -ic. Doublet of Serican.

parole.significato: Synonym of silken, made of silk.
parole.testo: From Latin sēricus, from Ancient Greek σηρῐκός (sērĭkós), from σήρ (sḗr, “silkworm”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”), possibly ultimately from the Old Chinese word for silk. Doublet of silk and serge.

parole.significato: Synonym of Chinese or Northern Chinese, chiefly in the context of ancient Greco-Roman knowledge of China.
parole.testo: From Latin Sēricānus, from Sērica (“Serica, China, ancient northern China”) + -ānus (“-an”), from Ancient Greek Σηρικά (Sēriká), from σήρ (sḗr, “silkworm”), and possibly ultimately from Old Chinese 絲 (*sə, “silk”). Equivalent to Serica + -an. Doublet of Seric.

parole.significato: Of or relating to silk; consisting of, or resembling silk; silky.
parole.testo: From Latin sēricus (“silken”), sēricum (“Seric material; silk”), from Sēricus (“belonging to the Seres”): Sērēs, Ancient Greek Σῆρες (Sêres, “a people of Eastern Asia, the modern Chinese, celebrated for their silken fabrics”). Compare silk, serge.

parole.significato: A silk gland, as in the silkworms.
parole.testo: Late Latin sericterium, from Ancient Greek σηρικόν (sērikón, “silk”).

parole.significato: A nonessential amino acid, CH₂OH.CH(NH₂)COOH, found in most animal proteins, notably silk.
parole.testo: From Latin sericus (“silken”). The compound was first obtained from silk protein, a particularly rich source, in 1865. See also serge.

parole.significato: A tropical Asian plant (Sesamum indicum) bearing small flat seeds used as food and as a source of oil.
parole.testo: From late Middle English sisamie, from Latin sīsamum, sēsamum, from Ancient Greek σήσαμον (sḗsamon), from Aramaic שושמא (šūššmā), shortening of שומשומא (šumššumā), from Akkadian 𒊭𒈦𒌑𒈬 (šamaššammū, “oil plant”), compound of 𒉌𒄑 (šaman, “oil”) and 𒌑 (šammum, “plant”). The modern pronunciation is perhaps

parole.significato: Herpes zoster, caused by Human herpes virus 3, in genus Varicellovirus.
parole.testo: From Latin cingulus, variant of cingulum (“girdle”), translating Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē), ζωστήρ (zōstḗr).

parole.significato: A pagan female oracle or prophetess, especially the Cumaean sibyl.
parole.testo: From Latin Sibylla, from Ancient Greek Σίβυλλα (Síbulla).

parole.significato: A member of an Italic tribe who inhabited eastern Sicily during the Iron Age.
parole.testo: From Latin Siculi, from Ancient Greek Σικελός (Sikelós). See also Sicily. Greek historians including Thucydides suggested Siculus, a legendary king and son of Italus, as the progenitor of the Sicels.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Silenus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Sīlēnicus, from Ancient Greek Σῑληνῐκός (Sīlēnĭkós). By surface analysis, Silenus + -ic.

parole.significato: A fine fiber excreted by the silkworm or other arthropod (such as a spider).
parole.testo: From Middle English silk, sylk, selk, selc, from Old English sioloc, seoloc, seolc (“silk”). The immediate source is uncertain; it probably reached English via the Baltic trade routes (cognates in Old Norse silki (> Danish silke, Swedish silke (“silk”)), Russian шёлк (šolk), obsolete Lithuanian zilk

parole.significato: A plant, thought to be extinct, used in Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome in cooking and as a contraceptive.
parole.testo: From Latin silphium, from Ancient Greek σίλφιον (sílphion).

parole.significato: A fish of the genus Silurus, such as the sheatfish.
parole.testo: From Latin silurus (“a sort of river fish”), from Ancient Greek σίλουρος (sílouros, “a very large sort of river fish”).

parole.significato: The scientific study of forests.
parole.testo: From silva + -o- + -logy. From Latin silva (“forest”) + Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía, “study of”). Coined by Roeloff Oldeman in 1990 in his book Forests: elements of silvology.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to apes and monkeys.
parole.testo: From Latin sīmia (“ape, monkey”), from Ancient Greek σιμός (simós, “snub-nosed”).

parole.significato: snub or snub-nosed
parole.testo: From Latin simus, from Ancient Greek σιμός (simós, “flat-nosed, snub-nosed”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Chinese.
parole.testo: From Sinae + -an, from Latin Sinae, from Ancient Greek Σῖναι (Sînai), q.v.

parole.significato: An alkaloidal amine found in seeds of black mustard (Brassica nigra, syns. Rhamphospermum nigrum, Sinapis erysimoides,…
parole.testo: Latin sinapi, sinapis (“mustard”), Ancient Greek: compare French sinapine.

parole.significato: An essential or indispensable element, condition, or ingredient.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin [condiciō] sine quā nōn (“[condition] without which not”), an expression which originated in the works of Boethius as a translation of some Aristotelian expression (perhaps Ancient Greek οὗ οὐκ ἄνευ (hoû ouk áneu); compare also Modern Greek εκ των ων ουκ άνευ (ek ton on ouk ánef)

parole.significato: Synonym of Sinitic, of or related to the family of Chinese languages.
parole.testo: From Latin Sinensis (“Chinese”) + -ian, from Sinae (“Southern Chinese; Southern China”) + -ensis (“-ese”), from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Chinese.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Sinicus, from Sina (“China”) + -icus (“-ic”), from Late Latin Sinae (“the Southern Chinese; Southern China”), from Ancient Greek Σῖναι (Sînai), q.v. Equivalent to Sino- + -ic.

parole.significato: An inhabitant of the city of Šianu (identified with modern Siano on the coast of Syria).
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin Sineum, from Ancient Greek Ασενναῖον (Asennaîon), from Biblical Hebrew סִינִי (sînî).

parole.significato: Related to pronunciations for reading Chinese in Japan, Korea and Vietnam, originating in medieval times and the source…
parole.testo: From Sino- + xeno- + -ic, from Late Latin Sīnae (“the Chinese”) + Ancient Greek ξένος (xénos, “foreign”); coined by American linguist Samuel Martin in 1953.

parole.significato: A tube that connects adjacent chambers in the shells of some cephalopods.
parole.testo: From Latin sīphunculus (“little tube”), from sīphō (“tube, pipe”) + -culus (diminutive suffix), from Ancient Greek σίφων (síphōn), of uncertain and possibly non-Indo-European Mediterranean substrate origin.

parole.significato: sunstroke
parole.testo: From Latin sīriāsis, from Ancient Greek σειρίᾱσις (seiríāsis, “heatstroke”)

parole.significato: An ancient Egyptian musical instrument, to be shaken, consisting of a metal frame holding percussive metal beads.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sīstrum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σεῖστρον (seîstron), from σείω (seíō, “shake”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the family Sittidae, or nuthatches.
parole.testo: From New Latin sitta (“the nuthatch”), from Ancient Greek σίττη (síttē, “nuthatch”) + -ine.

parole.significato: A skeleton.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin sceletus, from Ancient Greek σκελετός (skeletós).

parole.significato: To reduce to a skeleton; to skin; to skeletonize.
parole.testo: From New Latin sceleton, from Ancient Greek σκελετόν (skeletón), the neuter of σκελετός (skeletós, “dried up, withered, dried body, parched, mummy”), from σκέλλω (skéllō, “dry, dry up, make dry, parch”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelh₁- (“to parch, wither”); compare Ancient Greek σκληρός (sklērós

parole.significato: An emerald.
parole.testo: From Latin smaragdus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos), μάραγδος (máragdos), from a Semitic language.

parole.significato: Emerald.
parole.testo: From Latin smaragdinus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδινος (smáragdinos), from σμάραγδος (smáragdos). See emerald for more.

parole.significato: Cleansing.
parole.testo: From Latin smecticus, from Ancient Greek σμηκτικός (smēktikós), from σμήχειν (smḗkhein, “to wipe, to cleanse”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”).

parole.significato: A whitish sebaceous secretion that collects between the glans penis and foreskin or in the vulva.
parole.testo: From Latin, borrowed from Ancient Greek σμῆγμα (smêgma), alternative form of σμῆμα (smêma, “soap, detergent”), from σμάω (smáō, “to wipe, clean”).

parole.significato: The lack of aspiration on a vowel or semivowel in Ancient Greek.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin spīritus lēnis, from Ancient Greek ψιλὸν πνεῦμα (psilòn pneûma).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of the philosopher Socrates or his philosophy or methods.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Sōcratic(us). By surface analysis, Socrat(es) + -ic.

parole.significato: A person of unusual wisdom.
parole.testo: From Latin Solomōn (variant of Salomon), from Ancient Greek Σολομών (Solomṓn), from Biblical Hebrew שְׁלֹמֹה (šĕlōmōʰ), from שָׁלוֹם (šālōm, “peace”). Doublet of Shlomo and Suleiman.

parole.significato: The whole axial portion of an animal, including the head, neck, trunk, and tail.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek σῶμα (sôma, “body”).

parole.significato: Wise men; sages.
parole.testo: From the Latin sophī, the nominative plural form of sophus, from the Ancient Greek σοφός (sophós).

parole.significato: Synonym of sophistical, of or related to the ancient Sophists, characterized by fallacious reasoning.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin sophisticus, borrowing of Ancient Greek σοφιστικός (sophistikós). Equivalent to sophist + -ic and sophism + -istic.

parole.significato: To make (something) less innocent or natural; to artificialize.
parole.testo: From Middle English sophisticaten (“to mix (something) with a foreign or inferior substance, adulterate”), from Medieval Latin sophisticātus, the perfect passive participle of sophisticāre (“to disguise; to tamper with; to trick using words”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more). Sophisticāre i

parole.significato: wisdom, knowledge, learning
parole.testo: From the Middle English sophie, from the Latin sophia, from the Ancient Greek σοφῐ́ᾱ (sophĭ́ā, “high knowledge”: “learning”, “wisdom”); compare Sophia.

parole.significato: The awkward or humorous use of different languages mixed together, often using a foreign term incorrectly or in an inap…
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A series of propositions whereby each conclusion is taken as the subject of the next.
parole.testo: From the Latin sōrītēs, from the Ancient Greek σωρῑ́της (sōrī́tēs, “fallacy of the heap”), from σωρός (sōrós, “heap”).

parole.significato: Any reproductive structure, in some lichens and fungi, that produces spores.
parole.testo: From New Latin sōrus, from Ancient Greek σωρός (sōrós, “heap”).

parole.significato: iron(II) sulfate, or some earth impregnated with it
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sory, from Ancient Greek σῶρυ (sôru, “a kind of ore”).

parole.significato: A fleshy spike (inflorescence) with reduced flowers, usually enclosed by a spathe, characteristic of aroids.
parole.testo: Via Latin spādīx from Ancient Greek σπᾱ́δῑξ (spā́dīx, “palm branch”).

parole.significato: Someone who has been castrated; a eunuch or castrato.
parole.testo: From Latin spadō, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Pertaining to alchemy; alchemical, especially regarding medicine.
parole.testo: From Late Latin spagyricus, from Ancient Greek σπάω (spáō, “I draw, pull”) + ἀγείρω (ageírō, “I assemble”).

parole.significato: A Spartan, especially a full citizen.
parole.testo: From Middle English Sparciate, from Latin Spartiātēs, from Ancient Greek Σπᾰρτῐᾱ́της (Spărtĭā́tēs), from Σπᾰ́ρτη (Spắrtē) + -ᾱ́της (-ā́tēs).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a spasm; resembling a sudden contraction of the muscles.
parole.testo: From New Latin spasmōdicus, from Ancient Greek σπασμώδης (spasmṓdēs, “spasmodic”), from σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or affected by spasm.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin spasticus, from Ancient Greek σπαστικός (spastikós, “drawing in”). By surface analysis, spasm + -tic. Cf. French spastique and see also spasm.

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Spathiphyllum of peace lilies.
parole.testo: From New Latin, shortening of the genus name Spathiphyllum, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “blade”) + φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”).

parole.significato: A type of straight sword originating from the first-century Roman Empire. It was worn typically by cavalry officers and…
parole.testo: From Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “any broad blade, of wood or metal”). Doublet of spade, spathe, and epee.

parole.significato: A large bract that envelops or subtends a whole inflorescence, typically a spadix.
parole.testo: From Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “blade”). Doublet of epee, spatha, and spade.

parole.significato: A kitchen utensil consisting of a flat surface attached to a long handle, used for turning, lifting, or stirring food.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin spatula (“a flat piece”), the diminutive form of spatha (“broad or flat tool”), from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “a broad wood or metal blade”). Doublet of spauld; compare spatha and spathe.

parole.significato: The reproductive cell or gamete of the male; a spermatozoon.
parole.testo: From Middle English sperme, from Latin sperma, from Ancient Greek σπέρμα (spérma, “seed, semen”). Compare also Old French esperme, sparme.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling sperm.
parole.testo: From Middle English spermatik, from Latin spermaticus, from Ancient Greek σπερματικός (spermatikós). By surface analysis, spermat- + -ic.

parole.significato: A spherical aggregation of raphides in a plant cell
parole.testo: Derived from Latin sphaera + Ancient Greek ῥαφίς (rhaphís).

parole.significato: Having a wedge shape.
parole.testo: From New Latin sphenoides, from Ancient Greek σφηνοειδής (sphēnoeidḗs, “wedge-shaped”), from σφήν (sphḗn, “wedge”) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-form, -like”).

parole.significato: Shaped as a sphere; being a sphere.
parole.testo: English spheric [from Latin sphaericus, from Ancient Greek σφαιρικός (sphairikós)] + -al.

parole.significato: A ringlike band of muscle that surrounds a bodily opening (such as the anus or the openings of the stomach), constricti…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin sphinctēr (“the muscle of the anus”), from Ancient Greek σφῐγκτήρ (sphĭnktḗr, “lace, band; contractile muscle”), ultimately of Pre-Greek origin. Possibly related to sphinx (“the strangler”).

parole.significato: An aluminous earth of a grayish yellow color; a medicinal clay.
parole.testo: From Latin sphragis, sphragidis (“Lemnian earth”), from Ancient Greek σφραγίς (sphragís, “a seal”), so called because sold in sealed packets.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the circulatory pulse.
parole.testo: From Latin sphygmicus, from Ancient Greek σφυγμικός (sphugmikós), from σφυγμός (sphugmós, “pulse”), whence sphygm-.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to sex or fornication (especially homosexual) between three or more people.
parole.testo: From Latin spintria (“male prostitute”), from Ancient Greek σφιγκτήρ (sphinktḗr, “something which binds”), referring to the anal sphincter.

parole.significato: Any of the many flowering shrubs of the genus Spiraea, that have clusters of white or pink flowers.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek σπεῖρα (speîra, “coil”).

parole.significato: Synonym of rough breathing.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin spīritus asper, from Ancient Greek δασὺ πνεῦμα (dasù pneûma).

parole.significato: Synonym of smooth breathing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin spīritus lēnis, from Ancient Greek ψιλὸν πνεῦμα (psilòn pneûma).

parole.significato: Resembling or having the form of a spiral or helix.
parole.testo: From Latin spiroïdes, from Ancient Greek Ancient Greek σπειροειδής (speiroeidḗs). By surface analysis, spire + -oid.

parole.significato: Of, in, near or pertaining to the viscera or intestines.
